comment: 34 pages, 5 figures. Pre-registered predictions, code and data checksums are described in Appendix C
summary: LLM-guided search loops propose a modified candidate, score it, and keep it if it scores better. When both candidates are re-scored at every comparison, as in the minibatch acceptance gates of prompt optimizers, keep-if-better is a reversible Markov chain if the score difference is logistic and the mutation operator is reversible, and its stationary law is the mutation equilibrium tilted by exp(beta f). For any continuous symmetric noise difference the same tilt is the stationary law of a small-step diffusion limit, with beta = 4F'(0); for a minibatch gate beta grows with the square root of the minibatch size. Caching the incumbent's score instead inflates the recorded score. We test the tilt as a prediction for LLM-guided program search, committing each prediction from calibration data before the search runs. The level after 150 steps rises with the minibatch size in six of seven settings, but its predicted value fails: on bin packing, search attains 62-88% of the predicted gain when the proposer edits the parent and 109-119% when it writes new heuristics. The attained fraction falls with the parent-child quality correlation of unselected mutation; a registered test on two new settings confirmed the direction, but not the quantitative agreement after a correction. Further registered tests found that runs started from a good program kept losing quality over 300 steps, more so from starts that search had selected, by a margin that passed its registered rule narrowly. Runs from different starts had not reached a common level, so whether the tilt describes the stationary law of LLM editing remains open. A registered test in prompt optimisation on frozen task-model scores failed: search exceeded the tilt, and the bin-packing relation did not transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper frames keep-if-better LLM-guided search with re-scored candidates as a Markov chain whose stationary law is the mutation equilibrium tilted by exp(beta f), and tests this tilt as a pre-committed prediction. The tilt predicts the level after 150 steps poorly on bin packing, where search attains 62-88% or 109-119% of the predicted gain depending on the proposer, and the prediction does not transfer to prompt optimisation.
AI.motivation: Prompt optimizers and LLM-guided program search accept mutations by noisy re-scored comparisons, and it is unknown whether the resulting stationary distribution has a tractable form that predicts search outcomes.
AI.method: The authors derive a tilt under logistic or continuous symmetric noise, with beta equal to 4F'(0) and growing with the square root of minibatch size in minibatch gates, then commit predictions from calibration data and test them on bin packing and new settings with registered tests.
AI.result: The level after 150 steps rises with minibatch size in six of seven settings, but the quantitative prediction fails on bin packing; the attained fraction falls with the parent-child quality correlation, and runs from good starts keep losing quality over 300 steps. A registered test in prompt optimisation on frozen task-model scores failed, with search exceeding the tilt.
AI.conclusion: Whether the tilt describes the stationary law of LLM editing remains open, since runs from different starts did not reach a common level and the bin-packing relation did not transfer.

title: Empirical Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in SSH Infrastructure
summary: With the anticipated arrival of Q-day, quantum computers threaten current cryptographic schemes for encryption and digital signatures. In response, major content delivery networks and cloud service providers are already adopting Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The current state-of-the-art focuses on benchmarking the operational performance of implementing PQC, but the real-world adoption status remains under-researched. This work utilizes large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool to analyze PQC adoption across 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities. Our study shows that the PQC transition in the SSH protocol is underway but highly polarized: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC, while 54.8% remain classical-only. At the entity level, 39.9% have enabled PQC on at least one host, whereas 60.1% have no PQC support. By correlating PQC adoption with industry, geography, and organizational size (digital and financial), this study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of PQC adoption status in SSH infrastructure.

AI.tldr: A large-scale measurement of SSH hosts finds that post-quantum cryptography adoption is underway but polarized: 45.2% of hosts on port 22 support PQC, and 39.9% of 27,012 entities have enabled PQC on at least one host. The study also correlates adoption with industry, geography and organization size.
AI.motivation: CDNs and cloud providers are adopting PQC ahead of Q-day, but prior work benchmarks PQC performance rather than measuring real-world deployment status.
AI.method: The authors analyze large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool covering 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities, and correlate PQC support with industry, geography, and digital and financial organizational size.
AI.result: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC and 54.8% are classical-only; at the entity level 39.9% have PQC on at least one host and 60.1% have no PQC support.
AI.conclusion: The SSH PQC transition is in progress but highly uneven across hosts and entities, and the study gives a comprehensive empirical baseline of PQC adoption in SSH infrastructure.

title: Empirical Assessment of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in TLS
summary: Anticipating Q-day security concerns, major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While existing literature benchmarks PQC performance, empirical research evaluating real-world adoption data remains scarce. We present an empirical assessment of PQC deployment across seven critical protocols (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS, and RDP) using 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol. At the origin-server level, PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS, while falling below 1% for all other evaluated protocols. At the entity level, PQC support is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, while the remaining protocols have less than 5% of entities supporting PQC on the hosted servers. We further correlate these adoption trends against organizational digital and financial footprint, and industry sectors, yielding a multi-dimensional empirical assessment of PQC deployment. Finally, at the domain level, we perform a comparative analysis of PQC adoption in Cloudflare-hosted domains against baseline Cloudflare datasets. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into the current state of PQC readiness over Transport Layer Security (TLS).

AI.tldr: An empirical scan of PQC deployment across seven TLS-based protocols finds that adoption is concentrated in HTTPS and LDAPS, with all other protocols below 1% at the origin-server level. The study also compares Cloudflare-hosted domains against Cloudflare baseline datasets.
AI.motivation: Major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to PQC, but empirical data on real-world PQC adoption across protocols is scarce, and prior work mainly benchmarks performance.
AI.method: The authors probe 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol across HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS and RDP, correlate adoption with organizational digital and financial footprint and industry sectors, and run a domain-level comparison for Cloudflare-hosted domains.
AI.result: PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% of origin servers for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS and is below 1% for the other protocols; at the entity level it is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, with under 5% of entities for the rest.
AI.conclusion: PQC readiness over TLS is low outside HTTPS and LDAPS, and the findings give a multi-dimensional snapshot of current PQC deployment.

title: ICare-DT: a digital twin for continuous forecasting of intensive care patients
summary: Digital twins of intensive care patients should update forecasts from new data and predict treatment responses, but few studies test whether routine records support either. We propose ICare-DT, a Transformer-based twin that updates a latent patient state hourly from new measurements without retraining. We trained it on 140,473 eICU-CRD stays to forecast vital signs crossing their training-set means. On test data, later forecasts beat the twin's own hour-6 forecasts of the same windows in all 12 settings (+0.073 to +0.153 AUROC). On validation data, controls that withheld or swapped the new hours traced the gain to the patient's own measurements. Without refitting, the model kept its gain on a second database (8 of 9 settings, +0.025 to +0.114 AUROC) in a prespecified evaluation of the previously analyzed MIMIC-IV test split. Refitted within MIMIC-IV, a twin state fine-tuned on clinical endpoints gave gradient boosting a significant gain for acute kidney injury (+0.0035 AUROC; hypotension +0.0010, not significant). To test response prediction, we built a benchmark that replaces the treatments in real records with simulated doses and injects responses of known size, visible only at measurement times. Ridge models supervised with injected effects recovered them from real records only through frequently measured variables (heart rate) read at their measurement times. We asked standard learners to predict these effects for a dosing regime no patient had received. No standard learner outperformed predicting zero effect at an out-of-support query. When told how the simulated responses were generated, a separate learner recovered the effects from the same records without seeing their true values (R2 0.30 to 0.40 at one effect size). Routine records support forecasts that improve with each patient's new data, and our benchmark is a testbed for models that learn how responses are generated.

AI.tldr: ICare-DT is a Transformer-based digital twin that updates a latent ICU patient state hourly without retraining and forecasts vital-sign threshold crossings, with gains that persist on a second database. A benchmark with injected treatment responses shows that standard learners cannot predict effects for unseen dosing regimes, while a learner told how responses were generated recovers them with R2 of 0.30 to 0.40.
AI.motivation: Digital twins of intensive care patients should update forecasts with new data and predict treatment responses, but few studies test whether routine records support either.
AI.method: The Transformer twin updates a latent patient state from new hourly measurements without retraining; the authors train it on 140,473 eICU-CRD stays and build a benchmark that replaces real treatments with simulated doses and injects responses of known size visible only at measurement times.
AI.result: On test data, later forecasts beat the twin's own hour-6 forecasts in all 12 settings (+0.073 to +0.153 AUROC); without refitting, gains hold on MIMIC-IV in 8 of 9 settings (+0.025 to +0.114 AUROC); for acute kidney injury a refitted twin state gives gradient boosting +0.0035 AUROC, while hypotension is not significant; no standard learner beats predicting zero effect at an out-of-support query.
AI.conclusion: Routine ICU records support forecasts that improve with each patient's new data, and the benchmark is a testbed for models that must learn how treatment responses are generated, a task standard learners do not yet solve.

title: Safety Is $Π_1$, Provability Is $Σ_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
summary: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $\Pi_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $\Sigma_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $\Sigma_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $\Pi_1$ and not $\Sigma_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI safety is a Pi1 statement and provability is a Sigma1 statement, and uses this to read a security breach and a set of AI-generated mathematical proofs under one hybrid deductive framework. It proves that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier leaves Turing's undecidability result unchanged, however good the proposer is.
AI.motivation: The same company's AI systems produced a security breach and hundreds of mathematical proof manuscripts, which are read as a security failure and a mathematical success, and no unified logical account of the two outcomes exists.
AI.method: Within the hybrid framework of the authors' earlier paper, coding, proving and learning are derivations by one deductive mechanism, and the authors analyze the logical form of safety (no exploit exists, a Pi1 statement) and provability (a proof exists, a Sigma1 statement) using the halting set and its complement.
AI.result: The authors prove that a statistical proposer attached to a deductive verifier does not change the undecidability result, however good the proposer is; the abstract states no empirical numbers.
AI.conclusion: Safety cannot be assured by any finite list of passed tests, and the proposer-verifier loop cannot overcome undecidability; the paper then discusses what does assure safety and where residual risk goes.

title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Replication package: this https URL
summary: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like this http URL and this http URL, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.

AI.tldr: A study of documentation debt in coding agents finds that agents follow stale repository instruction files when they are relevant to the task, adding tool calls, and that task success alone hides this cost. The stale-instruction test with Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, roughly a third more than with the corrected command.
AI.motivation: Repository instruction files read by coding agents such as Claude Code can fall behind the code, and evaluations that check only task success can miss the cost this stale guidance adds to every later session.
AI.method: The authors take three real stale instructions from open-source repositories (a test command, a code location and a component-addition procedure) and have agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under stale, corrected and removed versions, analyzing 732 trajectories from two models at the level of tool calls.
AI.result: Agents followed stale guidance when relevant, sometimes even when correct information was available elsewhere; on the stale test command Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, and no detectable difference appeared in the other cases; no agent repaired the instruction file, and correcting the file eliminated operations on obsolete paths while removing it prevented most.
AI.conclusion: Task success can hide documentation debt costs, so agent evaluations should look beyond final outcomes, and maintainers should correct or remove stale instructions.

title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FiLSim is a scalable GNN framework for graph similarity (Graph Edit Distance and Maximum Common Subgraph) that uses a simplified GNN pipeline, remains accurate on graphs with over 150,000 nodes, and scores all test pairs within seconds on one GPU. The authors also release four large-scale datasets with reliable GED labels created by sequential graph editing.
AI.motivation: GNN-based approaches to graph similarity have been evaluated mainly on small graphs, and GED and MCS are NP-hard, so scalability to large graphs is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose FiLSim, a simplified GNN pipeline, and a sequential graph-editing strategy that constructs large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels for evaluating scalability.
AI.result: FiLSim is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four new large-scale datasets; it stays accurate on graphs with more than 150,000 nodes, where baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: A simplified GNN pipeline can stay competitive on standard benchmarks while scaling to very large graphs, and the new datasets provide a testbed for scalability.

title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
summary: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

AI.tldr: LLM agent teams synthesize and formally verify quantum programs in a Lean library, producing order-of-magnitude improvements on several scientific applications. The reported gains include 1.4x on parallel search, 290x on quantum arithmetic, and 11x, 8x and 2.5x on simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithm progress depends on slow expert collaboration, and quantum algorithms can usually be evaluated classically only on restricted or small instances, which limits automated discovery.
AI.method: The authors build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which LLM agents synthesize programs against formal specifications and verify correctness and cost, while agent teams share results through wikis and organized conferences.
AI.result: Results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations for fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively.
AI.conclusion: Combining human and AI effort under formal proof lets researchers design quantum algorithms that current classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

title: Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures
summary: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: this https URL

AI.tldr: Grasp-TAGS trains a PPO policy across multiple initial grasps and distills its critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that picks the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility before contact. It reaches an average success rate of 89.84% on goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement, versus 79.87% for the best single-grasp policy.
AI.motivation: Loco-manipulation performance depends strongly on the initial grasp, yet existing learning methods usually assume a fixed or predefined grasp, even though different stable grasps lead to very different manipulation outcomes.
AI.method: A unified PPO-based policy is trained over multiple initial grasp configurations, and its learned critic is distilled into a grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only grasp configuration and goal information.
AI.result: Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, with 89.84% average success versus 79.87% for the best single-grasp policy (a 9.97 percentage point gain), and it also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware grasp selection before contact is an effective way to improve large-object rearrangement performance over fixed-grasp policies.

title: GRAC: Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning for Surgical Scene Description
comment: 20 Pages and 4 Figures
summary: Purpose: Surgical operative reports support procedural documentation, surgical training, performance assessment, and workflow review. However, extracting meaningful information often requires extensive manual review and clinical expertise. Automated surgical scene descriptions could reduce this burden by leveraging recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge. Methods: We propose GRAC (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning), a framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs capturing relationships among instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. Given an input scene graph, GRAC learns to retrieve relevant graph-caption pairs from training data. It compares instrument-tissue interactions between retrieved examples and the input scene, using comparison features to condition retrieved-caption representations during generation. Results: On the EndoVis-18 benchmark, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.88, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest conventional Transformer baseline. Exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy reached 52.6%, compared with 32.7% for SGT and 26.2% for the strongest conventional baseline. These results demonstrate improvements in language quality and factual agreement. On TORS, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.06, compared with 3.80 for the strongest baseline. Conclusion: GRAC demonstrates that combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves surgical scene captioning and produces more contextually meaningful descriptions.

AI.tldr: GRAC is a graph-based retrieval-augmented captioning framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs and retrieves graph-caption pairs to condition caption generation. It achieves a CIDEr-D of 5.88 on EndoVis-18, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest Transformer baseline, and also improves on TORS.
AI.motivation: Surgical operative reports require heavy manual review, and automated scene descriptions could reduce this burden by exploiting recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge.
AI.method: GRAC encodes instrument, action and anatomy relationships as scene graphs, retrieves relevant graph-caption pairs from training data, and uses comparison features of instrument-tissue interactions to condition the retrieved-caption representations during generation.
AI.result: On EndoVis-18, GRAC reaches a CIDEr-D of 5.88 (SGT 4.23, strongest conventional Transformer 3.36) and exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy of 52.6% (SGT 32.7%, strongest conventional baseline 26.2%); on TORS it reaches a CIDEr-D of 5.06 versus 3.80 for the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves both language quality and factual agreement in surgical scene captioning, yielding more contextually meaningful descriptions.

title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
comment: Videos and code available at: this https URL
summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

AI.tldr: AMP1 is a reference harness in which a generalist AI model commands manipulators directly, achieving 85.6% zero-shot success on RoboLab-120 without demonstrations or task-specific training, compared with 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. It succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials and gains further from a persistent memory store across episodes.
AI.motivation: Robot manipulation research centers on specialist policies trained on demonstrations, and the paper asks whether generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably.
AI.method: The authors analyze agentic manipulation policies, in which a generalist model adapts its actions as the task unfolds, and present AMP1, a harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual and mobile manipulation, optionally with a memory representation carried across episodes.
AI.result: AMP1 reaches 85.6% zero-shot success on RoboLab-120 (49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies) and succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials across twelve tasks and three robots, cutting failure rates 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines; the memory-augmented harness lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual tasks by 4.6x versus zero-shot deployment.
AI.conclusion: Agentic manipulation policies are more general and robust than specialist policies, and cross-episode memory allows learning from experience, offering a foundation for robot manipulation.

title: Dynamic GPU Voxel Grids and Voxel-sequential Processing in NanoVDB
summary: We introduce two fundamental advances to the NanoVDB data structure: dynamic GPU-native topological updates, and a voxel-sequential access paradigm that dramatically accelerates point-wise and stencil-based operators on sparse grids. NanoVDB's linearized memory layout has delivered strong GPU performance, and the Index-Grid concept introduced in the fVDB framework [Williams et al 2024] provided topology/data separation and optimal compactness of storage in sparse machine learning workloads. However, all these prior iterations of NanoVDB assume a static topology that has precluded use of this data structure in simulation and dynamic geometric processes. We eliminate this limitation by introducing a suite of dynamic topology operators -- morphological dilation, grid merging, pruning, and cross-resolution coarsening and refinement. These operators use bit-parallel algorithms to reconstruct grids containing hundreds of millions of voxels in just a few milliseconds. We also introduce a voxel-sequential access paradigm and data structure for GPU kernels operating on sparse data. We stream active voxels as a flat linear sequence, minimizing or eliminating the need for tree traversal in the process. This achieves compute density and regularity that allow even complex stencil-based operators to approach peak memory bandwidth, with minimal storage overhead. Together, these contributions remove the read-only constraint from NanoVDB, establishing it as a high-performance primary representation for dynamic GPU simulation and geometry manipulation. We evaluate the efficacy of our newly introduced operators in benchmarks sourced from applications such as 3D reconstruction, fluid simulation, and large-scale mesh voxelization.

AI.tldr: The paper extends NanoVDB with dynamic GPU-native topology operators and a voxel-sequential access paradigm that streams active voxels as a flat sequence, removing the read-only limitation of the format. The operators rebuild grids with hundreds of millions of voxels in a few milliseconds, and stencil operators approach peak memory bandwidth.
AI.motivation: Earlier NanoVDB versions assume static topology, which rules out simulation and dynamic geometric processing on GPUs.
AI.method: The authors add morphological dilation, grid merging, pruning, and cross-resolution coarsening and refinement, implemented with bit-parallel algorithms, and introduce a voxel-sequential data structure that streams active voxels as a flat linear sequence to reduce tree traversal.
AI.result: The operators reconstruct grids with hundreds of millions of voxels in a few milliseconds, and voxel-sequential stencil operators approach peak memory bandwidth with minimal storage overhead; the paper evaluates on 3D reconstruction, fluid simulation and large-scale mesh voxelization.
AI.conclusion: The changes make NanoVDB a high-performance primary representation for dynamic GPU simulation and geometry manipulation, not only a read-only format.

title: Segmenting Geometric Textures of 3D Meshes
comment: Pacific Graphics 2026
summary: Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.

AI.tldr: The paper segments middle-level geometric textures on 3D meshes by fine-tuning SAM3 on a new texture benchmark, then clusters the 2D texture regions with DINO features and lifts them to 3D.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D model segmentation targets high-level semantic parts and misses middle-level textures, and current vision-language models still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures.
AI.method: Texture regions are segmented in 2D by SAM3 fine-tuned on a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark, clustered by DINO feature similarity, and lifted from 2D to 3D; an interactive tool supports 3D model editing and retrieval by geometric and texture similarity.
AI.result: Experiments show the method significantly outperforms existing methods at segmenting geometric textures and supports various applications; the abstract reports no quantitative numbers.
AI.conclusion: Texture-level segmentation of 3D meshes is feasible and useful for heritage protection, model editing and 3D printing.

title: Audiovisual Disparities in VR: Impact on Spatial Perception
comment: 2025 IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR)
summary: Virtual reality (VR) experiences often leverage rich and spatialized multimodal environments to increase immersion and engagement. This demands a consistent spatial perception of audiovisual stimuli, since perceived discrepancies can disrupt the sense of presence. In this work, we investigate the consequences of two types of spatial audiovisual disparities: true disparity, where there is a measurable spatial offset between auditory and visual cues, and perceptual disparity, where users report misalignment despite cues being colocated. Unlike most previous studies that employed controlled but simplified experimental setups, our research focuses on complex, realistic VR environments, allowing us to assess the actual implications for VR content design. Our experiments indicate that users are highly sensitive to true audiovisual disparities in controlled environments, detecting even minor misalignments. However, when engaged in additional tasks within realistic settings, their ability to notice such discrepancies diminishes significantly. We also observed that previously found perceptual disparities persist in complex audiovisual environments. However, we identify self-initiated head rotations as a key factor; its absence prevents the effect entirely. We hope our findings offer practical insights for designing more immersive and perceptually coherent VR experiences.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how true spatial audiovisual offsets and perceived misalignment with colocated cues affect spatial perception in realistic VR environments.
AI.motivation: Previous studies used controlled but simplified setups, so the consequences of audiovisual disparities for realistic VR content design were unclear.
AI.method: Experiments in complex, realistic VR environments compare true disparity (a measurable spatial offset between audio and visual cues) with perceptual disparity (reported misalignment despite colocated cues), including conditions with an additional task and with or without self-initiated head rotation.
AI.result: Users are highly sensitive to true disparities in controlled settings, but their ability to notice them drops significantly when engaged in additional tasks in realistic settings; perceptual disparities persist in complex environments, and self-initiated head rotations are a key factor, since without them the effect disappears.
AI.conclusion: The findings give practical guidance for designing more immersive and perceptually coherent VR experiences.

title: Real-Time Self-Penetration Repair for Skinned Characters with Soft Contact Budgets
comment: 4 figures, 9 tables
summary: Motion that is plausible on one body can penetrate another after a change in shape, and motion models can produce self-penetration on their native characters. We present a training-free post-process that reduces these artifacts through pose correction followed by bounded skin compression. The module attaches to any motion model whose native character and output character have compatible character packs, without access to model internals. Each pack is built offline from the rig and skin without training. A vertex-level pose layer solves a local quadratic program in plain C on one CPU core, and a stateless contact deformer acts on the host's final skinned mesh. A part-dependent soft-tissue budget allocates correction between pose and skin through a static convention. Source penetration contributes no extra allowance; optional cloth thickness and compliance modify the pose layer's collision surface. Operation is causal or uses a short buffered lookahead, with frame-exact pass-through at the native interface for clean, inactive frames in the zero state. Across 320 unseen clips and 3 body shapes, the fraction of frames with hand-torso depth above 20 mm falls from 15.53% for copied motion to 0.00%, with final maximum depth 9.3 mm over every frame. Mean pose and skin costs are 1.11 and 1.18 ms, respectively, and their sum of 2.29 ms is a sub-frame processing cost. The median joint-velocity high-frequency ratio relative to copied target motion is 1.008.

AI.tldr: A training-free, real-time post-process repairs self-penetration in skinned characters produced by motion models, using pose correction followed by bounded skin compression.
AI.motivation: Motion that is plausible on one body can penetrate another after a change in shape, and motion models can also produce self-penetration on their native characters.
AI.method: A vertex-level pose layer solves a local quadratic program on one CPU core, and a stateless contact deformer acts on the final skinned mesh; a part-dependent soft-tissue budget divides correction between pose and skin; the module attaches to any motion model with compatible character packs and needs no access to model internals.
AI.result: Across 320 unseen clips and 3 body shapes, frames with hand-torso depth above 20 mm fall from 15.53% for copied motion to 0.00%, with final maximum depth 9.3 mm; mean pose and skin costs are 1.11 and 1.18 ms (2.29 ms total), and the median joint-velocity high-frequency ratio relative to copied target motion is 1.008.
AI.conclusion: The module removes the evaluated penetration artifacts at sub-frame cost while leaving high-frequency joint-velocity content nearly unchanged (ratio 1.008).

title: The Drawing You Watch Is the Portrait You Keep: A Replayable Machine Portrait Studio
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Live system: this https URL
summary: Ask an image model for your portrait and a finished picture arrives: no first line, no second thoughts, no record of how it got there, and a different picture if you ask again. I built a portrait studio that works the other way. A sitter chooses one of eight fictional artists, each written with a city, a medium and a tempo of its own, holds still for 8 to 12 seconds, and watches a drawing of themselves appear over 44 seconds. One still is sent after consent, a hosted image model returns a private study the sitter never sees, and a compiler turns that study into one drawing document. The live drawing, the saved sheet, the vector export and the film all read that document, and a replay makes no model call, so the drawing you watch is the portrait you keep. I describe the compiler in enough detail to rebuild it and say plainly what it is: an authored reconstruction at a compressed speed, not a recorded hand. On 16 generated test studies a sheet holds 8,784 to 16,378 timed contacts, about three quarters of them fixed-grid fills and nearly all shorter than one video frame, and recompiling one study gave byte-identical output four times on one machine. The paper also traces a bug that matters more than any of that. The earlier compiler estimated the paper colour tile by tile, read dark skin as paper, and in all eight hands kept less of a deep-complexioned face than a fair one (13 to 48 percent against 41 to 56). On 80 generated studies the rebuilt engine keeps the complexion difference the study already has (raw retention 89 to 120 percent), so the fairness question has moved upstream, to the study and the hosted model. The two test sitters are generated and differ in more than complexion, and no real-face or perceptual study exists yet. The studio is live at this https URL.

AI.tldr: A replayable portrait studio has a sitter watch a drawing of themselves appear, compiled from one hosted image-model study into a single drawing document, so replays make no model call.
AI.motivation: Image models return a finished picture with no record of how it was made, and re-asking gives a different picture, so the portrait cannot be replayed or kept as a process.
AI.method: A sitter chooses one of eight fictional artists, holds still for 8 to 12 seconds, and watches a 44-second drawing; one still is sent after consent to a hosted image model that returns a private study, and a compiler turns that study into one drawing document read by the live drawing, saved sheet, vector export and film.
AI.result: On 16 generated test studies a sheet holds 8,784 to 16,378 timed contacts, about three quarters of them fixed-grid fills; recompiling one study gave byte-identical output four times on one machine. An earlier compiler under-kept deep-complexioned faces (13 to 48 percent retention against 41 to 56 for fair complexions); on 80 generated studies the rebuilt engine keeps the complexion difference the study already has (raw retention 89 to 120 percent). The two test sitters are generated, and no real-face or perceptual study exists yet.
AI.conclusion: The fairness question moves upstream to the study and the hosted model, and the drawing is an authored reconstruction at compressed speed rather than a recorded hand.

title: InstaGen: Group-Shared Importance Sampling for Fast Video Generation
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).

AI.tldr: InstaGen replaces top-p key block selection in permuted block-sparse attention with an exact top-scoring set plus a weighted sample, which speeds up attention in video diffusion transformers.
AI.motivation: Top-p block selection is sample inefficient in the high-entropy attention regimes common in video generation.
AI.method: Block selection is cast as importance sampling: top-scoring keys are computed exactly, and the remaining keys are sampled in proportion to estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability; each query cluster shares one sample so the sampled keys form GPU-efficient blocks; it is instantiated on the SVG family of methods.
AI.result: On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time; on the 14B model it beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
AI.conclusion: Under the same computational budget, sampling gives a better attention approximation than top-p selection in high-entropy video attention.

title: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.

AI.tldr: BEVCast refines a coarse bird's-eye-view grid only in the cells the predicted driving path crosses, giving a mixed-resolution BEV for end-to-end driving without HD maps or navigation commands.
AI.motivation: A dense BEV grid spends the same computation on every cell, although the vehicle crosses only a few cells within the planning horizon.
AI.method: A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells; a heat head trained on the recorded path scores each coarse cell, and the highest-heat cells are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget while the rest keep coarse resolution; the trajectory head reads this mixed-resolution BEV.
AI.result: At a 10% refinement budget, compared with a full 1.024 m grid, BEVCast encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1; on nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%; on NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28; it reaches error comparable to published planners on both benchmarks without a navigation command.
AI.conclusion: The resolution of a driving BEV can follow the task rather than the fixed grid.

title: An Anatomy-guided 3D Segmentation Pipeline for Prostate Surgical Phantoms from CT Scans
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables, 10 algorithms. Extended abstract accepted at SPIE Medical Imaging 2027: Image Processing
summary: Full autonomy has been a long-term goal in robotic surgery and a near-to-medium-term goal for prostatectomy. Due to the relatively closed structure of the procedure, its standard-of-care robotic/laparoscopic solutions, and procedure economics, prostate procedures are an optimal early target for surgical automation. Prototyping and testing of possible solutions is done in constructed laboratory phantoms, either synthetic tissues or animal phantoms. To enable measurement of perceptual and robotic motion error, phantoms undergo volumetric imaging; these images are critical to both a potential deployed automatic system, used in planning motion and treatment (cutting, ablation, suturing, etc.), as well as post-hoc assessment of system performance. Rapid iteration on these phantom models yields small, inconsistent datasets, while the current workflow for human annotation is often anatomically unreliable and prohibitively time-consuming, rendering deep learning unsuitable at reasonable scales. To address these limitations, we present an automated 3D segmentation pipeline that uses classical medical image-processing techniques to encode the known anatomy of the phantoms as explicit geometric and intensity priors, which requires no training corpus and is transferred to each new phantom revision without re-annotation. Across 57 scans spanning multiple phantom revisions, our pipeline recovers the capsule interior at 0.83 median Dice on 11 contrast-suppressed scans and detects all 32 annotated focal lesions without false positives, completing a full scan in 2-8 minutes on commodity CPU hardware versus 1-2 hours by hand.

AI.tldr: An automated, training-free 3D segmentation pipeline for CT scans of prostate surgical phantoms encodes the known phantom anatomy as geometric and intensity priors.
AI.motivation: Rapid phantom iteration yields small, inconsistent datasets, and manual annotation is anatomically unreliable and slow, which makes deep learning unsuitable at reasonable scales.
AI.method: Classical medical image-processing techniques encode the known anatomy as explicit geometric and intensity priors; the pipeline needs no training corpus and transfers to each new phantom revision without re-annotation.
AI.result: Across 57 scans spanning multiple phantom revisions, it recovers the capsule interior at 0.83 median Dice on 11 contrast-suppressed scans and detects all 32 annotated focal lesions with no false positives; a full scan takes 2 to 8 minutes on commodity CPU hardware, against 1 to 2 hours by hand.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline gives a fast, annotation-free route to segmenting phantom volumes for prostatectomy automation work.

title: eSharp: Diffusion-based Sharp Monocular Metric Event-to-Depth Estimation
summary: Depth perception is fundamental for autonomous navigation, industrial inspection, and mixed-reality systems. It often operates under strict constraints on power and form factor. In such cases, monocular depth estimation (MDE) is often used. Even as recent advances continue to improve monocular depth quality, conventional frame-based MDE systems remain challenged by fast motion and high-dynamic-range scenes. This work introduces eSharp, an MDE framework that addresses these problems using an event camera. eSharp repurposes pretrained diffusion priors for event-only MDE and produces accurate metric depth with unparalleled sharpness on real data. Real-world event datasets provide only sparse LiDAR depth maps for ground-truth supervision, making dense prediction challenging. We address this limitation through cross-modal distillation, using LiDAR-calibrated dense pseudo-labels generated from a spatially co-registered frame camera to train eSharp. Experiments show that eSharp outperforms prior event-to-depth baselines in both metric-depth accuracy and spatial fidelity, establishing diffusion models as a promising foundation for event-driven 3D perception.

AI.tldr: eSharp is an event-only monocular metric depth framework that repurposes pretrained diffusion priors and is trained by distilling LiDAR-calibrated pseudo-labels from a co-registered frame camera.
AI.motivation: Frame-based monocular depth struggles with fast motion and high-dynamic-range scenes, and real event datasets provide only sparse LiDAR ground truth, which makes dense prediction challenging.
AI.method: Pretrained diffusion priors are repurposed for event-only depth estimation; cross-modal distillation trains the model with dense pseudo-labels generated from a spatially co-registered frame camera and calibrated with LiDAR.
AI.result: On real data eSharp outperforms prior event-to-depth baselines in both metric-depth accuracy and spatial fidelity; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models are a promising foundation for event-driven 3D perception.

title: FishSense Lite: A Camera-Based, Single Laser Hardware Framework with Software System for In Situ Fish Length Measurement
comment: 27 pages with 14 figures
summary: Fish stock assessments need fish lengths paired with species from far more places than trained surveyors can reach. Recreational divers already visit many of those places, but measuring a fish underwater has required trained observers or specialist equipment. We present FishSense Lite, which recovers fish length from a single photograph taken with a recreational dive camera, a dive laser pointer, and a 3D-printed mount. The diver aims the laser at a fish and takes a picture; afterward, the dot's position in the image gives the range to the fish, and the range turns the fish's size in the image into a length. A citizen-science program, trained by the system's builders, taught its own divers and collected lengths paired with species for 73 wild fish across seven open-water dives. On seven wild fish also measured by an underwater stereo-imaging system, the two instruments agreed without detectable bias (mean difference +0.8%). On rigid targets of known length, FishSense Lite recovered every target to within 1.3%, and 99% of 1,055 frames fell within a 15% error budget. From the error sources we measure, we derive a field protocol: calibrate against a dive slate on every dive, photograph fish within 15 degrees of perpendicular and beyond 1 m, and take at least ten frames of each.

AI.tldr: FishSense Lite recovers fish length from a single photograph taken with a recreational dive camera, a dive laser pointer and a 3D-printed mount, using the laser dot's position to estimate range.
AI.motivation: Fish stock assessments need fish lengths paired with species from far more places than trained surveyors can reach, but measuring fish underwater has required trained observers or specialist equipment.
AI.method: The diver aims the laser at a fish and takes a picture; the dot's position in the image gives the range, and the range converts the fish's image size into length; a citizen-science program trained by the builders collected the data.
AI.result: Divers collected lengths paired with species for 73 wild fish across seven open-water dives; on seven wild fish also measured by an underwater stereo-imaging system the two agreed without detectable bias (mean difference +0.8%); on rigid targets of known length every target was recovered to within 1.3%, and 99% of 1,055 frames fell within a 15% error budget.
AI.conclusion: From the measured error sources the authors derive a field protocol: calibrate against a dive slate on every dive, photograph fish within 15 degrees of perpendicular and beyond 1 m, and take at least ten frames of each fish.

title: Extrapolation Matters: Sparse-Only Depth Completion Beyond LiDAR Coverage
summary: Extrapolation beyond LiDAR coverage is an important yet under-evaluated challenge of depth completion. In real camera--LiDAR systems, partial sensor overlap, occlusions, and limited field coverage often leave large image regions weakly observed or completely unobserved by LiDAR. Thus, we investigate depth completion in this beyond-coverage regime using only sparse supervision from raw single-sweep LiDAR, without dense depth labels, LiDAR accumulation, or pseudo-LiDAR generation. Our approach leverages a frozen monocular depth foundation model, lightweight per-frame alignment to sparse LiDAR geometry, and a refinement module that fuses the aligned prior with sparse LiDAR anchors to predict dense metric depth. To regularize learning under raw sparse supervision, we introduce a high-frequency normal-consistency loss defined as the image-space gradient of the per-pixel normal cosine discrepancy. This term penalizes spatial variation in scalar angular error; it does not directly match changes in neighboring normal vectors. We further introduce an evaluation protocol that explicitly separates LiDAR-supported and beyond-coverage regions, revealing extrapolative behavior that conventional depth-completion metrics can obscure. Our method achieves strong depth accuracy beyond LiDAR coverage while remaining competitive in LiDAR-covered regions, providing a practical way to deploy monocular foundation priors in multi-sensor systems.

AI.tldr: A sparse-only depth completion method extrapolates beyond LiDAR coverage by aligning a frozen monocular depth foundation model to single-sweep LiDAR and fusing the aligned prior with sparse LiDAR anchors.
AI.motivation: In real camera-LiDAR systems large image regions are weakly observed or unobserved by LiDAR, and conventional depth-completion metrics can obscure how a method behaves in those regions.
AI.method: A frozen monocular depth foundation model, lightweight per-frame alignment to sparse LiDAR geometry, and a refinement module that fuses the aligned prior with sparse anchors; a high-frequency normal-consistency loss, defined as the image-space gradient of the per-pixel normal cosine discrepancy, regularizes learning under raw sparse supervision; an evaluation protocol separates LiDAR-supported and beyond-coverage regions.
AI.result: The method achieves strong depth accuracy beyond LiDAR coverage while remaining competitive in LiDAR-covered regions; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a practical way to deploy monocular foundation priors in multi-sensor systems.

title: Scale as a Modality: Multi-Scale Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
summary: Latent diffusion models rely on pretrained autoencoders that introduce lossy compression and constrain spatial granularity. Pixel-space diffusion avoids this bottleneck and enables flexible tokenization at multiple spatial scales, yet existing approaches largely adopt two-level coarse-to-fine architectures with limited cross-scale interaction. We introduce MS-pDiT, a multi-scale pixel-space diffusion transformer that treats spatial scale as a modality. MS-pDiT tokenizes the same noisy image at multiple patch sizes, processes each scale in a dedicated transformer stream, and enables bidirectional information exchange through compacted MM-DiT-style joint attention, with attention cost independent of the finest patch size. This design establishes the number of scales as a new architectural scaling dimension. On ImageNet $256\times256$, increasing the number of scales from two to five consistently improves FID from 4.39 to 2.31, 2.26, and 2.19, while adding an intermediate scale substantially outperforms increasing depth under comparable parameter budgets. Further analysis highlights the importance of bidirectional cross-scale interaction and late introduction of fine-grained streams. MS-pDiT achieves FID scores of 1.43 and 1.44 on ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, respectively, and naturally extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.86 on GenEval and 83.9 on DPG-Bench.

AI.tldr: MS-pDiT is a pixel-space diffusion transformer that treats spatial scale as a modality, tokenizing the same noisy image at several patch sizes and exchanging information across scales through joint attention.
AI.motivation: Latent diffusion models rely on lossy pretrained autoencoders that constrain spatial granularity, while existing pixel-space approaches use two-level coarse-to-fine designs with limited cross-scale interaction.
AI.method: The same noisy image is tokenized at multiple patch sizes, each scale is processed in a dedicated transformer stream, and bidirectional exchange uses compacted MM-DiT-style joint attention whose cost is independent of the finest patch size; late introduction of fine-grained streams is part of the design.
AI.result: On ImageNet 256x256, increasing the number of scales from two to five improves FID from 4.39 to 2.31, 2.26 and 2.19; adding an intermediate scale outperforms increasing depth under comparable parameter budgets; FID is 1.43 and 1.44 on ImageNet 256x256 and 512x512; for text-to-image it reaches 0.86 on GenEval and 83.9 on DPG-Bench.
AI.conclusion: The number of scales establishes a new architectural scaling dimension for diffusion transformers.

title: Impact of color in computer and human-based object recognition under occlusion
summary: Partial occlusions challenge object recognition in both human and computer vision (CV), but the impact is largely dependent on the occlusion and model design. Properties relating to color are particularly important in biological recognition and frequently leveraged for camouflage, however there are still open questions about what makes them effective and how they translate to CV. This work studies partial occlusions that create camouflage, including those that blend in with target objects or with scenes, which alter object representations in distinct ways. Experiments evaluate recognition performance on both human participants and models ranging from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformers, and additional analysis is performed on models to uncover trends in processing and object representations under multiple occlusion types. Novel metrics offer explainability of model behavior under occlusion: non-occlusion precision (NOP) and non-occlusion recall (NOR) measure alignment of model activations with and without occlusion, and activation in occlusion (AIO) measures the percentage of activations that occur in occluded regions. Findings show that human recognition, and most transformers, are negatively impacted by generated camouflaging occluders, with scene-based camouflage performing worse than object-based. Classical CNNs show a strong opposite trend, performing the worst on neutral-colored occlusions, suggesting that contextually-related colors, particularly scene-based, benefit object recognition rather than disrupting shape or boundary cues. Additionally, generated camouflaging occluders for training augmentation improves robustness to unseen camouflage for selected CNN model, and occlusion metrics suggest trends about learned mechanisms. Findings have interesting implications for alignment in human and computer vision, model vulnerabilities, and explainability.

AI.tldr: The paper compares human and computer-vision object recognition under generated camouflage occlusions, finds opposite trends for transformers and classical CNNs, and introduces occlusion-alignment metrics.
AI.motivation: Color-based camouflage affects biological recognition, but it is unclear what makes it effective and how it translates to computer vision.
AI.method: Human participants and models from CNNs to transformers are tested under object-based and scene-based camouflaging occluders; the new metrics NOP and NOR measure activation alignment with and without occlusion, and AIO measures the share of activations inside occluded regions; generated camouflaging occluders are also used for training augmentation.
AI.result: Human recognition and most transformers are negatively impacted by generated camouflage, with scene-based camouflage worse than object-based; classical CNNs perform worst on neutral-colored occlusions; training augmentation with camouflaging occluders improves robustness to unseen camouflage for a selected CNN.
AI.conclusion: Contextually related colors may benefit CNN object recognition rather than disrupt shape cues, with implications for human-machine alignment, model vulnerabilities and explainability.

title: The APL Doesn't Fall Far From The Tree: Unsupervised Artefact Prototype Learning in Histopathology
summary: Histopathology foundation models provide rich representations of tissue morphology, but technical artefacts in whole slide images introduce noise that may impact diagnostic accuracy. We introduce Artefact Prototype Learning (APL), a novel approach to detecting these artefacts that exploits the geometry of pre-trained embedding spaces without manual labels or fine-tuning. Rather than treating artefacts as isolated outliers, APL computes prototypes of out-of-distribution patches and uses them to distinguish artefact-associated patterns from tissue. Evaluation on a single-centre dataset shows that APL outperforms prior methods GrandQC and HistoART in detecting artefacts such as blur, dark spots, slide edges and pen marks, but struggles with tissue folds and blood. These results show that frozen pre-trained embeddings already carry information that allows artefact detection without expensive labels or vast computational resources.

AI.tldr: APL detects technical artefacts in histopathology whole slide images by computing prototypes of out-of-distribution patches in the embedding space of frozen pretrained models, without labels or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Artefacts in whole slide images may affect diagnostic accuracy, and existing treatments tend to regard artefacts as isolated outliers.
AI.method: APL exploits the geometry of pre-trained embedding spaces, computes prototypes of out-of-distribution patches, and uses them to distinguish artefact-associated patterns from tissue, with no manual labels or fine-tuning.
AI.result: On a single-centre dataset APL outperforms the prior methods GrandQC and HistoART at detecting blur, dark spots, slide edges and pen marks, but it struggles with tissue folds and blood.
AI.conclusion: Frozen pre-trained embeddings already carry enough information for artefact detection without expensive labels or large computational resources.

title: Align3D: Image-Structure Co-Aligned 3D Scene Generation with Observability-Aware Fidelity-Preserving Guidance
summary: We present Align3D, an image-conditioned diffusion model that generates 3D indoor layouts that are both faithful to a single input photograph and physically plausible beyond the observed view. From the photograph we infer a confidence-calibrated scene graph and train a set-diffusion layout denoiser with image-structure co-alignment where confidence-weighted modality fusion balances image and scene-graph alignment using predicted confidences, while observability-aware fidelity-preserving guidance projects conflicting scene-quality gradients and reweighs them with an object-level confidence mask so under-observed degrees of freedom absorb physical priors without undoing the image-graph match. On 3D-FRONT, Align3D improves image-alignment and scene-quality metrics over recent baselines; once trained, it maps previously unseen photographs to layouts in a single feed-forward pass.

AI.tldr: Align3D generates 3D indoor layouts from a single photograph that stay faithful to the image while remaining physically plausible beyond the observed view.
AI.motivation: Layout generation from a photo must match the image yet plausibly fill unobserved regions, and conflicting image and physical-prior objectives can undo each other.
AI.method: A confidence-calibrated scene graph is inferred from the photograph, and a set-diffusion layout denoiser is trained with image-structure co-alignment, using confidence-weighted modality fusion; observability-aware fidelity-preserving guidance projects conflicting scene-quality gradients and reweights them with an object-level confidence mask.
AI.result: On 3D-FRONT, Align3D improves image-alignment and scene-quality metrics over recent baselines, and once trained it maps previously unseen photographs to layouts in a single feed-forward pass; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Single-pass, image-faithful layout generation with physical priors filling the under-observed degrees of freedom is feasible.

title: GeoJeV: Unified Spatial Probability for Training-Free Efficient Evidence Acquisition in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
summary: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.

AI.tldr: GeoJeV is a training-free method for ultra-high-resolution remote sensing that treats evidence search as spatial probability decisions from a frozen JeV model, removing generative MLLM search control.
AI.motivation: Existing evidence acquisition relies on generative multimodal LLMs for search control, RLHF aligns them with human-preferred responses rather than region-level relevance, and repeated autoregressive decoding adds overhead.
AI.method: A frozen JeV model gives a probability distribution over candidate regions; Region Rank orders the candidates, Sparse Branch sets branching width from the sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth from branch sparsity and distribution concentration, all coordinated through the shared distribution with no intermediate decoding.
AI.result: Accuracies are 60.59% on LRS-GRO, 52.79% on MME-RealWorld-RS and 34.32% on LRS-VQA; across the three benchmarks it improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by 5.32 points with 1.12 additional seconds per question, and gives a 7.8-fold inference speedup over a recent method.
AI.conclusion: Spatial probability-driven search can replace generative search control, reducing reliance on RLHF-aligned generation while improving accuracy and speed.

title: Computer Vision by YOLOs for Detection of Major Diseases in Vietnamese Custard Apple Using Fruit Imagery
summary: Amid Vietnam rapid digital transformation in agriculture, the integration of artificial intelligence technologies for identifying, monitoring, and predicting crop pests and diseases has emerged as an inevitable trend.

AI.tldr: The title indicates YOLO-based computer vision is used to detect major diseases of Vietnamese custard apple from fruit images; the abstract itself gives no method or results.
AI.motivation: Amid Vietnam's rapid digital transformation in agriculture, integrating AI to identify, monitor and predict crop pests and diseases has become an inevitable trend.
AI.method: The abstract does not describe the method; the title names YOLO models applied to fruit imagery.
AI.result: The abstract reports no results.
AI.conclusion: The abstract only motivates AI-based pest and disease monitoring for Vietnamese agriculture, and no findings are stated.

title: Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables; 11-page supplementary information included as ancillary file
summary: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.

AI.tldr: Ca2REAL reconstructs natural movies from calcium imaging of mouse V1 by conditioning a pretrained video diffusion model on separate layout and semantic controls derived from neural activity.
