AI.tldr: UniMore is a post-training method for unified multimodal models that derives fine-grained generation and understanding tasks from image-text pairs to counter loss of specificity in both directions. The abstract reports gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: A pretrained unified model loses specificity: generated images contain the requested objects with incorrect attributes, and captions identify a scene without expressing its distinguishing details.
AI.method: The generation route predicts grounded crops from their corresponding phrases using the native visual objective. The understanding route combines positive-caption fitting with ranking against captions that omit or alter details, conditioned on the full image. The two routes are optimized independently and their learned updates are combined into a single model without changing inference.
AI.result: Gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Supervision that specifies both the visual content to realize and the descriptive differences to distinguish improves unified models without changing their inference procedure.

title: DobotTrack: Target-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Learning for Embodied Person Tracking
summary: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DobotTrack is a target-grounded vision-language-action framework for language-guided embodied person tracking that combines auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. Its 0.8B-parameter model reaches an average success rate of 77.9% on EVT-Bench, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Language-guided embodied tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and keep following it under egocentric observations.
AI.method: Five auxiliary tasks are studied (person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification, future DINO feature prediction and future-frame prediction), with mask and bounding-box supervision. Q-identity is a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that uses grounding predictions to keep identity-discriminative appearance and spatial cues in compact historical tokens.
AI.result: 77.9% average success rate on EVT-Bench across three tasks, 16.9 points above OmTrackVLA. A new real-world quadruped-robot person-tracking dataset has 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames, from which bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels are derived automatically.
AI.conclusion: The framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from both simulated and real-world data.

title: EventHOI: Event-Driven Resource-Efficient Hand-Object Interaction Logging on Smartglasses
comment: 15 pages, 21 figures, 3 tables
summary: Hand-object interactions (HOIs) can be captured by smartglasses to learn how people manipulate objects in daily life. Automatic logging of these interactions from an egocentric perspective provides time-stamped evidence of daily actions for applications like memory assistance. However, continuous RGB capture and wireless transmission exceed the energy and bandwidth budgets of smartglasses. We present EventHOI, an event-driven sensing and compression system that couples selective RGB capture with HOI-aware encoding to enable egocentric logging over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) while preserving downstream HOI logging performance. Our key insight is to use low-power event sensing both to determine when RGB capture is needed and to identify where visual detail must be preserved. A lightweight IMU-based egomotion cancellation pipeline suppresses egomotion-induced events so that residual HOI motion can guide RGB triggering and spatial compression. We build a smartglasses prototype and conduct an end-to-end evaluation of EventHOI on a 50-hour egocentric benchmark with 97 subjects and a 20-hour real-world dataset we collect from 10 participants, together covering a broad range of daily-life scenarios and environments. Compared to RGB-only baselines, EventHOI reduces always-on backend power consumption by 5.8-10.4x and uplink bandwidth by 2.9x, with minimal HOI recognition accuracy loss. The resulting RGB uplink of less than 130 kbps fits within commodity BLE bandwidth budgets, making stable BLE video streaming feasible for egocentric HOI logging. Demo video and project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: EventHOI is an event-driven sensing and compression system for smartglasses that captures RGB only when low-power event sensing indicates hand-object interaction, enabling egocentric HOI logging over BLE. Compared with RGB-only baselines it reduces always-on backend power by 5.8-10.4x and uplink bandwidth by 2.9x with minimal HOI recognition loss.
AI.motivation: Continuous RGB capture and wireless transmission exceed the energy and bandwidth budgets of smartglasses, which blocks always-on egocentric logging of daily actions for applications such as memory assistance.
AI.method: Low-power event sensing decides when RGB capture is needed and where visual detail must be preserved. A lightweight IMU-based egomotion cancellation pipeline removes egomotion-induced events so residual HOI motion guides RGB triggering and HOI-aware spatial compression. A smartglasses prototype was built.
AI.result: End-to-end evaluation on a 50-hour egocentric benchmark with 97 subjects and a 20-hour real-world dataset from 10 participants. Backend power reduced 5.8-10.4x and uplink bandwidth 2.9x against RGB-only baselines, with minimal HOI recognition accuracy loss. The RGB uplink stays under 130 kbps, within commodity BLE bandwidth.
AI.conclusion: Event-driven selective capture makes stable BLE video streaming feasible for egocentric HOI logging on smartglasses.

title: Semantic Extraction Framework for Goal-Oriented V2X Communication Supporting Safe Intersection Passage
comment: Accept by 2026 Asia-Pacific Conference on Communications
summary: This paper proposes a transmitter-side semantic extraction framework for goal-oriented Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication supporting safe intersection passage. Instead of transmitting raw sensory data, roadside infrastructure extracts task-relevant semantic information from video and traffic-signal sequences and organizes them into compact semantic packets for low-latency driving-decision assistance. The intersection-passing problem is formulated as a set of traffic tasks under Japanese traffic regulations, and the proposed pipeline generates perception and intent semantics through object detection, object tracking, region-of-interest (ROI)-based semantic extraction, and recommended-action generation. The framework is implemented and evaluated on a self-constructed, CARLA-based single-vehicle dataset collected under clear weather conditions. Experimental results show high recommended-action accuracy within the tested task set, while the mean processing latency remains below the frame interval of the 15~fps input video.

AI.tldr: A roadside transmitter-side framework extracts task-relevant semantics from video and traffic-signal sequences into compact packets for V2X intersection passage under Japanese traffic regulations. On a self-built CARLA single-vehicle dataset in clear weather it achieves high recommended-action accuracy, with mean processing latency below the 15 fps input frame interval.
AI.motivation: Transmitting raw sensory data is ill-suited to goal-oriented V2X communication that must support low-latency driving-decision assistance at intersections.
AI.method: Object detection, object tracking, ROI-based semantic extraction and recommended-action generation produce perception and intent semantics for a set of traffic tasks formulated under Japanese traffic regulations.
AI.result: High recommended-action accuracy within the tested task set on a self-constructed CARLA dataset under clear weather, with mean processing latency below the frame interval of the 15 fps input video.
AI.conclusion: Roadside semantic extraction is a feasible low-latency alternative to raw data transmission for intersection driving assistance, within the scope of the tested tasks and conditions.

title: Beyond Segmentation: Enriching ImageCAS with Coronary Ostia Landmarks, Rooted Centerline Graphs, and Open-Weight Localization Models
comment: 52 pages including the appendices. Dataset, centerlines, code and model weights: this https URL
summary: Coronary ostia and centerlines are key reference points for automated analysis of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA), from surgical planning to intraoperative vessel tracking. However, the only public ostium annotations cover 77 non-gated aortic scans, not CCTA, while CAT08 and ASOCA (32 and 40 CCTA scans) mark the ostia only implicitly, as centerline start points. This work enriches ImageCAS, the largest public dataset for coronary artery segmentation, with ostium annotations for its 1000 patients and centerline graphs rooted at these new ostia, making it, to the authors' knowledge, the largest public dataset for ostium localization and the only one with centerlines following the official ImageCAS masks and starting at annotated ostia. Three annotators marked each ostium in the first 500 volumes; in the next 500, the candidates of a model trained on the first batch were corrected (human-in-the-loop). Six 3D localization models, trained on ImageCAS, CAT08 and ASOCA, were benchmarked on 58 held-out volumes (50 ImageCAS, 4 CAT08, 4 ASOCA). SwinUNETR-V2 and nnResUNet localized all ostia without failure (>5 mm error), with median errors of 0.70-0.87 mm. Trained on CAT08 and ASOCA alone, SwinUNETR-V2 fails on 34% of right and 53% of left ostia, whereas adding 250 ImageCAS volumes removes all failures. The centerlines were extracted by a deterministic, quality-controlled minimal-path procedure; on ASOCA, they cover a median of 99.5% of the reference length, with a median per-patient mean distance of 0.22 mm between matched reference points and centerlines. Annotations, centerlines, code, and weights are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors add ostium annotations for all 1000 ImageCAS patients and centerline graphs rooted at those ostia, and benchmark six 3D localization models. SwinUNETR-V2 and nnResUNet localize all ostia without failure, with median errors of 0.70-0.87 mm.
AI.motivation: The only public ostium annotations cover 77 non-gated aortic scans, while CAT08 and ASOCA (CCTA scans) mark ostia only implicitly as centerline start points, so CCTA ostium localization lacked suitable public data.
AI.method: Three annotators marked ostia in the first 500 volumes; in the next 500, candidates from a model trained on the first batch were corrected by humans. Six 3D localization models trained on ImageCAS, CAT08 and ASOCA were benchmarked on 58 held-out volumes. Centerlines were extracted by a deterministic, quality-controlled minimal-path procedure.
AI.result: SwinUNETR-V2 and nnResUNet localized all ostia without failure (error above 5 mm counted as failure), with median errors of 0.70-0.87 mm. Trained on CAT08 and ASOCA alone, SwinUNETR-V2 fails on 34% of right and 53% of left ostia, whereas adding 250 ImageCAS volumes removes all failures. On ASOCA, centerlines cover a median of 99.5% of the reference length, with a median per-patient mean distance of 0.22 mm.
AI.conclusion: The enriched dataset is the largest public resource for ostium localization with centerlines starting at annotated ostia, and the results show that ImageCAS data is key to generalization.

title: Multiscale Closing Index (MCI) for measuring structural similarity between 2D point sets
summary: We introduce Multi-scale Closing Index (MCI), a new dissimilarity measure for evaluating the alignment of two 2D point sets. MCI is bounded between 0 and 1 and is based on multiscale mathematical morphology operations, with smaller values indicating greater structural agreement. The measure was motivated by the need to assess the quality of registration between point sets representing cell populations in biological images. To evaluate its behaviour under controlled conditions, we generated synthetic point clouds from Perlin-noise-based spatial structures, following established approaches for simulating biologically plausible spatial organization. We assessed MCI between those point clouds and different transformed versions, obtained by local perturbation, point removal, translation, rotation and addition of impulsive noise. Across these experiments, the dissimilarity MCI increased gradually and consistently with perturbation severity, while showing a clear discontinuity between clouds originating from the same underlying spatial structure and point clouds generated from different structures. We further compared MCI with commonly used point-set distances, including Hausdorff-based measures and Sliced Wasserstein distance. These experiments show the ability of MCI to capture structural agreement and quantify deviations between point sets, highlighting its potential as a complementary metric for evaluating two-dimensional point-set registration.

AI.tldr: The Multi-scale Closing Index (MCI) is a dissimilarity measure bounded between 0 and 1, based on multiscale mathematical morphology, for evaluating structural agreement between two 2D point sets. It increases gradually with perturbation severity and separates point clouds from the same spatial structure from those generated from different structures.
AI.motivation: Assessing the quality of registration between point sets representing cell populations in biological images motivated a dedicated measure.
AI.method: Synthetic point clouds were generated from Perlin-noise-based spatial structures and transformed by local perturbation, point removal, translation, rotation and impulsive noise. MCI was compared with Hausdorff-based measures and Sliced Wasserstein distance.
AI.result: MCI increases gradually and consistently with perturbation severity and shows a clear discontinuity between clouds from the same versus different underlying structures. The comparisons show its ability to capture structural agreement and quantify deviations between point sets.
AI.conclusion: MCI is a potential complementary metric for evaluating two-dimensional point-set registration.

title: AnimWeb-Bench: Benchmarking Animated Webpage Code Generation from Videos
summary: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at this https URL .

AI.tldr: AnimWeb-Bench is the first benchmark for generating animated webpage code from videos, with 124 real-world webpages and a two-dimensional evaluation protocol. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents, the authors find that reproducing webpage animations is substantially harder than reproducing static appearance.
AI.motivation: Existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions or isolated motion graphics, although the CSS animation property appears on over three-quarters of webpages, leaving full animated page reconstruction unexplored.
AI.method: 124 webpages across 7 application domains and 33 animation types, 91.9% combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the original static assets. Static Appearance Fidelity scores structure, text, color and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, and Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames on position, size, velocity and appearance.
AI.result: Reproducing animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve coding agents' reconstruction quality; rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark exposes a clear gap in reconstructing animated webpages from video, and its code and dataset are available.

title: Seeing What Matters: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation
comment: 22 pages (8 main + 14 supplement). Extended cross-domain evaluation and physical robot validation in progress
summary: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? Spatial-reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs something more specific: the ability to acquire the particular evidence that makes the current command executable. A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Matters, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Across three domains--coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance--the benchmark provides 860 frozen evaluation cases; expanding across methods, budgets, and inference repeats yields more than 115,000 evaluator episodes under two protocols: closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization. Each case pairs a set of candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, so the benchmark directly measures whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations its command actually needs. We also provide a diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, this pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; ablating the functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models, evaluated on the same cases, reach only 26-43%. Replacing the reference pipeline's coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores preserves 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling the visual scores collapses it to 15%/11%, confirming that the result depends on image content. These gaps suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated not by scene-level completeness, but by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires.

AI.tldr: Introduces Seeing What Matters, a benchmark of 860 frozen cases across three simulated tabletop domains that tests whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations a manipulation command needs. A diagnostic reference pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success, while seven vision-language models reach only 26-43%.
AI.motivation: Spatial-reasoning benchmarks test whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs the specific evidence that makes the current command executable, and a view that is informative for one task can be useless for another.
AI.method: Each case pairs candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills and hidden postconditions, so success measures whether the chosen views supply the evidence the command needs. The reference pipeline maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence; evaluation uses closed-loop actionability and same-object functional OOD protocols over more than 115,000 evaluator episodes.
AI.result: At primary budgets the reference pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success, and ablating its functional or command-binding components drops performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models reach 26-43%. Replacing coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores keeps 98.5%/98.9% success, while shuffling the visual scores drops it to 15%/11%.
AI.conclusion: Spatial belief for manipulation should be judged by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires rather than by scene-level completeness, and the reported gains depend on image content.

title: AdaptivePnP: Fast Auto-Tuned Plug-and-Play for Deconvolution
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Computational Imaging
summary: Plug-and-play (PnP) methods reconstruct images by alternating a data-fitting step with an image denoiser. Their performance depends on two parameters: the step size $\gamma$ and the measurement noise level $\sigma$. In practice, $\gamma$ is often tuned by grid search over validation images and must be retuned whenever the problem setting changes, and $\sigma$ is assumed known or estimated separately. We propose AdaptivePnP, a PnP framework that jointly estimates $\sigma$ and $\gamma$ at every iteration from the data-fitting residual. To do so, we apply the PnP virtual model to the data-fitting proximal map and show that the residual is zero-mean Gaussian with covariance parameterized by $\gamma$ and $\sigma$. However, when one parameter is much larger than the other, the residual carries little information about the smaller one and using the maximum likelihood (ML) estimator can degrade the PnP iterations. We therefore introduce the identifiable maximum likelihood (IML) estimator, which restricts the ML estimator to an identifiable window in which the normalized Cramér--Rao bound of every parameter is bounded by a user-specified tolerance. For the virtual model, this window is an interval of ratios $\rho = \gamma/\sigma$, so computing the IML estimate reduces to a one-dimensional search over $\rho$. We apply AdaptivePnP to two standard PnP methods, yielding algorithms that require neither a tuned $\gamma$ nor a known $\sigma$. On image deblurring and super-resolution, AdaptivePnP matches or outperforms PnP baselines tuned with the true $\sigma$. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes AdaptivePnP, a plug-and-play framework that jointly estimates the step size gamma and the noise level sigma at every iteration, so neither a tuned step size nor a known noise level is needed. It matches or outperforms PnP baselines tuned with the true sigma on deblurring and super-resolution.
AI.motivation: PnP performance depends on the step size and the noise level; the step size is usually grid-searched on validation images and retuned when the problem changes, and the noise level is assumed known or estimated separately.
AI.method: Using the PnP virtual model, the data-fitting residual is shown to be zero-mean Gaussian with covariance parameterized by gamma and sigma. Because the maximum likelihood estimator degrades when one parameter is much larger than the other, the authors introduce an identifiable maximum likelihood (IML) estimator restricted to a window of ratios rho = gamma/sigma where the normalized Cramer-Rao bound of each parameter stays below a user tolerance, which reduces estimation to a one-dimensional search. It is applied to two standard PnP methods.
AI.result: On image deblurring and super-resolution, AdaptivePnP matches or outperforms PnP baselines tuned with the true sigma.
AI.conclusion: Estimating both parameters from the data-fitting residual can remove the need for manual step-size tuning and a known noise level in PnP reconstruction, provided the estimator is restricted to an identifiable regime.

title: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level
comment: Appendices will be added in a future version
summary: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission measures three-dimensional forest structure with a LiDAR aboard the International Space Station. GEDI observations have geolocation errors of about 10 m, which cause misalignment with other remote sensing data and reduce the accuracy of downstream tasks. Matching GEDI ground elevations against high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) from airborne LiDAR is one way to correct these errors, but such DTMs exist in few regions. To widen this method's applicability, we super-resolved a more widely available low-resolution DTM and used it for the matching. Our question is whether a super-resolved DTM yields the same correction as a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR DTM and, if not, why. In steep forests of western Japan, we super-resolved an existing 10 m-resolution DTM to 1 m. Improving its accuracy required fusion with a global 30 m-resolution DTM from a different source. Using the resulting DTM, we corrected GEDI observation positions first by a single shift per ground track, then per observation. For most tracks, the shifts nearly matched those from the airborne LiDAR DTM, likely because DTM errors canceled out across many observations. Per-observation corrections, however, did not match. At a single observation, the error does not cancel out and is too large for the correction. This error likely originates mainly from the input DTM. Therefore, even without a 1 m-resolution DTM, a roughly 10 m-resolution DTM, fused with a global DTM and super-resolved to 1 m, should yield track-wise corrections nearly matching those from a 1 m-resolution DTM.

AI.tldr: Shows that a super-resolved 10 m DTM, fused with a global 30 m DTM, gives GEDI geolocation corrections that nearly match those from a 1 m airborne LiDAR DTM at the track level but not at the individual-observation level. The single-observation error is attributed mainly to the input DTM.
AI.motivation: GEDI geolocation errors of about 10 m misalign it with other remote sensing data, and the DTM-matching correction needs high-resolution airborne LiDAR DTMs, which exist in few regions.
AI.method: In steep forests of western Japan, an existing 10 m DTM was super-resolved to 1 m after fusion with a global 30 m DTM, then used to match GEDI ground elevations. Corrections were computed first as one shift per ground track and then per observation.
AI.result: For most tracks the per-track shifts nearly matched those from the airborne LiDAR DTM, likely because DTM errors cancel across many observations. Per-observation corrections did not match, because at a single observation the error does not cancel and is too large for the correction.
AI.conclusion: Track-wise GEDI corrections from a fused, super-resolved 10 m DTM should nearly match those from a 1 m DTM, but per-observation correction remains limited by input DTM error.

title: Drift-admissibility via Optimal Transport
comment: 10 pages; 3 figures; 2 tables
summary: We introduce structure-aware optimal transport diagnostics for assessing whether empirical time-series dynamics are compatible with a prescribed predictable-drift class. Our approach translates a pathwise property of stochastic processes into a finite-dimensional projection problem over empirical transition laws, encoding admissibility as row-wise moment constraints on local couplings and quantifying deviations via a Kullback--Leibler projection gap $G_{\lambda,k}$. This yields both a principled diagnostic and a scalable Bregman--Dykstra algorithm that retains the efficiency of Sinkhorn-type methods while incorporating structural constraints. Calibrated against a Brownian reference null, $G_{\lambda,k}$ separates process classes that are indistinguishable by second-order statistics alone---including fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes sharing identical Hurst indices---without asymptotic resampling or continuous-time recovery. This positions the method as a general tool for structure-aware model validation of sequential data.

AI.tldr: Introduces optimal-transport diagnostics that test whether empirical time-series dynamics are compatible with a prescribed predictable-drift class, using a Kullback-Leibler projection gap and a scalable Bregman-Dykstra algorithm. The gap separates processes that second-order statistics cannot distinguish, such as fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes with the same Hurst index.
AI.motivation: Whether a time series is compatible with a predictable-drift class is a pathwise property, and second-order statistics alone cannot assess it.
AI.method: The pathwise admissibility property is cast as a finite-dimensional projection over empirical transition laws, with row-wise moment constraints on local couplings, and deviations are quantified by the KL projection gap G_{lambda,k}. A Bregman-Dykstra algorithm computes it while keeping the efficiency of Sinkhorn-type methods, and the gap is calibrated against a Brownian reference null.
AI.result: The gap separates process classes that are indistinguishable by second-order statistics, including fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes sharing identical Hurst indices, without asymptotic resampling or continuous-time recovery.
AI.conclusion: The method is positioned as a general tool for structure-aware model validation of sequential data.

title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination
comment: NeurIPS 2026
summary: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.

AI.tldr: Presents ELPAC, a Bayesian framework that jointly infers latent disease stage, progression subtype and stage-varying multimodal coordination from partially observed cross-sectional aging-cohort data. On synthetic data and an ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort it recovers latent structure and gives calibrated prediction intervals.
AI.motivation: Aging cohorts combine imaging, plasma and cognitive measures, but most subjects give only a partially observed snapshot, and existing methods rarely address endpoint-anchored staging together with progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities.
AI.method: Subtype trajectories are integrated backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components with modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential-ordering priors. Residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis is factorized into sparse coordination axes, and scalable amortized variational inference enables cohort-scale posterior inference and single-pass deployment on new subjects.
AI.result: On synthetic data ELPAC shows accurate latent-structure recovery and well-calibrated prediction intervals. On the harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN cohort it yields biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.
AI.conclusion: Joint endpoint-anchored staging and residual multimodal coordination gives interpretable, subtype-specific accounts of how modalities interact across disease progression in aging cohorts.

title: pESTO: Iterative p-greedy kernel regression with risk-driven Early STOpping
summary: Kernel-based greedy algorithms select suitable approximation nodes by minimizing point-wise error indicators, such as the power function; in this context, they are usually referred to as p-greedy approaches. In the presence of noisy data, deterministic criteria may fail, as the discrepancy between the true solution and its estimate is influenced by both approximation error and noise amplification, and the balance between the two is unknown. This study explicitly separates these two contributions, which are governed by the power function and a Lebesgue-type term, respectively. These bounds motivate the use of the Stein's unbiased risk estimator (SURE) as a proxy of the mean squared error, which in turn provides a principled and computable stopping criterion for the number of nodes to select in the p-greedy procedure. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively balances deterministic accuracy and statistical noise contributions.

AI.tldr: Proposes pESTO, a p-greedy kernel regression method that uses Stein's unbiased risk estimator (SURE) as a computable stopping criterion for the number of nodes to select under noisy data. Numerical experiments show it balances deterministic accuracy and statistical noise.
AI.motivation: Deterministic p-greedy criteria may fail with noisy data, because the error mixes approximation error and noise amplification and the balance between the two is unknown.
AI.method: Bounds separate the two contributions, governed by the power function and a Lebesgue-type term respectively. SURE serves as a proxy for the mean squared error, giving a principled stopping rule for the p-greedy node selection.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that the approach effectively balances deterministic accuracy and statistical noise contributions. The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: SURE-based early stopping gives a principled, computable way to choose the number of approximation nodes in noisy kernel regression.

title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles
summary: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: Introduces BRINE, a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize noise variance under heteroskedasticity, restoring the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and amplifying weak signals without prior knowledge. Convergence is proven for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions.
AI.motivation: When noise variances differ across entries, the noise distorts the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals in low-rank approximation.
AI.method: BRINE iteratively rescales rows and columns, using the equalization of the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. A potential function characterizes the equalization at the population level and motivates an iterative minimization, and the updates are estimated directly from noisy data with probabilistic error bounds on the scaling factors.
AI.result: The iterations converge to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate its effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Blind rescaling can equalize heteroskedastic noise and restore the expected noise spectrum, improving low-rank inference on large noisy data matrices.

title: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction
summary: Reward models used for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are commonly selected using held-out data. When sample size and context dimension grow proportionally, the difference in test risk between models fitted on the full sample and on a fixed fraction of it need not vanish. Held-out evaluation can therefore consistently estimate the test risk of the model trained on the smaller sample, but because the relative ranking of candidate reward models can change after full-data refitting, held-out selection can be suboptimal. We develop an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates the full-data reward model's out-of-sample risk under the target policy using only its training observations. This enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory without sample splitting. For neural networks with fixed depth and hidden width under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies, and known context-independent logging, we prove uniform consistency of our criterion over a fixed finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. The same correction yields a doubly robust estimator that consistently estimates the true policy value without sample splitting, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, and improved reward-model selection relative to held-out baselines. Empirically, our correction also reduces the root mean squared error of doubly robust value estimates computed from the same data used to fit and select the reward models.

AI.tldr: Develops an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates a full-data reward model's out-of-sample risk from its training observations alone, enabling early stopping without sample splitting. It also yields a doubly robust off-policy evaluation estimator that is consistent without sample splitting.
AI.motivation: Held-out selection of reward models estimates the risk of the smaller-sample model, and the ranking of candidates can change after full-data refitting, so held-out selection can be suboptimal when sample size and context dimension grow proportionally.
AI.method: An Onsager correction, weighted by the target policy, is applied to the training observations to estimate the full-data model's risk, which enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory. The theory covers fixed-depth, fixed-width neural networks under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies and known context-independent logging.
AI.result: The authors prove uniform consistency of the criterion over a finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, improved reward-model selection over held-out baselines, and reduced RMSE of doubly robust value estimates.
AI.conclusion: The Onsager correction removes the need for sample splitting in both reward-model selection and doubly robust policy value estimation, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish.

title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology
comment: This is the published version of the article. Published in *International Journal of Topology*, MDPI, DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijt3040025. Link to the official version: this https URL
summary: In the lower-star filtration (LSF), simplices are assigned filtration values according to the maximum-vertex rule, with each simplex entering the filtration when its highest-valued vertex appears. A limitation of this construction is that some higher-dimensional simplices may enter simultaneously with their boundary faces, causing certain topological features to be filled immediately upon formation and thus not appear in the resulting persistence diagram. To address this limitation, we propose three alternative filtration methods: the \(\varepsilon\)-lower-star filtration (ELSF), the \(L_p\) filtration (LpF), and the softmax filtration (SMF). {ELSF introduces a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule,} allowing higher-dimensional simplices to enter the filtration after their boundary faces, whereas {LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather} than solely on their maximum. By modifying how filtration values are assigned, these methods allow simplices to enter the filtration more progressively, so that topological features such as loops and voids may persist over longer filtration intervals rather than being filled immediately. Consequently, the resulting persistence diagrams may include persistence features that are not observed under LSF, potentially providing useful information for distinguishing data populations. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed filtration methods are computationally efficient and can provide greater sensitivity to structural differences in the data than LSF.

AI.tldr: Proposes three alternative filtration methods for persistent homology, the epsilon-lower-star filtration, the Lp filtration and the softmax filtration, which let higher-dimensional simplices enter after their faces so that loops and voids can persist. Experiments show computational efficiency and greater sensitivity to structural differences than the lower-star filtration.
AI.motivation: In the lower-star filtration some higher-dimensional simplices enter together with their boundary faces, so the features they would create are filled immediately and never appear in the persistence diagram.
AI.method: ELSF adds a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule, while LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather than only the maximum.
AI.result: The alternative filtrations are computationally efficient on simulated and real-world datasets, can yield persistence features not observed under the lower-star filtration, and are more sensitive to structural differences in the data.
AI.conclusion: Changing how filtration values are assigned can expose topological information the lower-star filtration misses, which may help distinguish data populations.

title: Geometry-Aware Score-Repellent Monte Carlo
comment: To appear at NeurIPS 2026
summary: The recently proposed Score-Repellent Monte Carlo (SRMC) method improves MCMC sampling by tilting the target density $\pi$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the factor $\exp(-\alpha\,\theta_n^\top s(x))$, where the score function $s(x) = \nabla_x \log \pi(x)$, and $\theta_n$ is the score average from past samples. However, a single scalar repellence strength $\alpha\ge0$ cannot handle both the steep and the flat directions in anisotropic energy landscapes at once. We introduce \emph{Geometry-Aware SRMC} (GA-SRMC), which generalizes the Euclidean alignment to $\theta^\top M s(x)$ for any symmetric positive-definite matrix $M$. A stochastic-approximation central limit theorem under a trace constraint on $M$ identifies the trace-normalized inverse Fisher $M_{\rm opt}\propto S^{-1}$ as the unique minimizer of the worst-direction covariance bound, elevating the Fisher information $S=\text{Cov}_\pi(s,s)$ from a proposal-side preconditioner (e.g., FisherMALA, natural gradient) to the bound-optimal repulsion-side matrix, with a single online estimate $\widehat S_n$ serving both roles at no additional computational cost. The full-Fisher online metric $M_n$ converges almost surely to $M_{\rm opt}$ and satisfies a CLT, providing a theoretical guarantee for the online implementation of the GA-SRMC framework. On an $8$-target simulation spanning the condition number $\kappa\in[1.3,100]$ and dimension $d\in[2,785]$, GA-SRMC dominates SRMC in ESS by $\boldsymbol{4.3\times}$ on anisotropic Gaussian ($\kappa=100$) and $\boldsymbol{6.8\times}$ on MNIST under the MALA baseline, by $\boldsymbol{16\text{--}32\%}$ on three well-conditioned logistic-regression posteriors, and by up to $\boldsymbol{+48\%}$ under FisherMALA; gains peak on the most anisotropic targets, and posterior-mean MSE is lower than with SRMC in all $16$ full-Fisher implementations.

AI.tldr: Introduces Geometry-Aware SRMC, which replaces the scalar repellence strength of Score-Repellent Monte Carlo with a symmetric positive-definite matrix M, and identifies the trace-normalized inverse Fisher information as the bound-optimal choice. On an 8-target benchmark it gives effective-sample-size gains that peak on anisotropic targets.
AI.motivation: A single scalar repellence strength cannot handle the steep and flat directions of an anisotropic energy landscape at once.
AI.method: The Euclidean alignment term is generalized to theta^T M s(x). A stochastic-approximation central limit theorem under a trace constraint on M identifies M_opt proportional to S^{-1}, where S = Cov_pi(s,s) is the Fisher information, and a single online estimate of S serves both as the repulsion-side matrix and as the proposal-side preconditioner.
AI.result: The online metric converges almost surely to M_opt and satisfies a CLT. ESS improves 4.3x on an anisotropic Gaussian with condition number 100 and 6.8x on MNIST under MALA, by 16-32% on three well-conditioned logistic-regression posteriors, and by up to 48% under FisherMALA. Posterior-mean MSE is lower than with SRMC in all 16 full-Fisher implementations.
AI.conclusion: Using the Fisher information as the repulsion-side matrix is a theoretically justified improvement over SRMC at no extra computational cost, with the largest gains on the most anisotropic targets.

title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs
comment: 43 pages, 4 figures
summary: We study kernel-based learning of analytic operators from finite samples, with a focus on how the regularity of the target should determine the choice of the kernel. We establish embeddings of analytic operators into vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive finite-sample, high-probability guarantees that quantify the uncertainty due to random sampling: in the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. We apply the theory to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE, where the training data are themselves finite-element approximations, and obtain bounds that separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size. The results are illustrated numerically.

AI.tldr: Embeds analytic operators into vector-valued RKHSs and gives finite-sample, high-probability guarantees for kernel-based operator learning. Analytic kernels give rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, Sobolev-type kernels give polynomial rates, and the theory is applied to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE.
AI.motivation: The regularity of the target should determine the choice of kernel, and the uncertainty due to random sampling must be quantified for operator learning.
AI.method: Analytic operators are embedded into vector-valued RKHSs and finite-sample bounds are derived. For the parametric elliptic PDE the training data are finite-element approximations, and the bounds separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size.
AI.result: In the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. The results are illustrated numerically.
AI.conclusion: Matching the kernel to the target's regularity gives much faster sample-complexity rates, and the mesh size should scale with the sample size in PDE operator learning.

title: Where Should Learning Live? Regret Analysis for Text, Parameter, and Joint Adaptation
summary: Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt--parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate's own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.

AI.tldr: Analyzes repeated selection among preconstructed prompts and parameter adapters during deployment, splitting excess loss into selection regret, a family-restriction gap and the effect of the deployment history. Under stated assumptions, limiting the number of switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family.
AI.motivation: Language-model systems choose prompts and adapters repeatedly, and earlier choices change the context that later choices inherit, so a standard regret comparison against the best fixed configuration does not directly apply.
AI.method: Candidates are evaluated on the history each would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from switching effects. The bounds assume loss functions fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affecting loss for a bounded number of rounds, and each candidate's own-history loss being revealed; the costs of independent probing and deployment-only feedback are also quantified.
AI.result: Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can lower or raise deployed loss depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection but produces more failures, because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.
AI.conclusion: Lower regret within a family does not imply better deployed performance, since family restriction and deployment history can dominate, so the whole excess-loss decomposition should guide where learning is placed.

title: MEDALLION: Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON
summary: Dimensionality reduction is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data and guide scientific discovery, yet interpreting which original features contribute to low-dimensional representations remains challenging, particularly for black-box methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. We introduce \textbf{MEDALLION} (Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON), a novel framework for interpreting low-dimensional embeddings through knowledge distillation and neural feature attribution. MEDALLION distills any given embedding with a neural encoder which we explain via a broad range of existing neural feature attribution methods. Through experiments on MNIST and applications in single-cell transcriptomics, we show MEDALLION provides informative feature attributions that cast additional insights into the underlying embedding and compare its performance with existing interpretability approaches.

AI.tldr: Presents MEDALLION, a framework that interprets low-dimensional embeddings such as t-SNE and UMAP by distilling any given embedding into a neural encoder and applying neural feature attribution methods to that encoder. It is demonstrated on MNIST and on single-cell transcriptomics.
AI.motivation: Dimensionality reduction is widely used for visualization, but it is hard to tell which original features contribute to black-box embeddings such as t-SNE and UMAP.
AI.method: MEDALLION distills a given embedding with a neural encoder and then explains the encoder with a broad range of existing neural feature attribution methods.
AI.result: Experiments on MNIST and single-cell transcriptomics give informative feature attributions that add insight into the underlying embedding, and the performance is compared with existing interpretability approaches. The abstract reports no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Distillation followed by attribution offers a way to interpret arbitrary low-dimensional embeddings in terms of the original features.

title: Reweighting for Transfer Classification: Exact Risk Conversion and Minimax Adaptation
comment: 87 pages, 5 figures. Main text (32 pages) followed by the Supplementary Material
summary: A source can make a training mixture easier to learn while making its accuracy less valuable for the target. We study how the training problem a source creates and the finite-sample error of learning it jointly determine target-risk guarantees under reweighting. For binary classification, for each pair of laws and each positive target weight, we derive the sharpest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by mixture excess alone, uniformly over clipped predictors. This exact conversion curve is determined by density-weighted local votes. A two-sample oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines supplies the mixture excess, and the composition becomes explicit for Gaussian kernels. On a tilted-boundary class, we establish the all-procedure minimax classification rate $[n+s_+^2/(m^{-1}+\tau^2)]^{-1}$ in the transferable strength $s_+$ and the tilt $\tau$, separating source sampling uncertainty ($m^{-1}$) from relation uncertainty ($\tau^2$). A target-checked Gaussian-SVM selector adapts to unknown $s_+$ and $\tau$ up to a logarithmic factor for fixed dimension, and retains the target-only rate up to the same factor against arbitrary independent sources under the stated target model. On a separate smooth opposition class, the minimax risk within the family of exact Gaussian SVMs fitted to the original labels with nonnegative weights is exponentially larger than the unrestricted minimax risk whenever the target sample is at most half the source sample, despite arbitrary data-dependent weighting and tuning. The value of a source thus depends on the training problem it creates, on what accuracy there means for the target, and on whether the permitted use of the source can implement the needed correction.

AI.tldr: Derives the sharpest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by source mixture excess under reweighting for binary classification, and establishes an all-procedure minimax classification rate with a target-checked Gaussian-SVM selector that adapts up to a logarithmic factor. It also shows that exact Gaussian SVMs with nonnegative weights can be exponentially worse than the unrestricted minimax risk on a smooth opposition class.
AI.motivation: A source can make the training problem easier while making its accuracy less valuable for the target, so the value of a source depends on the training problem it creates and on what accuracy means for the target.
AI.method: For each pair of laws and each positive target weight, the exact conversion curve from mixture excess to target excess hinge risk is determined by density-weighted local votes. A two-sample oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines supplies the mixture excess, and the composition is made explicit for Gaussian kernels.
AI.result: On a tilted-boundary class the minimax rate is [n + s_+^2/(m^{-1}+tau^2)]^{-1}, separating source sampling uncertainty (m^{-1}) from relation uncertainty (tau^2). The selector adapts to unknown s_+ and tau up to a logarithmic factor in fixed dimension, and on a smooth opposition class the minimax risk within the family of exact Gaussian SVMs with nonnegative weights is exponentially larger than the unrestricted minimax risk when the target sample is at most half the source sample.
AI.conclusion: The usefulness of a source depends on the training problem it creates, on what accuracy means for the target, and on whether permitted weighting can implement the needed correction.

title: Enforcing Symmetries on Pre-trained ML Models for Physics
comment: 32 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables
summary: Post-hoc group averaging (or test-time augmentation) is a simple way to impose symmetry on a trained predictor without changing its architecture or retraining it. For finite and compact groups, averaging over a normalized Haar measure on the group gives the Reynolds operator: a canonical projection onto invariant or equivariant predictors with known non-increasing risk guarantees under certain assumptions. This paper provides numerical experiments on physics emulation models that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in this setting. We then extend this framework to non-compact group symmetries. For non-compact groups, the Haar measure cannot be normalized, so group averaging cannot be defined in the same way. We replace it with three alternatives: the Weyl unitary trick (which requires complexifying the space and extending the predictor), a data-dependent orthogonal projection (which involves a non-trivial optimization on the space of invariant or equivariant functions), and a frame averaging approach (which involves mapping each point to a set of orbit representatives). We illustrate the constructions theoretically and empirically on the unit-rescaling group and the Lorentz group. Our results show that in the non-compact case, the Weyl trick and frame averaging do not provide a consistent improvement over the baseline, except where the test data is out-of-distribution (an orders-of-magnitude improvement in this case) and, for the Weyl trick, in low-data regimes. The orthogonal projection can provide improvements in-distribution and out-of-distribution. We also observe that models trained directly on invariant features matched or beat the projection of an unconstrained one. We conclude that post-hoc symmetrization extends to non-compact groups, but it does not consistently outperform training a symmetric model.

AI.tldr: Extends post-hoc group averaging to non-compact symmetry groups using three alternatives, the Weyl unitary trick, a data-dependent orthogonal projection and frame averaging, and finds that these do not consistently beat the baseline except out-of-distribution and in some low-data cases. Post-hoc symmetrization therefore does not consistently outperform training a symmetric model.
AI.motivation: Group averaging via the Reynolds operator needs a normalizable Haar measure, which non-compact groups lack, so symmetry cannot be imposed post hoc in the same way.
AI.method: The three replacements are the Weyl unitary trick, which complexifies the space and extends the predictor; a data-dependent orthogonal projection onto invariant or equivariant functions; and frame averaging over orbit representatives. They are illustrated on the unit-rescaling and Lorentz groups, and numerical experiments on physics emulation models demonstrate the compact-group approach.
AI.result: For non-compact groups the Weyl trick and frame averaging give no consistent improvement over the baseline, except on out-of-distribution test data (an orders-of-magnitude improvement) and, for the Weyl trick, in low-data regimes. The orthogonal projection improves both in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance, and models trained directly on invariant features matched or beat the projection of an unconstrained model.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc symmetrization extends to non-compact groups, but it does not consistently outperform directly training a symmetric model.

title: Calibrating your confidence requires thinking of all the ways you could be wrong
comment: PhD Thesis, Technical University of Denmark (DTU), 2026
summary: A primary limitation of modern deep learning is the miscalibration of model confidence; traditional architectures fundamentally lack a mechanism to quantify their own uncertainty. Larger models and larger datasets mitigate this issue, but they do not resolve the underlying structural deficiency. Bayesian methods offer a principled uncertainty-aware learning framework through stochastic parameters. Yet, despite the established benefits, the inherent computational overhead often compromises either scalability or quality. This trade-off currently prevents the widespread adoption of Bayesian methods. This Thesis bridges the gap between high-quality and low-complexity by introducing a novel distribution on parameter space: a degenerate Gaussian whose covariance is a projection matrix aligned with the null space of the Fisher information matrix. We demonstrate the scalability of this Bayesian posterior through two numerically efficient algorithms: one for posterior sampling and another for the direct computation of predictive confidence. Empirically, we show State-Of-The-Art confidence calibration and out-of-distribution detection for large models. We provide theoretical grounding for this approach. We study the degeneracies inherent in Amari's information geometry and highlight its most relevant component: the split of parameter's perturbations into two orthogonal subspaces. From this perspective, our posterior naturally emerges as the simplest choice that captures this split, assigning unitary variance to one subspace and zero variance to the other. Moreover, through the tools of differential geometry, we utilize this split to identify and rectify a critical misalignment issue of the non-linearized Laplace Approximation. Finally, with a focus on PAC-Bayes generalization bounds, we pave the way for a deeper understanding of the learning capabilities of overparametrized models.

AI.tldr: Presents a thesis proposing a degenerate Gaussian posterior whose covariance is a projection onto the null space of the Fisher information matrix, with a sampling algorithm and a direct predictive-confidence algorithm. It reports state-of-the-art confidence calibration and out-of-distribution detection for large models.
AI.motivation: Modern deep networks are miscalibrated and lack a structural mechanism for quantifying their uncertainty, while Bayesian methods either scale poorly or give limited quality.
AI.method: The posterior assigns unit variance to one of two orthogonal subspaces of parameter perturbations, the one identified through the information-geometry split in Amari's framework, and zero variance to the other. Differential geometry is used to identify and rectify a misalignment in the non-linearized Laplace approximation, and PAC-Bayes generalization bounds are the focus of the broader analysis.
AI.result: The abstract reports state-of-the-art confidence calibration and out-of-distribution detection for large models, without specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The degenerate-Gaussian posterior offers a scalable, principled route to calibrated confidence, and the analysis supports a deeper understanding of the learning capabilities of overparametrized models.

title: k-Volume: a Unified Active Learning Strategy
summary: In the classification context where revealing the label of a sample is costly, we propose a new Active Learning (AL) strategy named k-Volume (kVol). It randomly selects a sample to be labeled according to the volume of the smallest ball containing its k nearest neighbors. kVol is highly versatile: it can be applied either in the input space or in the output space, and it enjoys the desirable properties of the three main families of AL strategies: density, diversity, and (when performed in the output space) uncertainty. From a theoretical perspective, we establish that kVol is asymptotically equivalent to uniform sampling over the support of the (input or output) data distribution. Based on experiments on various synthetic and real-life tabular datasets and images, we observe that kVol is surprisingly stable: whatever the classifier or the experimental setup, it still lies among the best AL strategies unlike other competitors that fail dramatically. In particular, kVol outperforms state-of-the-art competitors such as CoreSet, TypiClust or Uncertainty on several real-life datasets, at a low computational cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes k-Volume, an active-learning strategy that randomly selects samples according to the volume of the smallest ball containing their k nearest neighbours, and shows it is asymptotically equivalent to uniform sampling over the data support. It stays among the best strategies across classifiers and setups and outperforms CoreSet, TypiClust and Uncertainty on several real datasets.
AI.motivation: When labels are costly, existing active-learning strategies come from density, diversity or uncertainty families, and some of them fail dramatically depending on the classifier or setup.
AI.method: kVol selects a sample at random according to the volume of the smallest ball containing its k nearest neighbours. It can be applied in the input space or the output space, and in the output space it also captures uncertainty.
AI.result: kVol is stable across classifiers and experimental setups, lies among the best strategies, and outperforms CoreSet, TypiClust and Uncertainty on several real-life datasets at low computational cost.
AI.conclusion: kVol is a versatile, theoretically grounded strategy that combines density, diversity and uncertainty behaviour while staying robust across settings.

title: Marginal-Nonuniform Multiclass Learning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: We study the problem of multiclass classification within the framework of marginal-nonuniform learning, where the constants in the learning rate may depend on the unknown marginal distribution generating the unlabeled data, but not on the target concept. This notion naturally lies between classical PAC learning, where the constants are independent of both the marginal distribution and the target concept, and more recent universal learning, where the constants may depend on both. We give a complete characterization of the optimal marginal-nonuniform learning rates, establishing a fundamental trichotomy: exponential, linear, and arbitrarily slow rates. This characterization is witnessed by a new combinatorial dimension, termed the uncentered DS-eluder dimension. A key ingredient in the upper-bound proofs is a set of new distributional exhaustion lemmas that exploit the sequential nature of this dimension and may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: Characterizes the optimal rates of marginal-nonuniform multiclass learning, where the constants may depend on the unlabeled marginal but not on the target concept, and establishes a trichotomy of exponential, linear and arbitrarily slow rates. The characterization is witnessed by a new combinatorial dimension, the uncentered DS-eluder dimension.
AI.motivation: This setting lies between classical PAC learning, whose constants are independent of both marginal and target, and universal learning, whose constants may depend on both, and its optimal rates were not previously characterized.
AI.method: The rates are characterized through the new uncentered DS-eluder dimension, and the upper-bound proofs rely on new distributional exhaustion lemmas that exploit the sequential nature of this dimension.
AI.result: The paper gives a complete characterization with a trichotomy of exponential, linear and arbitrarily slow rates. The abstract reports no numbers.
AI.conclusion: The optimal rate in this setting is fully determined by the new dimension, and the exhaustion lemmas may be of independent interest.

title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables
summary: This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.

AI.tldr: Develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions, normalizing non-conformity scores with an auxiliary PCE trained on log-transformed leave-one-out residuals. For ordinary-least-squares PCEs the coverage guarantee carries over, and all required quantities are derived in closed form from a single model fit.
AI.motivation: Standard conformal intervals do not adapt locally, so they are statistically inefficient where prediction uncertainty varies across the input space, especially in high-uncertainty regions.
AI.method: The auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals so that the jackknife+ guarantee carries over to the adaptive intervals. For sparse PCEs, which require multiple fits, a heuristic simplification limits the computational overhead at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee.
AI.result: On an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset, the method attains the target coverage while giving intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty and are more statistically efficient, especially in high-uncertainty regions where non-adaptive methods degrade substantially.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive jackknife+ intervals give efficient, locally adaptive coverage for OLS-fitted polynomial chaos expansions without retraining, with a heuristic extension for sparse expansions.

title: Online Causal Configuration for Networked Systems via Doubly Robust Steady-State Learning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Measurement exploration reveals how interacting local controllers behave but can alter the steady-state regime a network operator seeks to optimize. Exploratory rewards may therefore fail to identify a configuration's no-exploration value: under full exploration, identical logged distributions can conceal different target values. Identification requires accounting for both action-law mismatch and shifts in the steady-state context distribution. We introduce CAUSAL-UCB, which selects configurations using optimistic bounds on target causal values. Its interference-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator produces predecision certificates separating statistical variation from calibrated identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. For any finite horizon and predetermined schedule of measurement-exploration rates $\{\eta_t\}$, we prove lower bounds of $\Omega((1+\sum_t\eta_t)^{-1/2})$ on minimax inference error and $\Omega(\sum_t\eta_t)$ on measurement-induced deployment loss in a stationary, potentially slow-mixing family. We bound regret under valid certificates and selected-information growth, and establish an anytime finite-sample certificate with a shared radius for estimation, selection, and reporting in a restricted known-local-interference model. In a high-mismatch benchmark with 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds, CAUSAL-UCB attains target regret of $1.732$ versus $6.326$ for certified IPS-UCB, with deployment gaps of $30.607$ and $23.217$, respectively. Independent-audit coverage tests and trace-driven semi-synthetic studies further assess certificate coverage and deployment trade-offs.

AI.tldr: Introduces CAUSAL-UCB, which selects network configurations using optimistic bounds on target causal values from an interference-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator. On a high-mismatch benchmark with 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds it attains target regret of 1.732, versus 6.326 for certified IPS-UCB.
AI.motivation: Measurement exploration alters the steady-state regime that the operator wants to optimize, so exploratory rewards can misidentify a configuration's no-exploration value because of action-law mismatch and shifts in the steady-state context distribution.
AI.method: The evaluator produces predecision certificates that separate statistical variation from calibrated identification, transport and temporal-dependence errors. Lower bounds of Omega((1+sum_t eta_t)^{-1/2}) on minimax inference error and Omega(sum_t eta_t) on measurement-induced deployment loss are proved for a given measurement-exploration schedule, and an anytime finite-sample certificate is established in a restricted known-local-interference model.
AI.result: CAUSAL-UCB attains target regret of 1.732 versus 6.326 for certified IPS-UCB in the high-mismatch benchmark, with deployment gaps of 30.607 for CAUSAL-UCB and 23.217 for IPS-UCB. Independent-audit coverage tests and trace-driven semi-synthetic studies further assess certificate coverage and deployment trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for action-law mismatch and steady-state shift yields lower regret and valid certificates, but exploration imposes a deployment cost that the bounds make explicit.

title: A Generalized Bayesian Approach to Clustering with Dimension Reduction
summary: Generalized Bayes product partition models provide a probabilistic counterpart to loss-based clustering. They update a prior over partitions through an exponentiated clustering loss rather than a likelihood, so allocation uncertainty can be quantified without a full generative model for the data. However, their performance depends on the space in which the loss is evaluated. For high-dimensional observations, a squared Euclidean loss on the raw features can be dominated by irrelevant coordinates or fail to reflect cluster structure lying near a nonlinear low-dimensional manifold. We propose an extension in which an autoencoder and the partition are learned together, so that the space in which the clustering loss is evaluated is shaped by the clustering itself. Our generalized posterior combines a reconstruction loss, which keeps the low-dimensional representation faithful to the observed data, with a within-cluster sum of squares in the latent representation, which encourages cluster separation. Posterior computation alternates between Gibbs sampling over partitions and gradient-based updates of the autoencoder network, with the learning rate estimated jointly. We illustrate the approach through simulation studies and applications to four benchmark datasets.
