AI.tldr: Proposes a generalized Bayes clustering method in which an autoencoder and the partition are learned jointly, so the clustering loss is evaluated in a latent space shaped by the clustering itself. The method is illustrated with simulations and four benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Generalized Bayes product partition models quantify allocation uncertainty through an exponentiated clustering loss, but their performance depends on the space where the loss is computed. A squared Euclidean loss on raw high-dimensional features can be dominated by irrelevant coordinates or fail to capture cluster structure near a nonlinear low-dimensional manifold.
AI.method: The generalized posterior combines a reconstruction loss that keeps the low-dimensional representation faithful to the data with a within-cluster sum of squares in the latent space that encourages cluster separation. Posterior computation alternates Gibbs sampling over partitions with gradient-based updates of the autoencoder network, and the learning rate is estimated jointly.
AI.result: The abstract reports simulation studies and applications to four benchmark datasets but does not state specific numbers or baseline comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Learning the autoencoder and the partition together lets the clustering loss operate in a representation shaped by clustering, extending generalized Bayes clustering to high-dimensional observations.

title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
comment: 32 pages
summary: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $\rho>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $\rho$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

AI.tldr: Gives quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for rho-decodable POMDPs and shows that decodability is a weaker, easy-to-check assumption that includes l1- and l2-observable POMDPs.
AI.motivation: Exact and approximate planning in finite-horizon POMDPs are computationally hard in general. Prior quasipolynomial-time results required l1-observability, whose optimal constant is NP-hard to compute in the worst case.
AI.method: For each fixed rho > 0, the authors give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for rho-decodable POMDPs. They show that decodability is implied by l1- and l2-observability, is strictly weaker than observability, and has an optimal constant computable in polynomial time.
AI.result: Decodability is implied by both l1- and l2-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. The optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal l1-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. The fast filter-forgetting guarantee does not extend directly from l1- to constant l2-observability.
AI.conclusion: Decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

title: FasterRW: An Efficient Prior-Assisted Random Walk Solver for Thermal Analysis
summary: Thermal simulation is becoming increasingly critical in modern IC design and manufacturing. Feynman--Kac random walk methods can estimate localized temperatures without solving the global field, but in practical settings without Dirichlet boundaries they require very long paths to control the truncation residual. This paper presents FasterRW, a continuation-value framework for accelerating Feynman--Kac thermal random walks. We prove a stopping-time residual identity showing that the expected tail after truncation equals the current attenuation weight multiplied by the temperature at the stopping location. This identity enables a prior-corrected single-point estimator: a cheap, noisy prior replaces the unknown continuation value, making the truncation bias scale with prior error rather than absolute temperature and yielding an error-controlled threshold-selection rule. For multi-point queries, FasterRW further converts cross-query pass-through tails into pseudo-samples and refines the resulting observations in prior-error coordinates through kriging. Compared with prior state-of-the-art methods, FasterRW achieves up to $28\times$ acceleration while maintaining accuracy. Our code is open-sourced at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents FasterRW, a prior-assisted random walk solver for Feynman-Kac thermal simulation that uses a cheap prior to reduce truncation bias, reporting up to 28 times acceleration over prior state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Feynman-Kac random walks estimate localized temperatures without solving the global field, but without Dirichlet boundaries they require very long paths to control the truncation residual.
AI.method: A continuation-value framework built on a proven stopping-time residual identity. A cheap, noisy prior replaces the unknown continuation value in a prior-corrected single-point estimator with an error-controlled threshold-selection rule. For multi-point queries, cross-query pass-through tails become pseudo-samples that are refined by kriging in prior-error coordinates.
AI.result: FasterRW achieves up to 28 times acceleration relative to prior state-of-the-art methods while maintaining accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Correcting truncation bias with a prior makes Feynman-Kac thermal random walks substantially faster for IC thermal analysis. The code is open-sourced.

title: Embedding Consistent Recurrent Neural Networks in Finite Element Simulations for Path-Dependent Damage Prediction
comment: Journal paper. 22 pages, 16 figures
summary: Capturing sheet-metal localisation physics with a trained surrogate inside a finite element (FEM) solver requires the surrogate to deliver consistent predictions irrespective of the solver's strain-increment count, which is difficult to control in non-linear explicit codes. We address this by re-implementing a trained recurrent neural network (RNN) damage criterion in Fortran and embed it as a live, increment-by-increment fracture criterion inside an Abaqus/Explicit user material subroutine (VUMAT), advancing the network state alongside the solver. Two architectures are compared: a SimpleRNN and the proposed Consistent RNN (ConsRNN), whose transition function is designed so that predictions converge as the strain path is refined rather than drifting with the increment count. Both are trained on bilinear strain paths and evaluated under varying temporal discretisations and nonlinear histories. SimpleRNN predictions drift as the increment count increases, which disqualifies it for embedding; ConsRNN converges under refinement, at a substantial fixed-resolution accuracy cost relative to SimpleRNN on multilinear paths. Deployed at structural scale, the embedded ConsRNN surrogate governs element deletion in a clamped steel plate and reaches the same peak force and peak displacement as an established two-parameter fracture criterion. This pre-peak agreement is expected by construction, since no element is deleted before the peak and the two runs therefore share an identical constitutive path; the responses diverge only on the post-peak softening branch. The results establish discretisation consistency as the decisive property for embedding recurrent surrogates in explicit FEM solvers, and report the first embedding of a customised, non-standard-transition recurrent cell at structural scale.

AI.tldr: Embeds a trained recurrent neural network damage criterion in an Abaqus/Explicit VUMAT and proposes a Consistent RNN whose predictions converge under strain-path refinement, unlike a SimpleRNN.
AI.motivation: A surrogate inside an explicit FEM solver must give predictions independent of the solver's strain-increment count, which is hard to control in nonlinear explicit codes. The SimpleRNN predictions drift as the increment count grows.
AI.method: The trained RNN is reimplemented in Fortran and advanced increment by increment inside a VUMAT. The proposed ConsRNN has a transition function designed so that predictions converge as the strain path is refined. Both architectures are trained on bilinear strain paths and tested under varying temporal discretisations and nonlinear histories.
AI.result: SimpleRNN drifts with the increment count, which disqualifies it for embedding. ConsRNN converges under refinement, at a substantial fixed-resolution accuracy cost relative to SimpleRNN on multilinear paths. In a clamped steel plate at structural scale, the embedded ConsRNN governs element deletion and reaches the same peak force and peak displacement as an established two-parameter fracture criterion; the runs diverge only on the post-peak softening branch.
AI.conclusion: Discretisation consistency is the decisive property for embedding recurrent surrogates in explicit FEM solvers, and the work reports the first embedding of a customised, non-standard-transition recurrent cell at structural scale.

title: Generative Reconstruction of Full-Field Sensor States for Safety-Critical Digital Twins
comment: 27 pages, 8 figures, and 7 tables
summary: Accurate reconstruction of incomplete sensor fields is critical for state awareness in safety-critical digital twins (DTs). Thermocouples in high-temperature and radiation environments may drift, fail, or become intermittently unavailable, causing partial observability. This study develops a sparse-sensor reconstruction framework for Oregon State University's High Temperature Test Facility (HTTF) and evaluates six methods under intra- and inter-experiment protocols: three conditional generative models (i.e., a diffusion model [DM], variational autoencoder [VAE], and generative adversarial network [GAN]), two deterministic recurrent neural-network models, and ridge regression. For intra-experiment reconstruction within the PG{-}29 depressurized conduction cooldown (DCC) test, the models combine graph-based spatial encoding with gated recurrent units. The graph neural network (GNN)--gated recurrent unit (GRU) VAE achieves the lowest error, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of $11.73,^\circ$C, a root mean square error (RMSE) of $20.54,^\circ$C, and an $R^2$ of 0.98. The deterministic GNN--GRU and plain GRU obtain RMSE values of $25.26,^\circ$C and $35.22,^\circ$C, respectively, demonstrating the benefit of spatial modeling. All three generative models reduce RMSE by more than half compared with ridge regression. The DM maintains an $R^2$ of 0.94 when known sensors decrease from 91 to 45. For inter-experiment reconstruction, models trained on PG{-}27 pressurized conduction cooldown (PCC) are evaluated on PG{-}29 using section-context conditioning. The section-context DM achieves the best transfer performance, with an RMSE of $42.84,^\circ$C and an $R^2$ of 0.91. These results demonstrate the value of spatiotemporal generative modeling for missing-sensor reconstruction in safety-critical DT applications.

AI.tldr: Develops a sparse-sensor reconstruction framework for a high-temperature test facility digital twin, finding that a GNN-GRU VAE gives the lowest error among six methods and a section-context diffusion model transfers best between experiments.
AI.motivation: Thermocouples in high-temperature and radiation environments may drift, fail or become intermittently unavailable, causing partial observability in safety-critical digital twins.
AI.method: Six methods are compared under intra- and inter-experiment protocols: three conditional generative models (diffusion model, VAE and GAN), two deterministic recurrent neural network models, and ridge regression. The models combine graph-based spatial encoding with gated recurrent units. Inter-experiment transfer trains on PG-27 pressurized conduction cooldown and evaluates on PG-29 using section-context conditioning.
AI.result: On the PG-29 depressurized conduction cooldown test, the GNN-GRU VAE achieves MAE 11.73 C, RMSE 20.54 C and R2 0.98, while the deterministic GNN-GRU and GRU reach RMSE 25.26 C and 35.22 C. All three generative models reduce RMSE by more than half compared with ridge regression. The diffusion model keeps R2 at 0.94 when known sensors fall from 91 to 45. For inter-experiment reconstruction, the section-context diffusion model achieves RMSE 42.84 C and R2 0.91.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporal generative modelling is valuable for reconstructing missing sensor data in safety-critical digital twin applications.

title: Adaptive Depth Aggregation in Graph Transformers for Long-Range Graph Reasoning
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE BigData 2026
summary: Graph Transformers improve long-range node-to-node communication through global or structure-aware interactions. However, improving cross-node communication does not determine how computations produced at different depths should be combined. Standard residual streams accumulate successive computations with fixed unit coefficients shared across nodes. This fixed aggregation is a residual-interface constraint: once intermediate contributions have been produced, the interface cannot explicitly reweight them by node. We hypothesize that this constraint can create a depth-wise aggregation mismatch when the relative utility of these intermediate contributions varies across nodes and structural contexts. To study this hypothesis, we formalize Graph Transformer residual computation as a causal node-wise history of graph-propagation and feed-forward network (FFN) contributions, making depth aggregation an explicit interface choice. We realize node-adaptive aggregation over this history with Attention Residuals (AttnRes) while preserving the backbone's graph-propagation and auxiliary-state machinery. Block AttnRes reduces the routing cost of long histories relative to Full AttnRes by pooling consecutive contributions. We instantiate the interface in GPS and GRIT and evaluate it on all five ECHO tasks. Both variants achieve lower mean absolute error (MAE) than their independently tuned backbones on every task, and at least one obtains the lowest mean among all compared methods in each task. Routing-only donor-swap interventions support the mismatch hypothesis, while additional ablations examine the key design choices. Together, these results support node-adaptive depth aggregation as a useful complement to cross-node communication in long-range graph reasoning.

AI.tldr: Proposes node-adaptive depth aggregation for Graph Transformers by replacing fixed residual coefficients with Attention Residuals over the causal history of graph-propagation and FFN contributions, improving GPS and GRIT on five ECHO tasks.
AI.motivation: Graph Transformers improve cross-node communication, but standard residual streams combine intermediate contributions with fixed unit coefficients shared across nodes. This can mismatch the varying utility of those contributions across nodes and structural contexts.
AI.method: Graph Transformer residual computation is formalized as a causal node-wise history of propagation and FFN contributions, and node-adaptive aggregation over this history is realized with Attention Residuals. Block AttnRes pools consecutive contributions to reduce routing cost relative to Full AttnRes. The interface is instantiated in GPS and GRIT.
AI.result: Both variants achieve lower MAE than their independently tuned backbones on all five ECHO tasks, and at least one obtains the lowest mean among all compared methods in each task. Routing-only donor-swap interventions support the depth-wise aggregation mismatch hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: Node-adaptive depth aggregation is a useful complement to cross-node communication for long-range graph reasoning.

title: Emergent Low-Dimensional Topological Dynamics Dictate Generalization and Escape Mechanics in Billion-Parameter Neural Networks
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures
summary: The remarkable generalization of modern over-parameterized neural networks defies classical statistical learning bounds. Here we establish that optimization trajectories in billion-parameter models do not sample the ambient dimension $\mathbb{R}^N$ homogeneously; instead, they are dynamically constrained to a low-dimensional execution submanifold $\mathcal{M}_{\text{exec}}$ (with empirically observed effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}} \le 12$). By equipping the parameter space with a regularized Hessian metric $g_{ij} = \nabla_i \nabla_j L + \epsilon \delta_{ij}$ and analyzing stochastic Langevin diffusion on loss sublevel sets, we derive a rigorous Topological Generalization Bound grounded in projected subspace persistent homology. Furthermore, by linking Morse index transitions to Betti number annihilation ($\beta_1 \to 0$), we formulate an exact mathematical mechanism for exponential escape from strict saddles under anisotropic noise. We validate our framework across 80+ architectures (ResNets, Vision Transformers, and 7B LLMs). To bridge theoretical topology with computational feasibility, we resolve the curse of dimensionality by computing projected persistent homology proxies via randomized Lanczos iterations restricted strictly within active Hessian subspaces. Building upon this mathematical foundation, we introduce Topological-Adaptive Optimization (Top-SGD and Top-AdamW)---a family of wrapper algorithms that dynamically modulate learning rates using active curvature signatures. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate a 14.1\% reduction in total wall-clock training time on ImageNet with all computational and memory overheads fully accounted for. Code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Argues that optimization trajectories in billion-parameter networks lie on a low-dimensional execution submanifold, derives a topological generalization bound and a saddle-escape mechanism, and proposes Top-SGD and Top-AdamW, which cut ImageNet wall-clock training time by 14.1 percent.
AI.motivation: Classical statistical learning bounds do not explain the generalization of over-parameterized networks. The paper claims that optimization does not sample the ambient parameter dimension homogeneously.
AI.method: The parameter space is equipped with a regularized Hessian metric, and stochastic Langevin diffusion on loss sublevel sets is analysed. A topological generalization bound is derived from projected subspace persistent homology, and Morse index transitions are linked to Betti number annihilation to explain exponential escape from strict saddles. Persistent homology proxies are computed with randomized Lanczos iterations inside active Hessian subspaces. Top-SGD and Top-AdamW wrap base optimizers and modulate learning rates using active curvature signatures.
AI.result: The abstract reports an empirical effective dimension of at most 12 and validation across more than 80 architectures, including ResNets, Vision Transformers and 7B LLMs. Top-SGD and Top-AdamW give a 14.1 percent reduction in total wall-clock training time on ImageNet, with computational and memory overheads accounted for.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a topology- and curvature-based account of generalization and saddle escape, together with a wrapper optimizer that uses active curvature signatures to adapt learning rates.

title: Does Country Matter? Evaluating Geographic Sensitivity of Large Language Models in Zero-Shot Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
comment: Accepted to ACM HIKM-2026, 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) show strong zero-shot reasoning capabilities, yet their sensitivity to prompt context raises questions about reliability in deployment. This study investigates whether geographic context embedded in prompts influences LLM-based chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening, independent of any change in patient features. Using a community-based CKD dataset from Bangladesh (284 participants with 112 CKD and 172 non-CKD), we systematically varied the country attribute across 25 global contexts while holding all clinical inputs constant, and evaluated two open-weight LLMs (Qwen3 8B and Mistral 7B). Experiments were conducted on a common-correct subset of 156 participants for whom both models produced correct baseline predictions. Results show that non-CKD predictions were highly stable across geographic contexts, with both models maintaining consistent non-CKD predictions in nearly all settings. In contrast, CKD-positive predictions were considerably more sensitive. For Qwen3, CKD prediction dropped from a baseline of 65 to as low as 50 across country contexts, while Mistral showed smaller but non-negligible variation. Country contexts did not group according to known epidemiological or healthcare similarities; instead, groupings appear to reflect how country tokens are internally represented within each model. These findings demonstrate that geographic tokens can systematically shift clinical screening outcomes despite identical patient inputs, with implications for the deployment of LLM-based decision support in diverse healthcare settings.

AI.tldr: Shows that the country named in a prompt shifts zero-shot chronic kidney disease screening outcomes of open-weight LLMs even when clinical inputs are identical, mainly through changes in CKD-positive predictions.
AI.motivation: LLMs are sensitive to prompt context, which raises reliability concerns for deployment. It is unclear whether geographic context alone changes clinical screening decisions.
AI.method: On a Bangladeshi community CKD dataset (284 participants, 112 CKD and 172 non-CKD), the country attribute was varied across 25 global contexts with clinical inputs held constant. Two open-weight models, Qwen3 8B and Mistral 7B, were evaluated on a common-correct subset of 156 participants for whom both models predicted correctly at baseline.
AI.result: Non-CKD predictions were highly stable across geographic contexts. CKD-positive predictions were more sensitive: for Qwen3, CKD prediction dropped from a baseline of 65 to as low as 50, while Mistral showed smaller but non-negligible variation. Country groupings did not follow epidemiological or healthcare similarity and appear to reflect how country tokens are represented inside each model.
AI.conclusion: Geographic tokens can systematically shift clinical screening outcomes despite identical patient inputs, with implications for LLM-based decision support in diverse healthcare settings.

title: Interpretable Multifidelity Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Spatiotemporal Nuclear Reactor Flow Modeling
comment: 33 pages, 15 figures,9 tables, and a preprint under peer review
summary: High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of nuclear reactor systems are computationally expensive, motivating machine learning methods that reduce cost while preserving accuracy. Multifidelity surrogate modeling addresses this by combining inexpensive low-fidelity data with limited high-fidelity data. This work investigates whether the high-fidelity data required to predict the spatiotemporal mass flow rate across all 193 fuel assemblies of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) core can be reduced, comparing black-box multifidelity feedforward neural networks (MFNNs) with interpretable multifidelity Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (MFKANs). Cross-fidelity correlation across the core is weak, making this a challenging multifidelity problem, and neither architecture predicts the transient particularly well in absolute terms. MFKAN nonetheless performs comparably to MFNN for one-time-step-forward prediction while also providing closed-form symbolic equations unavailable with MFNN. To address the scarcity of CFD transients, with only one available per fidelity level, TabDDPM-generated synthetic data was used to augment cross-fidelity forecasting. KAN and FNN achieve comparable self-evaluation accuracy (Pearson correlation of roughly 0.73--0.81), but both perform poorly at true cross-fidelity forecasting (correlations of 0.03--0.06). Assembly-level analysis shows that each assembly's forecast correlation tracks its real cross-fidelity correlation for both architectures ($r=0.840$--$0.896$ for KAN, $r=0.804$--$0.903$ for FNN), confirming that forecasting accuracy is fundamentally limited by how correlated the fidelity levels already are. Overall, KAN-based multifidelity modeling achieves accuracy consistently comparable to MFNN across all settings, while additionally providing symbolic equations that match or exceed the spline representation's accuracy.

AI.tldr: Compares multifidelity Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with multifidelity feedforward networks for predicting spatiotemporal mass flow rates across the 193 fuel assemblies of a PWR core. KANs match the accuracy of FNNs and yield closed-form symbolic equations, but both architectures forecast cross-fidelity poorly.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity CFD of reactor cores is expensive, so multifidelity surrogates should reduce the high-fidelity data required. Cross-fidelity correlation across the core is weak, and only one CFD transient is available per fidelity level.
AI.method: Black-box multifidelity feedforward networks (MFNN) are compared with interpretable multifidelity Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (MFKAN). TabDDPM-generated synthetic data are used to augment cross-fidelity forecasting.
AI.result: MFKAN performs comparably to MFNN for one-time-step-forward prediction, but neither predicts the transient well in absolute terms. KAN and FNN reach self-evaluation Pearson correlations of roughly 0.73 to 0.81 yet only 0.03 to 0.06 in true cross-fidelity forecasting. Assembly-level forecast correlation tracks the real cross-fidelity correlation for both (r = 0.840 to 0.896 for KAN, 0.804 to 0.903 for FNN).
AI.conclusion: KAN-based multifidelity modelling is consistently comparable to MFNN across settings and additionally provides symbolic equations, while forecasting accuracy is fundamentally limited by how correlated the fidelity levels already are.

title: What Are LLM Agents Actually Learning on Low-Budget Molecular Optimization Benchmarks?
summary: Recent work reports large gains for LLM agents on low-budget molecular optimization. We measure the contributions of online optimization, retrievable task information, and permissive oracle landscapes. On PMO at 50 oracle calls, a GPT-4o mini agent's sum AUC falls from 14.44 to 4.85 after task names and curated reference compounds are hidden. An identity-blinded condition that states only the oracle form (e.g., similarity to a hidden reference) scores 5.39, while a deterministic retrieval-only baseline with no LLM reaches 12.16 (84% of the full agent). A full 23-task 2x2 ablation and a three-seed replication on eight tasks support this interpretation. On a protein-targeted benchmark with an AutoDock Vina composite oracle, a single-edit random walk is a strong lower bound; across three seeds it obtains composite 0.636 +/- 0.008 and docking improvement -1.11 +/- 0.04 kcal/mol. As a positive control, a retrieval-free population agent exceeds REINVENT at a matched 50-call AUC budget, with its strongest result at 100 calls. These results motivate two inexpensive sanity checks: retrieval-safe PMO prompts and a random-walk floor for docking-based optimization.

AI.tldr: An ablation study showing that LLM-agent gains on low-budget molecular optimization come largely from retrievable task information rather than online learning, and that a random walk is a strong floor for docking-based optimization.
AI.motivation: Recent work reports large gains for LLM agents on low-budget molecular optimization, but the sources of those gains are unclear.
AI.method: The contributions of online optimization, retrievable task information and permissive oracle landscapes are measured with a 2x2 ablation over 23 PMO tasks, a three-seed replication on eight tasks, an identity-blinded condition that states only the oracle form, and a retrieval-only baseline with no LLM. On a protein-targeted benchmark with an AutoDock Vina composite oracle, a single-edit random walk serves as a lower bound, and a retrieval-free population agent serves as a positive control against REINVENT.
AI.result: On PMO at 50 oracle calls, a GPT-4o mini agent's sum AUC falls from 14.44 to 4.85 when task names and curated reference compounds are hidden. The identity-blinded condition scores 5.39, and the deterministic retrieval-only baseline reaches 12.16, 84 percent of the full agent. On the docking benchmark, the random walk obtains composite 0.636 +/- 0.008 and docking improvement -1.11 +/- 0.04 kcal/mol across three seeds. The retrieval-free population agent exceeds REINVENT at a matched 50-call AUC budget, with its strongest result at 100 calls.
AI.conclusion: The results motivate two inexpensive sanity checks: retrieval-safe PMO prompts and a random-walk floor for docking-based optimization.

title: Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning: A Multi-Objective Framework for Learning Local Distance Functions in Nearest Neighbor Classification
summary: Nearest neighbour classifiers inherit the geometry of their distance function. Fixed distances and globally learned metrics apply the same geometry throughout the input space, although relevant feature directions may vary across regions. We propose EAML (Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning), a framework that learns instance-dependent positive-definite metrics through a low-dimensional parameterization. Each local metric combines an input-dependent diagonal scaling, generated by softmax interpolation between anchor points, with a global low-rank correlation component. A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes the parameters using a scalar objective combining leave-one-out prediction error, robustness, metric smoothness, and regularization. We establish positive definiteness, metric equivalence, existence of an optimal solution, and Lipschitz continuity of the metric field. We further investigate prediction stability, generalization bounds, and evolutionary convergence under explicit assumptions. Experiments on synthetic data with region-dependent feature relevance show that EAML can recover local metric variations and outperform global metrics. Evaluation on thirteen public datasets using nested 5-fold cross-validation reveals a more nuanced picture: EAML improves performance on selected datasets but does not significantly outperform global metric baselines overall. Additional experiments show that global diagonal metrics can be preferable under nuisance features and test-time noise. These findings identify the conditions under which evolutionary local metric learning is beneficial and highlight its practical limitations.

AI.tldr: Proposes EAML, which learns instance-dependent local metrics for nearest neighbour classification through an evolutionary, low-dimensional parameterization. It helps on selected datasets but does not significantly outperform global metric baselines overall.
AI.motivation: Fixed or globally learned distance functions apply one geometry across the whole input space, although relevant feature directions may vary across regions.
AI.method: Each local metric combines an input-dependent diagonal scaling, produced by softmax interpolation between anchor points, with a global low-rank correlation component. A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes the parameters using a scalar objective that combines leave-one-out error, robustness, metric smoothness and regularization. Positive definiteness, metric equivalence, existence of an optimal solution and Lipschitz continuity of the metric field are established.
AI.result: On synthetic data with region-dependent feature relevance, EAML recovers local metric variations and outperforms global metrics. On thirteen public datasets under nested 5-fold cross-validation, it improves selected datasets but does not significantly outperform global metric baselines overall. Global diagonal metrics can be preferable under nuisance features and test-time noise.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary local metric learning is beneficial only under certain conditions, and the paper identifies those conditions along with its practical limitations.

title: Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation for Wind Energy Predictive Analysis
comment: To be published in IEEE BigData 2026 Conference
summary: Resource-constrained cyber-physical decision systems often apply fixed sensing, knowledge, and computational pipelines despite state-dependent information needs. We introduce Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation (MSKC), a resource-aware computing principle: select the least-costly route meeting decision-risk and deployment constraints, escalating only when cheaper routes are insufficient. As proof of concept, we isolate adaptive knowledge routing, the decision underlying Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning (KGML), which conventionally injects external knowledge unconditionally rather than only where needed. We instantiate this for wind ramp-event predictive analysis, an edge-oriented decision-support task, evaluating local, relational, and physics-informed routes with a state-aware gate on publicly available real data from two wind farms. We establish conditions for feasibility preservation, cost dominance, and strict expected savings over always-on routing. At a 35.9% relational-knowledge injection rate, adaptive routing is statistically indistinguishable from always-on injection on the reported metrics while reducing knowledge calls by 64%, supporting sustainable, Green-IT-aligned deployment. These results support MSKC's premise that uniformly maximal intelligence is unnecessary. This offers intelligent data analysis for big data streams: the analysis itself decides, per state, how much knowledge and computation the data warrant.

AI.tldr: Introduces Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation, a principle that selects the least costly route meeting decision-risk constraints, and demonstrates it with adaptive knowledge routing for wind ramp-event prediction, which cuts knowledge calls by 64 percent without a statistically distinguishable loss.
AI.motivation: Resource-constrained cyber-physical systems often apply fixed sensing, knowledge and computation pipelines regardless of state-dependent information needs. Knowledge-guided machine learning injects external knowledge unconditionally rather than only where needed.
AI.method: The principle escalates to costlier routes only when cheaper routes are insufficient. Local, relational and physics-informed routes are evaluated with a state-aware gate on public data from two wind farms. Conditions are established for feasibility preservation, cost dominance and strict expected savings over always-on routing.
AI.result: At a 35.9 percent relational-knowledge injection rate, adaptive routing is statistically indistinguishable from always-on injection on the reported metrics while reducing knowledge calls by 64 percent.
AI.conclusion: Uniformly maximal intelligence is unnecessary, and adaptive routing supports sustainable, Green-IT-aligned deployment of data analysis on big data streams.

title: Not All Misalignment Is Alike: A Decomposed Benchmark for Emergent Misalignment
summary: Emergent misalignment (EM), in which fine-tuning on a narrow task induces misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts, has been demonstrated across a wide range of datasets, model families, and training setups. Yet, most studies continue to rely on the evaluation approach introduced in the original EM paper, producing rates that are sensitive to the small set of evaluation questions used, the choice of judge, and the thresholds applied. These evaluations can also conflate misalignment with capability loss and offer little insight into the specific ways misalignment manifests. Differences in datasets, models, and fine-tuning configurations further make findings difficult to compare across studies. We introduce EMERGE, a decomposed benchmark that tracks changes in eight distinct misaligned behaviours from base to fine-tuned models. It evaluates these behaviours on out-of-domain prompts against matched benign controls and tracks capability, coherence, and refusal to account for potential confounders. Applying EMERGE to 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets, we find that models with similar broad misalignment rates can exhibit very different behavioural profiles that a single score cannot capture. We hope EMERGE can help establish a shared and robust standard for measuring EM, making findings more comparable and helping move research from detecting the phenomenon towards understanding it.

AI.tldr: Introduces EMERGE, a decomposed benchmark that measures eight distinct misaligned behaviours in emergently misaligned models against matched benign controls, showing that similar overall misalignment rates can hide very different behavioural profiles.
AI.motivation: Emergent misalignment studies mostly rely on the evaluation approach of the original EM paper, whose rates are sensitive to the question set, the judge and the thresholds, and can conflate misalignment with capability loss. Differences in datasets and setups also make findings hard to compare.
AI.method: EMERGE tracks changes in eight misaligned behaviours from base to fine-tuned models on out-of-domain prompts, against matched benign controls, and tracks capability, coherence and refusal as potential confounders. It is applied to 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets.
AI.result: Models with similar broad misalignment rates can show very different behavioural profiles that a single score cannot capture.
AI.conclusion: The authors hope EMERGE can serve as a shared, robust standard for measuring emergent misalignment, moving research from detecting the phenomenon toward understanding it.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning for Chaotic Three-Body Dynamics in Astrophysics
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Sim2Science: ML with Imperfect Scientific Models
summary: Machine learning (ML) and generative AI have recently made impressive progress in understanding physics. We explore a hierarchy of prediction problems stemming from chaotic three-body systems and benchmark existing ML approaches, including general-purpose prediction algorithms and those that build on top of foundational physics models. We first simulate the trajectories of triple systems near the critical boundary of stable/unstable initial conditions. We then design a hierarchy of learning tasks, focusing mainly on two broad problems: stability prediction and trajectory prediction. The former classifies whether a given triple system has diverged or not up to a specific horizon, while the latter predicts the exact trajectory, both given suitable input features. We benchmark a range of ML approaches, from simple regression methods to state-of-the-art foundational physics models, across these tasks, and compare them against astrophysical methods such as the Mardling-Aarseth stability criterion. Our experiments reveal a clear order of task difficulties in chaotic three-body dynamics: early dynamics enable strong stability prediction, while precise long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains difficult. Code and dataset are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks machine learning methods on chaotic three-body systems across a hierarchy of stability and trajectory prediction tasks, finding that early dynamics support strong stability prediction while long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains difficult.
AI.motivation: Machine learning and generative AI have made progress in understanding physics, but their performance on chaotic three-body dynamics near the stable/unstable boundary has not been benchmarked systematically against astrophysical methods.
AI.method: Triple-system trajectories are simulated near the critical boundary between stable and unstable initial conditions. Two task families are defined: stability prediction, which classifies whether a system has diverged up to a given horizon, and trajectory prediction. Regression methods, general-purpose prediction algorithms and foundational physics models are compared, including against the Mardling-Aarseth stability criterion.
AI.result: The experiments show a clear order of task difficulty: early dynamics enable strong stability prediction, while precise long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains difficult.
AI.conclusion: The code and dataset are publicly available as a benchmark for machine learning on chaotic three-body dynamics.

title: Higher Order Component Attribution via Learned Surrogates in High Energy Physics
summary: Experimental High Energy Physics (HEP) has adopted the transformer architecture for identification of jets, particularly the state-of-the-art Particle Transformer (ParT) which injects explicit information about particle correlations into the attention mechanism. While able to achieve state-of-the-art results in accuracy, interpretability to its effectiveness has been limited. In this paper we propose component attribution methods using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) that directly tie back to the physical descriptors of jets, to probe whether mechanisms such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), or the ParT architecture, are able to learn these as discriminating features.

AI.tldr: Proposes component attribution methods based on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks to test whether attention mechanisms in the Particle Transformer, used for jet identification, learn physically meaningful jet descriptors.
AI.motivation: The Particle Transformer achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in jet identification for high energy physics, but its interpretability has been limited.
AI.method: Component attribution methods that tie directly back to the physical descriptors of jets are built on KANs and used to probe whether Multi-Head Attention or the ParT architecture learns these descriptors as discriminating features.
AI.result: The abstract does not report results.
AI.conclusion: The abstract does not state a conclusion; the work asks whether ParT's mechanisms learn physical jet descriptors.

title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies
comment: 33 pages, 10 figures
summary: Execution algorithms are calibrated asset by asset, because the queues, trade rates and bid-ask spreads they face differ by orders of magnitude across assets. For reinforcement learning this is zero-shot generalisation across contexts of very different scales, and microstructure invariance proposes a normalisation fixed by theory: measured in each asset's own units of time, size and price, markets look alike. In an exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data, we train policies once, on 954 stocks in 2019, to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread, and evaluate them unchanged on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020-21, 2,629 stocks in 2025-26, crypto pairs and a second exchange. First, a policy that sees a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and price increment (tick) costs within 0.015 spreads per share (a fifth of what learning saves) of a policy whose training data included the stock, and the stock's own history does not help it; it comes within a similar margin of policies trained on the second exchange when every episode counts equally, and within a wider one on crypto. Second, in mean cost before fees, invariant units beat raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors, but by under a basis point: most of their advantage is information and a common cost scale that a learner can also take as plain inputs, and none of the representations tested extrapolates to unseen spread regimes. Third, a near-zero transfer gap to a pooled comparator is weak evidence that a representation is right: we show that such a comparator detects only a small share of what a poor representation loses, and confirm it in synthetic markets and on pendulums.

AI.tldr: Shows that an execution policy using only asset-normalised microstructure features transfers zero-shot to thousands of unseen stocks, crypto pairs and a second exchange, with invariant units giving only a marginal advantage over plain inputs.
AI.motivation: Execution algorithms are calibrated asset by asset because queues, trade rates and spreads differ by orders of magnitude. Microstructure invariance proposes a theory-fixed normalisation that could allow zero-shot generalisation across assets.
AI.method: Policies are trained once on 954 stocks in 2019 to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread, using exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data. A policy sees a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and price increment (tick). Invariant units are compared with raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors.
AI.result: The tick-based policy costs within 0.015 spreads per share of a policy whose training data included the stock, a fifth of what learning saves, and the stock's own history does not help it. It stays within a similar margin of policies trained on the second exchange when every episode counts equally, and within a wider margin on crypto. In mean cost before fees, invariant units beat raw units, z-scores and descriptors by under a basis point, and no tested representation extrapolates to unseen spread regimes. A pooled comparator with a near-zero transfer gap detects only a small share of what a poor representation loses.
AI.conclusion: A near-zero transfer gap to a pooled comparator is weak evidence that a representation is right, and most of the invariant units' advantage comes from information and a common cost scale that a learner can also take as plain inputs.

title: Foundation-Model Residuals as Signals of Urban Bus Irregularity
comment: 2-page extended abstract accepted, but not presented as a poster at NetMob 2026
summary: Pretrained trajectory models encode mobility patterns learned across cities, but their errors when transferred to a new city are usually treated only as performance limitations. We instead ask whether these residuals reveal systematic local conditions. Architectures such as UniTraj and TrajFM learn transferable trajectory representations, although cross-context transfer remains challenging. Using the NetMob26 bus location, ticketing, weather, network, and socioeconomic data for Niteroi, we analyze spatial and travel-time residuals of these recent trajectory foundation models. We test whether high residuals concentrate spatially, whether spatial and travel-time residuals overlap, and which urban-context variables explain their distribution. We interpret high residuals as candidate proxy signals of transit irregularity rather than direct evidence of service disruption, and analyze their contextual associations using Explainable AI (XAI). Insights into such varied environments are increasingly valuable for evaluating new urban paradigms; for instance, the 15-minute-city perspective serves as a key motivation for our approach, guiding our methods and expanding the analysis beyond standard mobility metrics.

AI.tldr: Uses residuals of pretrained trajectory foundation models on Niteroi bus data as candidate proxy signals of transit irregularity, and analyses their spatial concentration and contextual drivers with explainable AI.
AI.motivation: Errors of pretrained trajectory models transferred to a new city are usually treated as performance limitations, whereas they may reveal systematic local conditions. Cross-context transfer of such models remains challenging.
AI.method: Spatial and travel-time residuals of recent trajectory foundation models, including UniTraj and TrajFM, are analysed on NetMob26 bus location, ticketing, weather, network and socioeconomic data for Niteroi. The tests check whether high residuals concentrate spatially, whether spatial and travel-time residuals overlap, and which urban-context variables explain their distribution, using explainable AI.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: High residuals are interpreted as candidate proxies for transit irregularity rather than direct evidence of service disruption, and the approach is positioned as a way to evaluate new urban paradigms such as the 15-minute city.

title: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting. In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$. In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^{\omega})$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space. We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}{\epsilon})$ for $\epsilon$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness of this canonical task. Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets shows that the accuracy of our continual observation mechanism clearly outperforms any other known differentially private mechanism for this problem such as rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.

AI.tldr: Introduces ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained least-squares linear regression under continual differential privacy, with suboptimality proportional to sqrt(d) polylog(n), and gives new lower bounds for box-constrained regression.
AI.motivation: Private linear regression is well studied in the batch setting but underexplored in the continual observation setting, where prior work covered only constrained regression with update time polynomial in n.
AI.method: The mechanism uses O(d^2 log n) space and O(d^2 log n + d^omega) update time for unconstrained regression under continual DP. The lower bounds are derived by a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem of Peter et al. (2024).
AI.result: The suboptimality gap is proportional to sqrt(d) polylog(n). The lower bounds for box-constrained regression are proportional to min(n, sqrt(d)/log^1.5 d) for (1, O(1/n))-DP and min(n, d/epsilon) for epsilon-DP. On real-world datasets the continual mechanism clearly outperforms other known private mechanisms, including rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.
AI.conclusion: The work gives the first continual-DP mechanism for unconstrained regression and new insight into the inherent hardness of this canonical task.

title: TopoSHAP: Shapley for Explainable and Efficient Topological Deep Learning
summary: Topological deep learning (TDL) extends learning on graphs, such as molecules or social networks, to higher-order structures, such as rings in a molecule or groups in a social network. Explaining which of these structures drive a model's predictions, and which architectural components matter most for its performance, remains challenging. We introduce TopoSHAP, an efficient and general explanation framework that addresses both questions across topological domains and model architectures. TopoSHAP-cell assigns Shapley values to topological data cells and extracts compact explanations. These explanations match or outperform graph-based counterparts on GraphXAI benchmark data while running up to 112$\times$ faster. They also reveal advantageous topological feature design, leading to measured improvements in explanation recovery and predictive accuracy. On the architecture side, TopoSHAP-neighbor explains how neighborhoods contribute to model performance, and turns these evaluations into a backward-elimination search that identifies smaller, competitive architectures early in training. This is up to $11.3\times$ cheaper than traditional TDL training sweeps.

AI.tldr: Proposes TopoSHAP, a Shapley-based explanation framework for topological deep learning that explains both topological cells and architecture components, matching or beating graph-based explanations while running up to 112 times faster.
AI.motivation: In topological deep learning, it remains challenging to explain which higher-order structures drive a model's predictions and which architectural components matter most for its performance.
AI.method: TopoSHAP-cell assigns Shapley values to topological data cells and extracts compact explanations. TopoSHAP-neighbor explains how neighbourhoods contribute to model performance and turns these evaluations into a backward-elimination search for smaller architectures early in training.
AI.result: Explanations match or outperform graph-based counterparts on GraphXAI benchmark data while running up to 112 times faster, and reveal advantageous topological feature design with improved explanation recovery and predictive accuracy. The architecture search identifies smaller competitive architectures early and is up to 11.3 times cheaper than traditional TDL training sweeps.
AI.conclusion: TopoSHAP offers an efficient and general way to explain both topological structures and architectures in topological deep learning.

title: MotionBench-XAI: Benchmarking What Shapes Shapley Explanations in Spatiotemporal Machine Learning
summary: Predicting outcomes from spatiotemporal data, such as assessing Parkinson's severity from human motion, often requires explainability in addition to accuracy. Practitioners need to know what drove the prediction, whether it be spatial (a body joint), temporal (a specific window), or both. Shapley values are attributions computed by treating input features as players in a cooperative game and measuring how the model output changes as coalitions of players are removed. Computing them involves choosing what counts as players, how absent players are imputed, and how the game is evaluated. How these choices affect explanation quality is poorly understood for spatiotemporal data, and real data carries no ground-truth attributions to check against. We present MotionBench-XAI, a benchmark built on i) five synthetic spatiotemporal datasets with exact ground-truth Shapley values, ii) three real datasets across clinical gait, electrocardiogram, and audio, iii) ten attribution methods across three player sets, and iv) three trained architectures. We show that grouping features into players, across time, space, or both, matters more than the choice of imputer. Generative imputers improve explanations only when their conditional models are accurate. On real data, the standard proxy metrics select contradictory best methods. We distill these findings into practical insights and provide an open-source pipeline.

AI.tldr: Presents MotionBench-XAI, a benchmark for Shapley explanations of spatiotemporal models, finding that how features are grouped into players matters more than the choice of imputer, and that standard proxy metrics can select contradictory best methods on real data.
AI.motivation: Explaining spatiotemporal predictions, such as Parkinson's severity from human motion, requires attributing outcomes to spatial, temporal or joint units. How the design choices in Shapley computation affect explanation quality is poorly understood, and real data carries no ground-truth attributions.
AI.method: The benchmark combines five synthetic spatiotemporal datasets with exact ground-truth Shapley values, three real datasets (clinical gait, electrocardiogram and audio), ten attribution methods across three player sets, and three trained architectures.
AI.result: Grouping features into players across time, space or both matters more than the choice of imputer. Generative imputers improve explanations only when their conditional models are accurate. On real data, the standard proxy metrics select contradictory best methods.
AI.conclusion: The findings are distilled into practical insights, and an open-source pipeline is provided for the analysis.

title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
comment: Under review at ICLR 2027
summary: Fine-tuned (FT) derivatives of large language models (LLMs) are now released in large numbers, yet their provenance relies on self-reports and cannot be verified. Misattributed lineage leaves a verifier unable to audit outsourced fine-tuning, confirm license compliance of derived models, or trace vulnerabilities that a parent passes to its children. All three require the direction of derivation, not merely its presence. Existing output-only methods are limited to pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage estimation, while recovering a directed tree requires white-box access to model weights. We formalize the problem of reconstructing a directed model tree, including internal nodes, under gray-box access, where only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and a child inherits this increase from its parent. Building on this property, we define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it an edge weight for each ordered pair of models. We propose TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these edge weights, with neither hyperparameters nor tree-structure constraints. We evaluate it on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks. TRACE-Edge achieves a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples, and on average outperforms an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes drawn from the same distribution as the training data.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes reconstructing a directed model tree of fine-tuned LLMs under gray-box access, using only teacher-forced log-likelihoods, and proposes TRACE-Edge, which recovers the parent structure by solving for a maximum spanning directed tree. On 25 model trees it reaches 0.74 parent-match accuracy with fine-tuning probes.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuned LLM provenance relies on self-reports that cannot be verified, and existing output-only methods only give pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage, while recovering a directed tree was thought to require white-box weight access.
AI.method: Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of training data and a child inherits this increase from its parent, so an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between two models gives a directed edge weight for each ordered pair, and TRACE-Edge exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree with no hyperparameters or tree-structure constraints.
AI.result: On five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks, TRACE-Edge reaches a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 with fine-tuning-example probes and outperforms an output-similarity baseline on average, including with held-out probes drawn from the training distribution.
AI.conclusion: Directed lineage of derived LLMs can be audited from output likelihoods alone, which supports verifying outsourced fine-tuning, license compliance, and vulnerability tracing without weight access.

title: Learning to Restart: Differentiable Restart Policies for Optimization Dynamics
summary: Adaptive restart mechanisms, which reset the momentum or other auxiliary state of an iterative optimizer, play a central role in the empirical performance of accelerated first-order methods, yet existing restart rules remain almost entirely hand-designed. The obstruction to learning restart policies is that, unlike the typical Learning to Optimize (L2O) setting, the discrete restart events make the resulting trajectory non-differentiable in the algorithm parameters and thus block gradient-based optimization of the restart policy. We resolve this obstruction by developing a differentiable framework for restart policies through their continuous-time limit. We introduce surrogate gradients for the restart events and optimization trajectories that are efficient to compute and provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts. We validate the effectiveness of our surrogate gradients in L2O settings, training restart policies that improve upon standard handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs, and that transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper learns restart policies for accelerated first-order optimizers by making restart events differentiable through a continuous-time limit and introducing surrogate gradients. Learned policies beat handcrafted adaptive restart rules on quadratic and linear programs and transfer zero-shot to logistic regression on real datasets.
AI.motivation: Adaptive restart rules that reset momentum in accelerated methods are hand-designed, and discrete restart events make the trajectory non-differentiable, which blocks gradient-based learning of restart policies unlike typical Learning to Optimize settings.
AI.method: A differentiable framework for restart policies is developed through their continuous-time limit, with surrogate gradients for the restart events and optimization trajectories that are efficient to compute and provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts.
AI.result: Restart policies trained in L2O settings improve upon standard handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs and transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-based learning of restart policies is feasible once restart events are given surrogate gradients, offering a route to replace hand-designed restart criteria in accelerated optimization.

title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning
summary: Machine learning methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) significantly improve computational efficiency over traditional numerical solvers such as finite element method (FEM). However, PDE dynamics inherently span both local and global dynamics: disturbances propagate and decay gradually through the domain, while global coupling effects can influence the whole system simultaneously. Capturing both types of dynamics with a low complexity model remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose the Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network (SSF-Net), built around a dual-branch Spatial-Spectral Fusion (SSF) block comprising a spatial branch and a spectral branch. The spatial branch employs a multi-directional Mamba, which mitigates its inherent causal, single-direction scanning bias and capture local interactions with reduced directional bias at linear complexity. The spectral branch leverages a Fourier transform with a block-diagonal MLP to efficiently capture global spectral features with reduced parameter count and complexity. The SSF block is embedded in a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder, which extracts multi-scale features. We evaluate SSF-Net on a comprehensive PDE benchmark spanning multiple task types and assess its long-horizon stability. Compared with attention-based and convolution-based baselines, SSF-Net achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters while retaining near-linear asymptotic complexity in the number of spatial tokens.

AI.tldr: SSF-Net is a neural operator for PDE solution learning that combines a multi-directional Mamba spatial branch with a Fourier spectral branch inside a multiresolution encoder-decoder. Compared with attention-based and convolution-based baselines it achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: PDE dynamics mix local propagation with global coupling, and capturing both with a low-complexity model is hard, while the causal single-direction scanning of Mamba introduces directional bias.
AI.method: A dual-branch Spatial-Spectral Fusion block pairs a spatial branch using multi-directional Mamba for local interactions at linear complexity with a spectral branch using a Fourier transform and block-diagonal MLP for global features, and the block is embedded in a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder.
AI.result: On a comprehensive PDE benchmark spanning multiple task types, SSF-Net achieves lower prediction error than attention-based and convolution-based baselines with fewer parameters, retains near-linear asymptotic complexity in the number of spatial tokens, and is assessed for long-horizon stability.
AI.conclusion: Combining directional spatial scanning with spectral global mixing gives an accurate and efficient operator learner for PDEs, with near-linear scaling in the number of tokens.

title: Composable Causality: A Toolkit for Systematic Time-Series Causal Discovery and Treatment-Effect Benchmarking
comment: 30 pages, 10 main text pages plus references and appendices, with figures and tables. Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Code and data at this https URL
summary: Real-world multivariate time series rarely come with verified ground-truth causal structure, so research on time-series causal discovery and treatment-effect estimation depends on synthetic data. Existing tools are either fixed datasets that cannot be modified after release or script-based generators in which each script fixes one combination of mechanism, confounding, and missingness. Neither supports controlled experiments that vary a single property, such as sparsity, noise distribution, or missingness mechanism, while holding the others fixed. Counterfactual evaluation has the same gap, since existing simulators are built per paper with hardcoded mechanisms or produce observational data only. We introduce DTCD (Datasets and Toolkit for Causal Discovery), a data generation library that produces multivariate time series with ground-truth contemporaneous and lagged adjacency matrices. Topology, mechanism, noise, observational mask, and intervention policy are independent components that compose through configuration alone. Paired counterfactual twins, produced by caching the stochastic realization during the factual rollout and re-injecting it during the interventional rollout, recover individual treatment effects to numerical precision. A reference benchmark of eight discovery algorithms on eighty-one configurations and four treatment-effect estimators on eighteen configurations exposes failure modes that aggregate metrics hide. These include the inability of standard discovery methods to handle missing values, regardless of whether the missingness mechanism is informative, and a marginal-variance shortcut (varsortability) that we measure and remove by standardization. Code and data: this https URL

AI.tldr: DTCD is a library that generates multivariate time series with ground-truth causal structure, where topology, mechanism, noise, missingness, and intervention are composable components, and it adds paired counterfactual twins for individual treatment effects. A reference benchmark exposes failure modes that aggregate metrics hide.
AI.motivation: Existing causal time-series datasets are either fixed and unmodifiable or script-based generators that fix one combination of mechanism, confounding, and missingness, so controlled experiments varying a single property are not supported, and counterfactual simulators are built per paper or produce only observational data.
AI.method: Independent components for topology, mechanism, noise, observational mask, and intervention policy compose through configuration alone, and paired counterfactual twins are made by caching the stochastic realization in the factual rollout and re-injecting it in the interventional rollout, with standardization used to remove varsortability.
AI.result: A benchmark of eight discovery algorithms on 81 configurations and four treatment-effect estimators on 18 configurations shows that standard discovery methods cannot handle missing values regardless of whether the missingness is informative, and that a marginal-variance shortcut (varsortability) exists and is removed by standardization; the counterfactual twins recover individual treatment effects to numerical precision.
AI.conclusion: Controlled, composable generation with ground truth and counterfactual twins enables systematic causal discovery and treatment-effect evaluation that reveals failures hidden by aggregate metrics.

title: Surrogate Quality Score: A Novel Composite Performance Metric for Model Selection
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables
summary: The growing reliance on high-fidelity, state-of-the-art machine learning based models for engineering decision-making necessitates robust and systematic approaches for model selection. While high predictive accuracy at untrained points is a necessary trait in the final model, other attributes such as model complexity, forecastability, explainability, scalability, and physics-awareness may be equally important or relevant criteria depending on application context and user requirements. In this work, we propose a novel composite performance metric, Surrogate Quality Score (SQS) for model selection based on predictive accuracy and model complexity simultaneously. SQS heuristically integrates these two attributes through a weighted product of normalized measures, yielding a unified score to reflect overall model quality. A user-specified parameter in SQS enables explicit control over the accuracy-complexity trade-off, thereby incorporating human judgement and preference in the model selection process. We extensively discuss and justify the formulation of SQS and demonstrate its utility through an illustrative example. By combining predictive accuracy and model complexity, SQS offers a systematic and objective approach for model selection based on both attributes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Surrogate Quality Score (SQS), a composite model-selection metric that combines predictive accuracy and model complexity as a weighted product of normalized measures, with a user parameter that sets the accuracy-complexity trade-off. It is illustrated with one example.
AI.motivation: Model selection for engineering decisions needs more than untrained-point accuracy, since complexity, forecastability, explainability, scalability, and physics-awareness can also matter depending on context, and a systematic single score balancing accuracy and complexity is lacking.
AI.method: SQS heuristically integrates predictive accuracy and model complexity through a weighted product of normalized measures, and a user-specified parameter gives explicit control over the accuracy-complexity trade-off so that human preference enters the selection.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the formulation is extensively discussed and justified and that its utility is demonstrated through an illustrative example, without reporting quantitative benchmark numbers.
AI.conclusion: SQS offers a systematic and objective way to select surrogate models that weighs both accuracy and complexity, with the trade-off set explicitly by the user.

title: Accuracy Is Not Value: Choosing Weak Supervisors by What the Student Inherits
summary: Weak supervisors are usually judged by their own errors, but what matters is what a student learns from them. For squared loss and any linear learner shared by all supervisors, we show that a supervisor's value is determined by its errors after they pass through the student's learning operator. Consequently, the inner products of the supervisors' raw errors can be compatible with every feasible value of the student's risk, and weighting supervisors by them can be arbitrarily worse than the best weighting in relative excess risk. This student-relative value is not identifiable from unlabeled data, but what is missing is small: one finite-dimensional projection of the target decides whether training on a weak aggregate helps, another decides how to weight the supervisors. Known teacher training rules, or a label-model condition stated in student-relative form, shrink it further. Clean labels close the remaining gap at a cost set by the geometry of the unresolved directions rather than by the dimension of the student's representation, with matching worst-case lower bounds. In Gaussian designs we also quantify when exact teacher structure beats ordinary stacking and when weak supervisors, combined with clean labels, beat every procedure that uses the clean labels alone. The guarantees extend to fitted ridge students and finite unlabeled data.

AI.tldr: For squared loss and linear learners, the paper shows that a weak supervisor's value is set by its errors after passing through the student's learning operator, so raw error inner products can mislead weighting. It characterizes the small unidentifiable part of the student-relative value and the cost of clean labels, with matching lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Weak supervisors are usually judged by their own errors, but what matters is what a student learns from them, and weighting supervisors by raw error inner products can be arbitrarily worse than the best weighting in relative excess risk.
AI.method: The analysis treats squared loss and any linear learner shared by all supervisors, reduces a supervisor's value to its errors after the student's learning operator, identifies one finite-dimensional projection of the target that decides whether training on a weak aggregate helps, and extends the guarantees to fitted ridge students and finite unlabeled data.
AI.result: The student-relative value is not identifiable from unlabeled data, but the missing part is small; known teacher training rules or a student-relative label-model condition shrink it further; clean labels close the remaining gap at a cost set by the geometry of unresolved directions with matching worst-case lower bounds; in Gaussian designs the paper quantifies when exact teacher structure beats ordinary stacking and when weak supervisors plus clean labels beat clean labels alone.
AI.conclusion: Choosing weak supervisors should be guided by what the student inherits rather than by supervisor accuracy, and the remaining unidentifiable gap is small and governed by the geometry of unresolved directions rather than the representation dimension.

title: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model
summary: Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345$\times$ less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

AI.tldr: Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs) learn an energy function over latent states of a looped recurrent model and treat looped updates as gradient descent on that energy, which gives a stopping signal. They match or outperform prior recurrent reasoners and reach 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with 345x less inference compute than the next-best model.
AI.motivation: Looped models scale effective depth for multi-step latent reasoning, but they lack an explicit measure of progress, so it is unclear when to stop looping or how to improve the current state.
AI.method: An energy function over latent reasoning states is learned, looped updates are formulated as gradient descent on this energy so that the gradient guides refinement and signals stopping, and exploration-based training is added to discover further modes and shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states.
AI.result: Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, reaching 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with 345x less inference compute than the next-best model at comparable training compute; on multi-solution benchmarks they achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions with near-100% single-sample accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Energy-based models are presented as a promising basis for strong recurrent reasoning, since an explicit energy supplies both a progress measure and a stopping criterion.

title: Action-Centered Causal Bandits for Budget-Constrained Promotion Targeting
comment: Accepted at the 20th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM 2027)
summary: Web platforms select among costly interventions for each user to maximize incremental outcomes under a global budget. We formulate this problem as a budget-constrained contextual bandit with heterogeneous treatment effects. Although an action-independent outcome baseline cancels from treatment comparisons, modeling a nonlinear baseline can increase statistical complexity. We propose DR-CATE-CBwK, an action-centered causal bandit that directly learns treatment contrasts. Its online update remains valid under baseline-model misspecification without inverse-propensity weighting.
