It combines an offline doubly robust learner to warm-start treatment-effect estimates, an online action-centered estimator for sequential contrast learning, and a primal-dual controller with an affordable-action rule to enforce the effective-cost budget pathwise. For linear conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) in a stationary i.i.d. setting, we prove a high-probability (\widetilde{O}(Kd\sqrt{T})) regret bound, where K is the number of priced actions, d the context dimension, and T the horizon. We benchmark against the fluid linear program (LP) under the coverage-guaranteed action rule. We further show that the action-centered estimating moment remains unbiased under any predictable baseline estimate, whereas a specified separate-arm reward regression can exhibit asymptotic contrast bias under action-dependent logging and shared-baseline misspecification. On a semi-synthetic job-marketplace benchmark with real logged features and simulated outcomes, our practical Thompson-restricted variant achieves the lowest regret among evaluated budget-feasible methods in the operating regime. It reduces regret by approximately 20% versus the strongest reward-based baseline, outperforming raw-reward contextual bandits, BwK baselines, and a static offline policy, while never exceeding the effective-cost budget.

AI.tldr: DR-CATE-CBwK is an action-centered causal bandit for budget-constrained promotion targeting that learns treatment contrasts directly and enforces the effective-cost budget with a primal-dual controller. On a semi-synthetic job-marketplace benchmark, its Thompson-restricted variant cuts regret by about 20% versus the strongest reward-based baseline.
AI.motivation: Platforms must pick costly interventions per user under a global budget, and modeling a nonlinear outcome baseline increases statistical complexity even though the action-independent baseline cancels in treatment comparisons, while separate-arm reward regression can be biased under action-dependent logging and baseline misspecification.
AI.method: The method combines an offline doubly robust learner that warm-starts treatment-effect estimates, an online action-centered estimator for sequential contrast learning that stays valid under baseline misspecification without inverse-propensity weighting, and a primal-dual controller with an affordable-action rule that enforces the budget pathwise.
AI.result: For linear CATEs in a stationary i.i.d. setting the paper proves a high-probability regret bound of order Kd sqrt(T) up to logarithmic factors, where K is the number of priced actions, d the context dimension, and T the horizon; on a semi-synthetic job-marketplace benchmark the Thompson-restricted variant has the lowest regret among evaluated budget-feasible methods and reduces regret by about 20% versus the strongest reward-based baseline, without exceeding the effective-cost budget.
AI.conclusion: Learning action-centered treatment contrasts with a budget-enforcing primal-dual controller gives a regret-guaranteed and budget-feasible approach that outperforms raw-reward bandits, BwK baselines, and a static offline policy in the studied setting.

title: When2What: A Timing-Conditioned Framework for Long-Horizon Forecasting of Continuous Cardiovascular Waveforms
comment: 31 pages (18 pages main text, 13 pages supplementary material), 7 figures, 31 tables. Code available at this https URL
summary: Long-horizon forecasting of quasi-periodic cardiovascular waveforms, such as the electrocardiogram (ECG), arterial blood pressure (ABP), and photoplethysmogram (PPG), requires predicting both when future cardiac events will occur (beat timing) and what the local structural pattern looks like around each event (beat morphology). However, standard sequence forecasters trained with pointwise mean squared error (MSE) average across uncertain future heartbeat phases, flattening sharp R peaks and pulse upstrokes into featureless baselines. Our analysis of intraoperative ECG reveals a clear temporal asymmetry: beat-time predictability from history decays within seconds due to stochastic heart-rate variability, whereas local beat morphology aligned at true beat times remains stable over several minutes. Guided by this insight, we introduce When2What, a timing-conditioned framework comprising three stages: Predict, Commit, and Generate. Given a 120-s history, When2What predicts a dense 60-s timing map, selects and sharpens discrete beat events into unit-height Gaussian impulses, and conditions a neural waveform generator on both these committed events and the observed history. Across intraoperative ECG, When2What substantially outperforms existing time-series and physiological forecasters, achieving a near-term waveform event skill of 0.644 and reproducing 95.62% of its predicted heartbeats in the generated waveform where direct long-horizon forecasters collapse into flat baselines. Furthermore, When2What transfers zero-shot to external hospital and atrial fibrillation cohorts, extends effectively to ABP and PPG pulse waveforms, and is supported by ablations and synthetic analyses that establish explicit timing conditioning as an effective paradigm for quasi-periodic long-horizon waveform forecasting.

AI.tldr: When2What is a three-stage framework (Predict, Commit, Generate) for long-horizon forecasting of quasi-periodic cardiovascular waveforms that first predicts beat timing and then conditions a waveform generator on committed beat events. It reaches a near-term waveform event skill of 0.644 and reproduces 95.62% of predicted heartbeats in generated waveforms.
AI.motivation: Pointwise MSE forecasters average over uncertain heartbeat phases and flatten sharp R peaks and pulse upstrokes, while beat-time predictability decays within seconds from heart-rate variability but local beat morphology stays stable for minutes.
AI.method: Given a 120-s history, When2What predicts a dense 60-s timing map, selects and sharpens discrete beat events into unit-height Gaussian impulses, and conditions a neural waveform generator on these committed events and the observed history.
AI.result: On intraoperative ECG, When2What substantially outperforms existing time-series and physiological forecasters, achieving a near-term waveform event skill of 0.644 and reproducing 95.62% of its predicted heartbeats in the generated waveform where direct long-horizon forecasters collapse to flat baselines; it transfers zero-shot to external hospital and atrial fibrillation cohorts and extends to ABP and PPG pulse waveforms.
AI.conclusion: Explicit timing conditioning is an effective paradigm for long-horizon forecasting of quasi-periodic waveforms, separating when beats occur from what they look like.

title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning Market Making: Lessons from Loss Function Experimentation
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures
summary: Market makers play a vital role in ensuring efficient trade within financial markets. Recent literature has delved into training market-making systems using reinforcement learning. This paper delves into the impact of various loss function formulations on risk management behavior within reinforcement-based market making. Through empirical evaluation, we contrast profit-maximizing strategies with risk-averse approaches, finding that penalties for inventory and cash management foster more resilient and adaptable market-making strategies. Our results underscore the significance of striking a balance between profit maximization and risk management in algorithmic trading, providing actionable insights for refining strategies in practical settings.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically compares how different loss function formulations affect risk management in reinforcement-learning market makers, finding that penalties for inventory and cash management yield more resilient strategies than pure profit maximization. It frames the result as a balance between profit and risk.
AI.motivation: Recent work trains market makers with reinforcement learning, but the effect of the loss function on risk-management behavior has not been well examined, and profit-only objectives may produce fragile strategies.
AI.method: Several loss function formulations for an RL market maker are compared empirically, contrasting profit-maximizing strategies with risk-averse ones that add penalties for inventory and cash management.
AI.result: Penalties for inventory and cash management foster more resilient and adaptable market-making strategies than profit-maximizing formulations, according to the empirical evaluation; the abstract reports no specific numbers or datasets.
AI.conclusion: Loss design for RL market making should balance profit maximization against risk management, and the findings are offered as practical guidance for algorithmic trading.

title: KnowEvo: Knowledge Evolution for Protein Optimization
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in scientific discovery, yet systematically accumulating and refining reusable scientific knowledge remains challenging. Existing approaches primarily improve LLM-based problem solving through parameter optimization or feedback-driven refinement of prompts, programs, and solution trajectories, leaving acquired expertise either embedded in model weights or scattered across iterative problem-solving processes. As a result,knowledge is difficult to systematically inspect, evaluate, and refine. We propose KnowEvo, a framework that treats externalized knowledge itself as the optimization target. Our key insight is that scientific knowledge is inherently modular: multiple interacting mechanisms jointly determine the design outcomes. This makes knowledge evolution fundamentally challenging, as improvements cannot be attributed to individual components in isolation. To address this, KnowEvo represents knowledge as executable expertise blocks and organizes their refinements into strategy mutation trees, enabling structured exploration over a combinatorial knowledge space. The framework combines a Thompson-style forward allocation strategy that adaptively distributes evaluation budgets across strategy variants with a backward revision process, in which a code agent operates in an isolated sandbox to translate rollout evidence into localized program updates. This design enables persistent accumulation, evaluation, and refinement of mechanistic expertise across iterative experimentation. We evaluate KnowEvo on protein optimization tasks including stability and solubility. Results show that knowledge evolution consistently improves over initial strategy blocks and outperforms monolithic program evolution and prior LLM-guided evolution baselines across metrics such as pass@k, MRR, MAP,and NDCG@5. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: KnowEvo treats externalized scientific knowledge as the optimization target, representing it as executable expertise blocks organized into strategy mutation trees refined by Thompson-style budget allocation and code-agent revision. On protein stability and solubility tasks it improves over initial strategy blocks and beats monolithic program evolution and prior LLM-guided evolution baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM-based scientific discovery leaves acquired expertise either in weights or scattered across iterative problem-solving, so knowledge is hard to inspect, evaluate, and refine, and improvements cannot be attributed to individual interacting mechanisms in isolation.
AI.method: Knowledge is stored as executable expertise blocks organized into strategy mutation trees, a Thompson-style forward allocation distributes evaluation budgets across strategy variants, and a backward revision process lets a code agent in an isolated sandbox turn rollout evidence into localized program updates.
AI.result: On protein optimization tasks including stability and solubility, knowledge evolution consistently improves over initial strategy blocks and outperforms monolithic program evolution and prior LLM-guided evolution baselines on pass@k, MRR, MAP, and NDCG@5.
AI.conclusion: Treating modular knowledge as an evolvable, attributable object enables persistent accumulation and refinement of mechanistic expertise across iterative experimentation.

title: Knowledge Distillation from Neural Networks to Differentiable Logic Networks
summary: Differentiable logic networks (DLNs) are interpretable, edge-friendly classifiers that learn both their logic operators and their connections through gradient descent, achieving accuracy competitive with multi-layer perceptrons at orders-of-magnitude lower inference cost. Their accuracy, however, is bounded by the problems of vanishing gradients, scalability, and lack of an ecosystem, leaving a gap relative to conventional neural networks on several datasets. We introduce knowledge distillation for DLNs to narrow this gap. We distill from a trained multi-layer perceptron teacher into a DLN student, integrating the distillation objective into a two-phase training loop without altering the architecture or the inference procedure. The teacher is discarded after training. Hence, the distilled model retains the interpretability, sparsity, and inference cost of a conventionally trained DLN. We investigate this approach through four variants: a joint hyperparameter search that optimizes the distillation weight and temperature alongside the architecture, a grid search over these two hyperparameters with the architecture fixed, and two single-phase variants that employ distillation during only the neuron-function or only the connection phase. On 20 public tabular classification tasks, distillation improves balanced-class accuracy at negligible cost to gate-level operation counts and model size, though the benefit varies by dataset. Performance improvements of up to 15% are observed, in some cases surpassing the teacher itself.

AI.tldr: The paper distills a trained multi-layer perceptron teacher into a differentiable logic network (DLN) student through a two-phase training loop, keeping the DLN architecture and inference unchanged. On 20 tabular classification tasks it improves balanced-class accuracy, with gains up to 15% and sometimes surpassing the teacher.
AI.motivation: DLNs are interpretable and cheap to run but their accuracy is limited by vanishing gradients, scalability, and a lack of ecosystem, leaving a gap to conventional neural networks on several datasets.
AI.method: Knowledge distillation from an MLP teacher is integrated into the two-phase DLN training loop without changing the architecture or inference, the teacher is discarded afterward, and four variants are studied: joint search over distillation weight and temperature with the architecture, a grid search over these two hyperparameters with the architecture fixed, and two single-phase variants applying distillation only in the neuron-function or only in the connection phase.
AI.result: On 20 public tabular classification tasks, distillation improves balanced-class accuracy at negligible cost to gate-level operation counts and model size, with benefits varying by dataset; improvements of up to 15% are observed, in some cases surpassing the teacher.
AI.conclusion: Distillation can narrow the accuracy gap of DLNs while preserving their interpretability, sparsity, and inference cost, though the benefit is dataset dependent.

title: Function-Space Certification for Neural Operators
comment: 45 pages, 6 figures
summary: Certifying the robustness and physical consistency of scientific machine-learning models ensures that their predictions remain reliable beyond the test set. For neural operators, which learn PDE solution operators by mapping infinite-dimensional function spaces, certification means establishing rigorous, domain-wide guarantees for their output functions. However, standard neural network (NN) verification methods are fundamentally designed for vector-to-vector mappings, and they can only certify neural operators at fixed grid resolutions and provide no guarantees over the entire domain or across another resolution. We close this gap by introducing a function-space certification framework that verifies neural operators across the entire continuous domain. We formulate interval bound propagation (IBP) and CROWN in function space, propagating upper and lower bound functions through each layer using rigorous numerical integration. In addition, we extend bound propagation to higher-order derivatives to certify PDE residuals and solution error bounds. Experiments across several neural operator architectures and scientific problems, including the 572.5-million-parameter spherical Fourier neural operator for global weather forecasting, show that our method produces tight, domain-wide guarantees efficiently, providing a foundation for trustworthy operator learning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a function-space certification framework for neural operators that propagates bound functions through interval bound propagation and CROWN over the continuous domain, with higher-order extensions to certify PDE residuals and solution error bounds. It yields domain-wide guarantees that standard grid-based verification cannot provide.
AI.motivation: Standard NN verification handles vector-to-vector maps at fixed grid resolutions and gives no guarantees over the whole domain or across resolutions, which is a gap for neural operators that map function spaces.
AI.method: Interval bound propagation and CROWN are formulated in function space, upper and lower bound functions are propagated through each layer using rigorous numerical integration, and bound propagation is extended to higher-order derivatives to certify PDE residuals and solution error bounds.
AI.result: Experiments across several neural operator architectures and scientific problems, including a 572.5-million-parameter spherical Fourier neural operator for global weather forecasting, show that the method produces tight, domain-wide guarantees efficiently.
AI.conclusion: Function-space certification provides a foundation for trustworthy operator learning by giving rigorous guarantees over the entire continuous domain.

title: When Can You Trust Neural Critics? Auditing Mutual Information Estimates of Higher-Order Epistasis in Protein Language Models
summary: Mutual information (MI) estimation is used to probe what neural representations encode, including in protein language models, but variational MI estimators have variance that scales at least exponentially in the true MI. We audit a prior neural-MI study of order-resolved epistasis in ESM-2 on the four-site GB1 landscape. Run-to-run differences show no systematic bias and a magnitude comparable to ordinary cross-seed retraining variability, and the evaluation-pairing scheme shifts scores substantially. At the original dimensionality, two of three alternative estimator families stabilize the estimate across seeds and one does not. In a synthetic calibration at the representation dimensionalities of two other protein language models (a Gaussian channel with known MI; no model representations), all three families recover materially less signal than required, despite correct signal ordering and stable seeds. A control critic given the true signal direction, which also reduces its input to one dimension, recovers 93.3% and 98.7% of the analytic MI at gain 1.5 (at 5,120 and 4,096 dimensions), so the signal is recoverable with privileged information, but the control does not identify why blind estimation fails. We package the checks into a reusable diagnostic protocol and conclude that even a stabilized estimator is not currently sufficient for order-resolved dependence claims made under blind search at this dimensionality and sample size.

AI.tldr: The paper audits a neural mutual-information estimate of order-resolved epistasis in ESM-2 on the GB1 four-site landscape and finds that stabilized estimators still cannot support order-resolved dependence claims under blind search at this dimensionality and sample size. It packages the checks into a reusable diagnostic protocol.
AI.motivation: Variational MI estimators have variance that scales at least exponentially in the true MI, so claims about what protein language model representations encode based on neural MI estimates need auditing before they can be trusted.
AI.method: The authors re-run a prior neural-MI study across seeds and evaluation pairings, compare three alternative estimator families at the original dimensionality, run a synthetic Gaussian-channel calibration at the representation dimensionalities of two other protein language models, and use a control critic given the true signal direction.
AI.result: Run-to-run differences show no systematic bias and a magnitude comparable to ordinary cross-seed retraining variability, and the pairing scheme shifts scores substantially; at the original dimensionality two of three alternative families stabilize the estimate; in the synthetic calibration all three recover materially less signal than required, while the privileged control critic recovers 93.3% and 98.7% of the analytic MI at 5,120 and 4,096 dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Even a stabilized estimator is not currently sufficient for order-resolved dependence claims under blind estimation at this dimensionality, although the signal is recoverable when privileged information is available.

title: LeanDojo-v2: A Comprehensive Library for AI-Assisted Theorem Proving in Lean
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, accepted to NeurIPS Math-AI workshop
summary: Building on recent progress in machine learning for formal theorem proving in Lean, we introduce LeanDojo-v2: an end-to-end framework that unifies repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted theorem proving in a single software library. In addition, we provide Lean4Code, a lightweight IDE that integrates the various features of LeanDojo-v2 through a simple, mathematician-friendly UI. These tools will enable mathematicians and researchers to easily fine-tune language models on domain-specific Lean codebases and experiment with LLM-assisted theorem proving without a complex setup.

AI.tldr: LeanDojo-v2 is an end-to-end library that unifies repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted theorem proving for Lean, and Lean4Code is a lightweight IDE built on it. The aim is to let mathematicians fine-tune models on domain-specific Lean codebases without complex setup.
AI.motivation: Machine learning for formal theorem proving in Lean has progressed, but using these methods on domain-specific codebases requires complex setup that mathematicians and researchers may not manage.
AI.method: A single software library integrates repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted proving, and a lightweight IDE, Lean4Code, exposes these features through a mathematician-friendly UI.
AI.result: The abstract describes the framework and tools and states their intended use, but reports no quantitative evaluation or benchmark numbers.
AI.conclusion: The toolkit is positioned to make fine-tuning and experimenting with LLM-assisted theorem proving accessible to mathematicians and researchers.

title: StreamTab: Training-Free Temporal Link Prediction with Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Temporal link prediction uses past interactions to predict whether two nodes will interact in the future. Temporal graph neural networks achieve strong results on this task, but they are trained separately for each graph. How a model should use interaction history also depends on the candidates it is compared with. A past interaction can distinguish a recurring link from a random pair that has never interacted, but when the negative candidates have also interacted before, other signals are needed. We propose StreamTab, a training-free framework built on a frozen tabular foundation model pretrained only on synthetic tables. StreamTab describes each candidate pair by statistics of its past interactions and shows the model recent observed interactions and sampled negative pairs as labeled examples, from which the model scores new candidates. Its central design, regime conditioning, samples the negative examples according to how the candidates are sampled, so the examples show the distinction the model must make. As new interactions arrive, StreamTab updates the statistics and refreshes the examples while the model parameters stay fixed. On thirteen datasets against 21 temporal graph baselines, StreamTab achieves the highest average precision on twelve datasets under historical sampling and eleven under inductive sampling, and ranks first or stays within one point of the best on seven datasets under random sampling. With the same features and model, regime conditioning raises average precision over examples with random negatives by a median of 12.6 points under historical sampling.

AI.tldr: StreamTab performs training-free temporal link prediction by describing candidate pairs with statistics of past interactions and feeding a frozen tabular foundation model, pretrained only on synthetic tables, with labeled examples whose negatives are sampled to match the candidate sampling regime. It achieves the highest average precision on most of thirteen datasets against 21 temporal graph baselines.
AI.motivation: Temporal graph neural networks are trained separately per graph, and how interaction history should be used depends on how negative candidates are sampled, since past interactions do not help when negatives have also interacted before.
AI.method: StreamTab builds pair statistics from past interactions and shows the frozen model recent observed interactions and sampled negatives as labeled examples; its regime conditioning samples negatives according to how candidates are sampled, and as new interactions arrive it updates statistics and refreshes examples while the parameters stay fixed.
AI.result: Across thirteen datasets against 21 temporal graph baselines, StreamTab achieves the highest average precision on twelve datasets under historical sampling and eleven under inductive sampling, and ranks first or within one point of the best on seven datasets under random sampling; with the same features and model, regime conditioning raises average precision by a median of 12.6 points over examples with random negatives under historical sampling.
AI.conclusion: A frozen tabular foundation model with regime-matched in-context examples can serve as a competitive training-free temporal link predictor.

title: WearableBridge: Task-Guided Latent Transport for Free-Living Activity Recognition
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code and interactive demo: this https URL
summary: Wrist-worn accelerometers make activity monitoring feasible at scale, but incidental arm motion, device orientation, and shifting context blur the signal that separates activities. Calibration studies supply higher-quality references such as concurrent thigh recordings or supervised laboratory wrist sessions, but they are expensive, cover few participants, and are rarely available at deployment. How can limited reference data improve recognition for participants who wear only a wrist device? We propose WearableBridge, which holds the reference encoder and classifier fixed and learns a task-guided transport map, the bridge, that carries each wrist feature into the region the classifier associates with its activity. Reference features or the classifier's predictions indicate the destination, and a classification loss penalizes wrist features that land in the region of another activity. We instantiate WearableBridge with three bridges: Mapper regresses onto reference features, Distillation matches the classifier's class probabilities, and MeanFlow learns a one-step flow from wrist toward reference features. On 40 held-out free-living PAAWS participants, all three bridges improve macro-F1 in every training run, and the strongest, MeanFlow, raises mean macro-F1 from 35.1% to 56.0% with concurrent thigh references (Thigh2Wrist), and from 54.0% to 63.5% with group-matched laboratory wrist references (Lab2Freeliving). Fitted only on PAAWS, MeanFlow also raises macro-F1 on the CAPTURE-24 cohort from 42.8% to 54.7%. The gains replicate on selfBACK, hold across four reference encoders, and grow with temporal context. A study can therefore collect reference recordings for a calibration subset and improve wrist-only recognition for every other participant, training only a bridge of 0.13 to 2.44 million parameters while the reference encoder and classifier stay unchanged.

AI.tldr: WearableBridge learns a fixed-encoder transport map that carries wrist accelerometer features into the region a reference classifier associates with each activity, improving wrist-only activity recognition using limited reference data. Its MeanFlow variant lifts mean macro-F1 from 35.1% to 56.0% with concurrent thigh references and from 54.0% to 63.5% with laboratory wrist references.
AI.motivation: Wrist accelerometers are easy to deploy but their signals are blurred by incidental arm motion, orientation, and context, while higher-quality references such as thigh recordings or lab sessions are expensive, cover few participants, and are rarely available at deployment.
AI.method: The reference encoder and classifier are held fixed and a bridge learns a task-guided transport map from wrist features to the classifier's destination region, with three instantiations: Mapper regresses onto reference features, Distillation matches the classifier's class probabilities, and MeanFlow learns a one-step flow from wrist toward reference features; a classification loss penalizes wrist features landing in another activity's region.
AI.result: On 40 held-out free-living PAAWS participants all three bridges improve macro-F1 in every training run, with MeanFlow strongest, raising mean macro-F1 from 35.1% to 56.0% with thigh references and from 54.0% to 63.5% with group-matched laboratory references; fitted only on PAAWS, MeanFlow raises CAPTURE-24 macro-F1 from 42.8% to 54.7%; gains replicate on selfBACK, hold across four reference encoders, and grow with temporal context, with bridges of 0.13 to 2.44 million parameters.
AI.conclusion: A calibration subset with reference recordings can improve wrist-only recognition for other participants by training only a small bridge, leaving the reference encoder and classifier unchanged.

title: BrainCoT: A Multi-Task Zero-Shot Brain Signal Foundation Model with Neurometric-Anchored Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
comment: 37 pages. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Brain signals exhibit substantial multi-center heterogeneity, strong inter-subject variability, and highly diverse task settings, which makes it difficult to build models that generalize beyond a single task. While recent brain signal foundation models leverage large-scale pretraining to learn generalizable representations, they often fall short in practice because they still require target-data-specific supervised adaptation, lack multi-task zero-shot capability, and rarely provide verifiable evidence to support their predictions. In this work, we present BrainCoT, a multi-task zero-shot Brain signal foundation model with neurometric-anchored Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. BrainCoT unifies heterogeneous tasks into an instruction-driven framework so that, after pretraining, a single model can be directly applied to multiple tasks in zero-shot settings without additional adaptation. It further introduces neurometric-anchored chain-of-thought grounded in neurometric evidence for verifiable reasoning, and adopts Decision-Consistent Rationale Training to keep process learning aligned with correct predictions. Across extensive evaluations, BrainCoT achieves an average ACC of 67.41% and AUC of 74.33% in zero-shot classification without downstream training data, outperforming the strongest linear-probing baseline trained with 1% labeled downstream data by 3.85% in ACC and 5.97% in AUC.

AI.tldr: BrainCoT is a brain-signal foundation model that unifies heterogeneous tasks in an instruction-driven framework and uses neurometric-anchored chain-of-thought reasoning to support zero-shot prediction with verifiable evidence. It reaches an average ACC of 67.41% and AUC of 74.33% in zero-shot classification without downstream training data.
AI.motivation: Brain-signal foundation models still need target-specific supervised adaptation, lack multi-task zero-shot capability, and seldom give verifiable evidence for their predictions, given multi-center heterogeneity, inter-subject variability, and diverse task settings.
AI.method: Heterogeneous tasks are unified into an instruction-driven framework so that one pretrained model can be applied directly to several tasks, neurometric-anchored chain-of-thought grounded in neurometric evidence provides verifiable reasoning, and Decision-Consistent Rationale Training keeps the reasoning process aligned with correct predictions.
AI.result: In zero-shot classification without downstream training data BrainCoT achieves an average ACC of 67.41% and AUC of 74.33%, outperforming the strongest linear-probing baseline trained with 1% labeled downstream data by 3.85% in ACC and 5.97% in AUC.
AI.conclusion: Instruction-driven pretraining combined with neurometric-anchored reasoning can give a single brain-signal model usable across tasks without adaptation, with evidence attached to its predictions.

title: TUGB: A Two-stage Uncertainty-aware Generative Auto-Bidding Framework
summary: Generative modeling, particularly Decision Transformers, shows promise in auto-bidding strategies. However, it struggles with limited exploration in static offline datasets, vulnerability to dynamic environmental shifts, and a reliance on heuristic return-to-go (RTG) specifications that may yield suboptimal performance on unseen traffic. To address these challenges, we propose the Two-stage Uncertainty-aware Generative Auto-Bidding (TUGB) framework. TUGB integrates generative sequence modeling with Reinforcement Learning (RL). It employs a two-stage pipeline where a pre-trained Generative Bidding Model is fine-tuned via an ensemble-based Uncertainty-aware Environment Model. This approach quantifies epistemic uncertainty to penalize high-risk trajectories and evolves the policy from RTG-conditioning to direct bidding optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TUGB significantly outperforms SOTA baselines. Notably, full-scale deployment on JD Search Ad achieved a 2.32\% increase in cost and 3.57\% in target cost, validating its industrial efficacy, while its successful adaptation to subsequent mechanism upgrades and JD Food Delivery Ad further validates TUGB's superior generalization capability.

AI.tldr: TUGB is a two-stage auto-bidding framework that fine-tunes a pretrained Decision Transformer-style generative bidding model with an ensemble-based uncertainty-aware environment model, moving the policy from return-to-go conditioning to direct bidding optimization. Full deployment on JD Search Ad raised cost by 2.32% and target cost by 3.57%.
AI.motivation: Decision Transformer auto-bidding has limited exploration in static offline data, is vulnerable to dynamic environment shifts, and depends on heuristic return-to-go specifications that may be suboptimal on unseen traffic.
AI.method: A pretrained Generative Bidding Model is fine-tuned via an ensemble-based Uncertainty-aware Environment Model that quantifies epistemic uncertainty to penalize high-risk trajectories, integrating generative sequence modeling with reinforcement learning in two stages.
AI.result: The abstract states that TUGB significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, and that full-scale deployment on JD Search Ad achieved a 2.32% increase in cost and a 3.57% increase in target cost, with successful adaptation to later mechanism upgrades and to JD Food Delivery Ad.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware fine-tuning of a generative bidder is industrially effective and generalizes across ad scenarios and mechanism changes, according to the deployment results.

title: COMBIO: Automated Discovery of a Compact Composite Biomarker from Routine Laboratory Panels
comment: 27 pages including supplementary material; 4 figures
summary: Machine-learning models based on routine laboratory panels can predict outcomes but can be difficult to interpret and operationalize. We present COMBIO, an automated pipeline that distils such a model into a compact closed-form biomarker. The composite is a product of laboratory measurements raised to integer powers from minus two to two. The sign of each exponent indicates whether higher values of the corresponding measurement increase or decrease the composite. Shapley additive explanation values from the gradient-boosted reference model rank five candidate measurements and guide eligible exponent signs. An exhaustive search over small integer exponents selects the formula on an inner validation set, before evaluation on the reserved test set. We evaluated COMBIO across six tasks: three National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey outcomes, liver-disease classification in the Indian Liver Patient Dataset, and Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV in-hospital mortality and sepsis case-finding, with external evaluation in the eICU Collaborative Research Database for the two hospital tasks. Across the six test sets, COMBIO's area under the receiver operating characteristic curve differed by at most 0.03 from logistic regression using the five candidate laboratory measurements. The hospital mortality composite had an area under the curve of 0.698 in the external database. A version restricted to widely available measurements in the source hospital database achieved an area under the curve of 0.786 in a cohort covering 92% of admissions. The multiplicative representation provides compactness rather than additional accuracy, and local validation and recalibration are required before clinical use.

AI.tldr: COMBIO distills a gradient-boosted model over routine laboratory panels into a compact closed-form biomarker, a product of laboratory measurements raised to integer exponents from minus two to two. Its area under the ROC curve differs by at most 0.03 from logistic regression on the same five measurements across six tasks.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning models on routine laboratory panels can predict outcomes but are hard to interpret and operationalize in clinical practice.
AI.method: Shapley additive explanation values from the gradient-boosted reference model rank five candidate measurements and guide the eligible exponent signs, and an exhaustive search over small integer exponents selects the formula on an inner validation set before evaluation on a reserved test set.
AI.result: Across six test sets, including three NHANES outcomes, Indian Liver Patient Dataset liver-disease classification, and MIMIC-IV in-hospital mortality and sepsis case-finding with external evaluation in eICU for the two hospital tasks, the AUC differs by at most 0.03 from logistic regression using the five candidate measurements; the hospital mortality composite reaches an AUC of 0.698 externally, and a version restricted to widely available measurements reaches an AUC of 0.786 in a cohort covering 92% of admissions.
AI.conclusion: The multiplicative form offers compactness rather than extra accuracy, and local validation and recalibration are needed before any clinical use.

title: Deep Learning Theory through the Lens of Statistical Physics: A Topical Review
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Topical review published in Front. Phys. 22(1), 011302 (2027); this version contains minor corrections
summary: The recent success of foundation models and deep learning has far outpaced our theoretical understanding of how large-scale neural networks learn and generalize. Statistical physics provides a natural language for describing such high-dimensional, nonlinear, and strongly coupled systems, offering concepts such as mean-field theory, phase transitions, energy landscapes, and stochastic dynamics. In this topical review, we adopt a statistical-physics way of thinking -- from concepts including phases and criticality, and free-energy viewpoints, to methods such as kernel and Gaussian-process limits, mean-field and dynamical mean-field theories, random-matrix tools, and Fokker-Planck formalisms, and to a mindset emphasizing universality, scaling, and tractable limits with explicit validity regimes. We survey recent progress on understanding modern deep learning through this lens, including mean-field analyses of wide networks, spectral and geometric perspectives on loss landscapes, stochastic-gradient-based training viewed as a dynamical process, and phase-transition analogies that organize phenomena such as overparameterization, generalization, and representation change. Our goal is to synthesize these threads into a coherent framework that clarifies what each approximation explains, when it is expected to hold, and how apparently competing narratives relate or diverge. Together, these perspectives form a unified physical framework that views representation learning as a collective phenomenon in high-dimensional systems, bridging deterministic and stochastic regimes of gradient-based optimization.

AI.tldr: This topical review surveys recent deep learning theory through a statistical-physics lens, organising mean-field, kernel, random-matrix and Fokker-Planck tools into one framework. It clarifies what each approximation explains and when it is expected to hold.
AI.motivation: Foundation models and deep learning have advanced far faster than the theoretical understanding of how large-scale neural networks learn and generalise.
AI.method: The review applies statistical-physics concepts such as phases, criticality, free energy and universality, and methods such as kernel and Gaussian-process limits, mean-field and dynamical mean-field theory, random-matrix tools and Fokker-Planck formalisms. It covers mean-field analyses of wide networks, spectral and geometric views of loss landscapes, and stochastic gradient training viewed as a dynamical process.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; the review synthesises existing threads and clarifies how competing narratives relate or diverge.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that representation learning can be understood as a collective phenomenon in high-dimensional systems, bridging deterministic and stochastic regimes of gradient-based optimisation.

title: Augmentron: Scalable Multi-View Visual Augmentation for Robot Learning
comment: Accepted to the 8th Robot Learning Workshop (WRL), NeurIPS 2026
summary: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive to environmental features that are unrelated to the task. Existing generative augmentation methods can introduce visual diversity, but processing every frame and camera view independently is computationally expensive and may produce inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps. We introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses. This produces temporally and multi-view consistent environ- ment and workspace variations while preserving the robot, task objects, actions, and annotations. Across three physical manipulation tasks, replacing half of the real world training dataset with Augmentron data improves model success across three tasks for both in out-of-distribution distractor objects, and out-of-distribution workspace variation evaluations. In a separate comparison against alternate augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions. The results show that introducing augmented data to a data training recipe can help policies generalize to dynamic real-world settings.

AI.tldr: Augmentron is a geometry-aware pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses, producing multi-view consistent visual augmentations for robot demonstrations. Replacing half of the real training data with its output improves policy success on three physical manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations are sensitive to task-irrelevant features, and existing generative augmentation processes every frame and camera view independently, which is computationally expensive and can produce inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps.
AI.method: Augmentron generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses, varying the environment and workspace while preserving the robot, task objects, actions and annotations.
AI.result: On three physical manipulation tasks, replacing half of the real training dataset with Augmentron data improves success under out-of-distribution distractor objects and out-of-distribution workspace variations. In a separate comparison with alternative augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions.
AI.conclusion: Adding augmented data to a training recipe can help policies generalise to dynamic real-world settings.

title: Beyond the Grid: Continuous Dictionary Pursuit for Interpretable Signal Decomposition
comment: 10 pages main paper, 3 pages references, 22 pages appendix, to be published in NeurIPS 2026
summary: Deep learning models achieve high accuracy in signal processing but remain difficult to interpret. Classical matching pursuit and sparse coding offer better transparency but suffer from spectral leakage and grid mismatch when signal frequencies do not align with discrete dictionary atoms. We introduce Continuous Dictionary Pursuit (CDP), a framework for interpretable signal decomposition that learns the parameters of closed-form functions directly from data. CDP optimizes over a continuous manifold of differentiable atoms and, unlike prior continuous pursuit methods that operate on a single analytic family, searches a heterogeneous library spanning periodic, trend, transient, and discontinuous structures. The algorithm employs a greedy iterative strategy using data-driven priors and gradient-based optimization to isolate individual signal components, with discontinuous waveforms made differentiable through spectral sharpness annealing. To ensure a sparse atom set for reconstruction, the framework utilizes a stopping criterion based on a predefined atom budget and residual error convergence. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show that CDP removes the grid discretization error for atom families contained in its library, recovers generative parameters to within $1\%$ on stationary synthetic signals expressible in that library, and achieves the best sparsity-accuracy trade-off among classical, continuous-pursuit, and neural baselines in the sparse regime. Beyond decomposition, we demonstrate that the extracted atoms can serve as structured curriculum targets for training sequence models, improving forecasting accuracy over standard end-to-end training on most evaluated datasets. The method offers a glass-box alternative for signal decomposition by providing high reconstruction fidelity alongside direct physical interpretability.

AI.tldr: Continuous Dictionary Pursuit (CDP) decomposes signals by learning the parameters of closed-form differentiable atoms from a heterogeneous library, removing grid discretisation error. The extracted atoms also serve as curriculum targets that improve sequence-model forecasting on most evaluated datasets.
AI.motivation: Deep learning signal models are hard to interpret, while classical matching pursuit and sparse coding suffer from spectral leakage and grid mismatch when signal frequencies do not align with discrete dictionary atoms.
AI.method: CDP optimises over a continuous manifold of differentiable atoms spanning periodic, trend, transient and discontinuous structures, using a greedy iterative strategy with data-driven priors and gradient-based optimisation. Discontinuous waveforms are made differentiable through spectral sharpness annealing, and a stopping criterion uses a predefined atom budget and residual error convergence.
AI.result: CDP removes grid discretisation error for atom families in its library and recovers generative parameters to within 1% on stationary synthetic signals expressible in that library. On synthetic and real-world data it achieves the best sparsity-accuracy trade-off among classical, continuous-pursuit and neural baselines in the sparse regime.
AI.conclusion: CDP offers a glass-box alternative for signal decomposition, combining high reconstruction fidelity with direct physical interpretability.

title: TOFS: Feature Selection with Swap Supervision for Semantic Communication over Fading Channels
summary: Task-oriented semantic communication transmits task-relevant features to support receiver inference under limited communication resources and adverse channel conditions. For image classification, the usefulness of a feature depends on the other transmitted features and the distortion introduced by the wireless channel. Effective feature prioritization should therefore account for classification performance after transmission of the selected features. This paper proposes a Task-Oriented Feature Selection (\textit{TOFS}) framework and method, which evaluates feature replacements using receiver classification loss. Loss differences confirmed under independent transmission samples provide pairwise ranking supervision for a selector network. The trained selector predicts priorities in a single forward pass. CIFAR-10 simulations demonstrate improved classification accuracy over an importance-based feature selection baseline at the same transmitted feature count and average transmit power. The proposed \textit{TOFS} framework shows 84\% accuracy performance under Rayleigh fading and Gaussian noise, compared with the 68\% performance of a SOTA method.

AI.tldr: TOFS selects task-relevant features for semantic communication over fading channels by learning from pairwise differences in receiver classification loss, and a trained selector predicts feature priorities in a single forward pass. On CIFAR-10 simulations it reaches 84% accuracy under Rayleigh fading and Gaussian noise, compared with 68% for a state-of-the-art method.
AI.motivation: Under limited communication resources and adverse channel conditions, the usefulness of a transmitted feature depends on the other transmitted features and on channel distortion, so feature prioritisation must account for classification performance after transmission.
AI.method: The Task-Oriented Feature Selection framework evaluates feature replacements using receiver classification loss. Loss differences confirmed under independent transmission samples provide pairwise ranking supervision for a selector network.
AI.result: At the same transmitted feature count and average transmit power, TOFS improves CIFAR-10 classification accuracy over an importance-based feature selection baseline. Under Rayleigh fading and Gaussian noise it shows 84% accuracy, compared with 68% for a state-of-the-art method.
AI.conclusion: Learning feature priorities from receiver-side loss differences is a promising route to robust task-oriented semantic communication over fading channels.

title: RoleWalk: training-free structural embeddings for directed graphs that transfer across graphs
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. Complete technical report (20 pages) as an ancillary file. Code: this https URL (pip install rolewalk)
summary: Structural role embeddings describe a node by its position in a graph - hub, bridge, periphery, member of a dense core - rather than by who its neighbours are. Existing methods either learn coordinates specific to one graph (struc2vec, Role2Vec, RESD) or read scales and normalisations from the whole graph (GraphWave, Digraphwave), so the same neighbourhood can receive different coordinates in two graphs; few read edge directions. We present RoleWalk, a training-free embedding that follows a short lazy random walk from each node and records, at each step, two distributions: that of the transition probabilities, through its characteristic function at a fixed grid of frequencies, and that of the walker's distance to its starting node. On directed graphs, walks that go forward then backward add who shares a node's targets or sources. The embedding depends only on a node's neighbourhood within a fixed radius, so its coordinates mean the same thing in every graph. We show that, without curvature, it is the kernel mean embedding of the walk's footprint, that it separates graphs that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot, and that pruning small probabilities comes with a per-node error certificate. Empirically, RoleWalk is competitive with the best role embeddings on five classification benchmarks at a fraction of their cost, has the highest scores on real directed roles in Wikipedia adminship, exceeds the published accuracy of Digraphwave at every noise level of its own Enron network-alignment benchmark, transfers centrality predictors to graphs four times larger better than existing inductive embeddings, hand-made features and a trained GIN, and embeds a million nodes in 20 s to 3 min on one CPU core. The code is open source (BSD license): this https URL

AI.tldr: RoleWalk is a training-free structural role embedding for directed graphs, built from a short lazy random walk, whose coordinates mean the same thing in every graph. It is competitive with the best role embeddings at a fraction of their cost and embeds a million nodes in 20 s to 3 min on one CPU core.
AI.motivation: Existing role embeddings either learn coordinates specific to one graph or read scales and normalisations from the whole graph, so the same neighbourhood can receive different coordinates in different graphs, and few methods use edge directions.
AI.method: From each node, RoleWalk follows a short lazy random walk and records at each step two distributions: that of the transition probabilities, through its characteristic function on a fixed frequency grid, and that of the walker's distance to its starting node. On directed graphs, walks that go forward and then backward capture which nodes share targets or sources. The embedding depends only on a fixed-radius neighbourhood.
AI.result: RoleWalk is competitive with the best role embeddings on five classification benchmarks and has the highest scores on real directed roles in Wikipedia adminship. It exceeds the published accuracy of Digraphwave at every noise level of Digraphwave's own Enron network-alignment benchmark, and it transfers centrality predictors to graphs four times larger better than existing inductive embeddings, hand-made features and a trained GIN.
AI.conclusion: Without curvature, the embedding is the kernel mean embedding of the walk's footprint, and it separates graphs that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot; pruning small probabilities comes with a per-node error certificate.

title: Provable State Estimation with Recurrent Models
summary: Estimating the state of a dynamical system from observations is a crucial task in robotics and control. Despite their empirical success, recurrent models often lack formal guarantees on convergence and robustness. We bridge this gap by analyzing these architectures from the perspective of nonlinear observer theory. By framing RNNs as a time-discretization of continuous latent dynamical systems (Neural ODEs), we demonstrate that enforcing a contraction condition on the latent flow guarantees the existence of a smooth, injective map of the true physical state into the latent space. We prove that this architecture acts as a tunable observer: by increasing a single scalar gain that scales the latent vector field, the estimation error can be driven to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of zero at an exponentially fast rate. We further establish quantitative bounds on the MLP complexity required to decode this latent state, and extend our formal guarantees to the discrete-time residual RNN implementation. We validate the theory on a real mobile robotic task, where a provably contracting model outperforms a vanilla GRU with substantially more stable training. We also report that unconstrained GRUs converge to contracting dynamics on this task, suggesting that contraction is an emergent property of well-trained sequence models.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that recurrent models written as time discretisations of contracting Neural ODEs act as tunable observers, whose estimation error can be driven to an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of zero at an exponential rate by increasing a single gain. On a real mobile robot task a provably contracting model outperforms a vanilla GRU with more stable training.
AI.motivation: Recurrent models are widely used for state estimation in robotics and control, but they often lack formal guarantees of convergence and robustness.
AI.method: The authors frame RNNs as time discretisations of continuous latent dynamical systems (Neural ODEs) and enforce a contraction condition on the latent flow, which guarantees a smooth injective map of the true physical state into the latent space. They also bound the MLP complexity needed to decode the latent state and extend the guarantees to the discrete-time residual RNN implementation.
AI.result: Increasing a single scalar gain that scales the latent vector field drives the estimation error to an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of zero at an exponentially fast rate. On a real mobile robotic task, the provably contracting model outperforms a vanilla GRU with substantially more stable training, and unconstrained GRUs converge to contracting dynamics on this task.
AI.conclusion: Contraction may be an emergent property of well-trained sequence models, since unconstrained GRUs converge to contracting dynamics in this task.

title: Cross-Layer TopK: Dynamically Allocating Sparsity Across Layers in Transcoders
summary: Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) decompose the activations of large language models into human-interpretable features and trace how these features interact across layers to form circuits, making them a key tool for mechanistic interpretability. However, training CLTs effectively and efficiently is hard. Beyond the usual trade-off between sparsity and reconstruction quality, a CLT has to model all layers at once, which adds a further challenge. The common JumpReLU recipe controls sparsity only indirectly through a penalty, while the direct extension of TopK selects a fixed number of latents in every layer. Yet reconstruction difficulty differs widely across layers, and intermediate layers are much harder than others, so giving every layer the same budget is suboptimal. We propose Cross-Layer TopK, which sets a single L0 budget for the whole model and dynamically allocates it across layers during training. In a comparison with JumpReLU and other TopK variants on Qwen3-8B-Base, this gives lower FVU while using 20% fewer active latents than JumpReLU. The better reconstruction carries over to circuit tracing, yielding more complete circuits with higher replacement and completeness scores. The fixed per-token budget of Cross-Layer TopK also makes it easy to pair with sparse decoding, which cuts both computation and communication and gives a 2.9x speedup per training step. We further show that Cross-Layer TopK follows scaling laws in both latent size and sparsity. We have open-sourced the weights of our CLT at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Cross-Layer TopK sets a single L0 budget for the whole model and dynamically allocates it across layers while training cross-layer transcoders. On Qwen3-8B-Base it gives lower FVU than JumpReLU while using 20% fewer active latents.
AI.motivation: Training cross-layer transcoders requires modelling all layers at once; the JumpReLU recipe controls sparsity only indirectly through a penalty, and the direct TopK extension gives every layer the same budget even though reconstruction difficulty differs widely across layers.
AI.method: The method sets a single L0 budget for the whole model and reallocates it across layers during training. It is compared with JumpReLU and other TopK variants, and its fixed per-token budget pairs easily with sparse decoding.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B-Base it gives lower FVU than JumpReLU with 20% fewer active latents. The better reconstruction carries over to circuit tracing, yielding more complete circuits with higher replacement and completeness scores. Pairing it with sparse decoding gives a 2.9x speedup per training step, and it follows scaling laws in both latent size and sparsity.
AI.conclusion: Cross-Layer TopK is a budget-controlled alternative for training cross-layer transcoders that improves reconstruction and circuit completeness, and its weights are open-sourced.

title: Controllable Molecule Generation via Sparse Representation Editing: An Interpretability-Driven Perspective
summary: Controllable molecule generation is crucial for diverse scientific applications, such as drug discovery and materials design. While large language models (LLMs) show great promise, their dense and entangled representations impede precise control over the generation of molecules with bespoke substructures or properties. To address this, we propose Sparse Representation Editing (SpaRE), an interpretability-driven framework for fine-grained and precise control in LLM-based molecule generation. The crux of SpaRE is to learn an overcomplete sparse feature space that disentangles LLM representations into a compact set of latent features corresponding to chemically meaningful concepts. Within this space, we can directly manipulate these concept-aligned latent features to achieve (1) local control, by generating target atoms and functional groups at specified positions; and (2) global control, by customizing the overall structural and physicochemical properties within defined ranges. In this way, our framework advances interpretability from post-hoc analysis to actionable generative control. Experiments show that SpaRE can generate chemically desirable molecules under complex constraints in real-world scenarios, while offering mechanistic insights for quantitative structure-property analysis. The code and demo are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SpaRE edits LLM representations in a learned overcomplete sparse feature space aligned with chemical concepts, enabling controllable molecule generation. Concept-aligned features allow local control over atoms and functional groups and global control over structural and physicochemical properties.
AI.motivation: LLM-based molecule generation relies on dense and entangled representations, which impede precise control over molecules with bespoke substructures or properties.
AI.method: SpaRE learns an overcomplete sparse feature space that disentangles LLM representations into a compact set of latent features corresponding to chemically meaningful concepts. These features are manipulated for local control, generating target atoms and functional groups at specified positions, and for global control, customising overall structural and physicochemical properties within defined ranges.
AI.result: Experiments show that SpaRE generates chemically desirable molecules under complex constraints in real-world scenarios and offers mechanistic insights for quantitative structure-property analysis.
AI.conclusion: The framework moves interpretability from post-hoc analysis to actionable generative control for applications such as drug discovery and materials design; code and a demo are available.

title: Practical Non-Stationary Graph Gaussian Processes
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Gaussian processes on graphs provide a principled framework for prediction and uncertainty estimation, but modelling heterogeneous networks often requires balancing flexibility against parameter complexity. Variability at a node may reflect useful signal that should propagate through the network, unreliable measurements whose influence should be suppressed, or a mixture of both. We introduce Variance-Coupled Gaussian Processes (VCGPs), which use a positive auxiliary signal to modulate graph interactions through a single learned coupling exponent. The exponent controls how strongly high-variability nodes propagate or attenuate information, while a cluster-wise extension accommodates different regimes within the same graph. Under stated structural assumptions, we characterize the unique stationary-rescaling point of the basic family, where correlations match those of a stationary graph kernel while node-dependent variances remain. Experiments on traffic, air-quality and weather datasets show competitive prediction and uncertainty estimation relative to stationary and per-node non-stationary baselines, with the largest gains on networks requiring multiple coupling regimes. Stationary correlations after variance rescaling remain sufficient on some data, and performance depends on the auxiliary signal and model selection.

AI.tldr: Variance-Coupled Gaussian Processes (VCGPs) use a positive auxiliary signal to modulate graph interactions through a single learned coupling exponent. They give competitive prediction and uncertainty estimation on traffic, air-quality and weather datasets, with the largest gains on networks that need multiple coupling regimes.
AI.motivation: Gaussian processes on heterogeneous networks must balance flexibility against parameter complexity, because node variability may reflect useful signal that should propagate, unreliable measurements whose influence should be suppressed, or a mixture of both.
AI.method: A positive auxiliary signal modulates graph interactions through one learned coupling exponent that controls how strongly high-variability nodes propagate or attenuate information, and a cluster-wise extension accommodates different regimes within one graph. Under stated structural assumptions, the authors characterise the unique stationary-rescaling point of the basic family, where correlations match those of a stationary graph kernel while node-dependent variances remain.
AI.result: Experiments show competitive prediction and uncertainty estimation relative to stationary and per-node non-stationary baselines. Stationary correlations after variance rescaling remain sufficient on some data, and performance depends on the auxiliary signal and on model selection.
AI.conclusion: VCGPs are a useful non-stationary option for heterogeneous graphs, with gains that depend on the network and on the auxiliary signal.

title: Topology as a Design Variable: Joint Architecture-Sizing Optimization for SRAM
comment: Accepted by ASPDAC2027
summary: SRAM's power-performance-area-stability trade-off depends on bitcell topology, a discrete architectural choice that interacts non-separably with continuous transistor sizing. However, no open-source SRAM tool treats topology as an optimizable variable. OpenRAM generates SRAM layouts but performs no optimization, while OpenYield supports high-fidelity evaluation but restricts optimization to scalar sizing of a fixed 6T cell. OpenYieldV2 closes this gap through three integrated contributions. First, a fully parameterized compiler generates complete 6T and 10T SRAM macros with peripheral circuits and replica-bitline self-timing, enabling topology comparison under identical simulation conditions. Second, a few-shot TabPFN surrogate learns topology-dependent PPA responses with limited full-macro SPICE samples. Third, a coarse-to-refined multi-objective optimizer combines global exploration of discrete architectural choices with local refinement of continuous transistor sizes. Experiments across varying design conditions reveal a topology decision boundary that shifts with operating constraints rather than following a fixed design rule. Jointly optimizing across this boundary improves hypervolume by up to 17.3\% over the strongest single-topology baseline. OpenYieldV2 is open-source to support reproducible SRAM design research.

AI.tldr: OpenYieldV2 is an open-source SRAM design framework that treats bitcell topology as an optimisable variable, combining a parameterised 6T and 10T compiler, a few-shot TabPFN surrogate and a coarse-to-refined multi-objective optimiser. Jointly optimising topology and sizing improves hypervolume by up to 17.3% over the strongest single-topology baseline.
AI.motivation: The SRAM power-performance-area-stability trade-off depends on bitcell topology, a discrete choice that interacts non-separably with continuous transistor sizing, yet OpenRAM performs no optimisation and OpenYield restricts optimisation to scalar sizing of a fixed 6T cell.
AI.method: The framework has three contributions: a fully parameterised compiler that generates 6T and 10T macros with peripheral circuits and replica-bitline self-timing, so topologies can be compared under identical simulation conditions; a few-shot TabPFN surrogate that learns topology-dependent PPA responses from limited full-macro SPICE samples; and a coarse-to-refined multi-objective optimiser that combines global exploration of discrete architectural choices with local refinement of continuous transistor sizes.
AI.result: Experiments across varying design conditions reveal a topology decision boundary that shifts with operating constraints rather than following a fixed design rule. Jointly optimising across this boundary improves hypervolume by up to 17.3% over the strongest single-topology baseline.
AI.conclusion: Topology should be treated as a design variable, because the best choice depends on operating constraints; the tool is open-source to support reproducible SRAM design research.

title: Rethinking MoE Load Balancing as Feedback Control
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training is often not stationary: the data mixture changes at curriculum boundaries, when a model is continually pretrained into a new domain, or when the corpus is refreshed. Routing is learned against the current mixture, so each such change disrupts the per-expert load the router had converged to, and existing balancing methods have only been evaluated on stationary data. We rethink load balancing as a feedback control problem, in which the deviation of each expert's load from its fair share is the control error and the per-expert routing bias is the control input, and define a family of controllers, the PID-Balancer, from the proportional, integral, and derivative terms of classical PID control. Two widely used methods belong to this family: the auxiliary balancing loss behaves like a proportional controller, and the loss-free bias update is an integral controller acting on the sign of the error. Reading the router as a static map with a one-step delay, we show that the integral term is the only one that both removes persistent imbalance and averages out the step-to-step fluctuation of the measured load, whereas the proportional and derivative terms pass or amplify that fluctuation into the routing bias. We therefore adopt PID (I), the pure-integral member of the family with a single gain. Two settings are evaluated: (i) training an OLMoE backbone from scratch with 16 to 64 experts per layer, through a mid-run mixture switch, and (ii) continual pretraining of the released OLMoE-1B-7B on a new corpus. PID (I) holds balance before the shift and restores it more tightly afterwards than either the auxiliary loss or loss-free balancing, at comparable perplexity.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts MoE load balancing as PID feedback control and proposes PID (I), a pure-integral controller, which holds balance under mid-run data-mixture shifts more tightly than the auxiliary loss or loss-free balancing, at comparable perplexity.
AI.motivation: MoE routing learned against one data mixture is disrupted when the mixture changes at curriculum boundaries, during continual pretraining into a new domain, or when the corpus is refreshed, and existing balancing methods have only been evaluated on stationary data.
AI.method: Each expert's load deviation from its fair share is treated as the control error and the per-expert routing bias as the control input, which defines a PID-Balancer family. The auxiliary balancing loss acts as a proportional controller and the loss-free bias update as an integral controller on the sign of the error. Treating the router as a static map with a one-step delay, the integral term alone removes persistent imbalance while averaging out step-to-step fluctuation, so PID (I) uses a single gain.
AI.result: In training OLMoE from scratch with 16 to 64 experts per layer through a mid-run mixture switch, and in continual pretraining of OLMoE-1B-7B on a new corpus, PID (I) holds balance before the shift and restores it more tightly afterwards than either the auxiliary loss or loss-free balancing, at comparable perplexity.
AI.conclusion: Integral control is the appropriate member of the PID family for non-stationary MoE training, since it removes persistent imbalance without passing measurement fluctuation into the routing bias.

title: Safety-Focused Reinforcement Learning Using Risk-Sensitive Coupled Control
summary: This paper investigates the coupled control problem within safety-focused reinforcement learning, addressing the essential challenge of achieving optimal performance while ensuring safety in systems operating within complex environments. We define safety as the requirement to prevent the system from reaching undesirable or hazardous states. We propose a coupled control approach that prioritizes safety by employing effective methods to prevent the system from entering unsafe states while optimizing the performance metric, defined as the average cost. We propose a novel problem transformation that reformulates it into a risk-sensitive problem combined with an average reward criterion. We present a two-timescale Q-learning algorithm where in the faster timescale, the algorithm solves a risk-sensitive control problem to ensure safety, while on a slower timescale, the algorithm focuses on average cost control. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of our algorithms, establishing their significance in ensuring safe, optimal control in dynamic environments. We validated the performance of our approach using GridWorld and CarGoal task in Safety Gymnasium.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-timescale Q-learning algorithm that pairs a faster risk-sensitive controller for safety with a slower average-cost controller for performance, and provides convergence guarantees. It is validated on GridWorld and CarGoal tasks in Safety Gymnasium.
AI.motivation: Safety-focused reinforcement learning must achieve optimal performance under an average-cost criterion while preventing the system from reaching undesirable or hazardous states.
AI.method: The authors reformulate the problem into a risk-sensitive problem combined with an average-reward criterion and apply a two-timescale Q-learning algorithm. The faster timescale solves a risk-sensitive control problem to ensure safety, while the slower timescale focuses on average-cost control.
AI.result: The abstract reports convergence guarantees for the algorithms and validation on the GridWorld and CarGoal tasks in Safety Gymnasium; it gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The approach is presented as a way to achieve safe and optimal control in dynamic environments, supported by the convergence analysis.

title: Stable probabilistic emulation of partially observed dynamical systems
summary: Predicting the long-term behavior of partially observed dynamical systems such as the coupled atmosphere-ocean system is central to societal decision-making. Motivated by the success of deep learning emulators in weather forecasting, data-driven climate models represent a promising approach. However, climate emulation poses distinct challenges: models must account for unresolved fast variables introduced by unavoidable coarse-graining, reproduce long-term statistics, and remain stable over arbitrarily long rollouts and under external perturbations. These requirements motivate stochastic data-driven emulators, but modern generative models lack stability guarantees. We introduce forced-dissipative stochastic interpolants, a generative framework for learning stochastic reduced dynamics. Its architecture uses structural constraints inspired by turbulent dynamics, which provide stability by design while retaining the flexibility of stochastic interpolants to represent complex probabilistic dynamics. Building on the theory of Markov-chain stability, we establish a Foster--Lyapunov drift condition and prove geometric ergodicity for our emulator, together with stability under steady external forcing. We evaluate the framework on the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system, a prototype of partially observed multiscale turbulence. The resulting emulator remains stable over long integrations and under finite-amplitude forcing, with accurate prediction of forced responses of both the mean and variance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces forced-dissipative stochastic interpolants, a generative emulator for partially observed dynamics whose architecture gives stability by design, and proves geometric ergodicity for it. On the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system it stays stable over long integrations and under finite-amplitude forcing.
AI.motivation: Climate emulators must account for unresolved fast variables, reproduce long-term statistics and remain stable over arbitrarily long rollouts and under external perturbations, but modern generative models lack stability guarantees.
AI.method: The framework learns stochastic reduced dynamics with structural constraints inspired by turbulent dynamics. Building on the theory of Markov-chain stability, the authors establish a Foster-Lyapunov drift condition for the emulator.
AI.result: The emulator is proved to be geometrically ergodic and stable under steady external forcing. On the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system it remains stable over long integrations and under finite-amplitude forcing, with accurate prediction of forced responses of both the mean and the variance.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a stable and flexible route to probabilistic emulation of partially observed multiscale turbulence, backed by theoretical guarantees.

title: DiffusionRef-IMU: Guide-Anchored Residual Diffusion for Cross-Location Inertial Measurement Unit Translation
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables
summary: Cross-location variation in wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals complicates learning when measurements from a desired target body location are unavailable. This study proposes DiffusionRef-IMU, a two-stage cross-location translation framework in which a deterministic Direct network first estimates the target signal and a guide-anchored residual diffusion model refines only the remaining target discrepancy. The evaluation comprises five subject-disjoint activity-location composition-held-out folds, capacity-matched deterministic and flow-based residual baselines, source-only activity conditioning, computational ablation, and true zero-shot evaluation on two independent datasets.
