By closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction, and counterfactual coaching, our framework provides a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Coachable Health Age, a wearable-derived health-age metric, and SensorWM, an action-conditioned wearable world model, and combines them into an agentic counterfactual coaching system that produces 12-week plans. Expert reviewers preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans based on wearable history alone.
AI.motivation: Retrospective wearable summaries do not give quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions for personalized health coaching. Existing approaches lack a way to forecast how candidate lifestyle changes would affect physiology.
AI.method: CHA is built from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals from consumer wearables. SensorWM is pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of sensor data from about 100,000 participants to forecast responses to lifestyle changes. Both feed an agentic system that synthesizes personalized counterfactual coaching plans.
AI.result: CHA aligns with cardiometabolic constructs and improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex and BMI across WEAR-ME (N=2,780), All of Us (N=22,748) and Fitbit (N=1,464) cohorts. SensorWM forecasts multi-week responses with R^2 of 0.664 and outperforms generic time-series foundation models. In blinded reviews, coaches preferred counterfactual plans for overall quality (71.4%) and anticipated adherence (71.0%), and clinicians judged 99.2% of them safe versus 97.6% for comparison plans.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction and counterfactual coaching offers a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health, according to the authors.

title: Just CaloCHILL: fast hadronic shower generation in a learned latent space
comment: 25 pages, 19 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL, data: this https URL
summary: Calorimeter showers are the most expensive part of detector simulation, and highly granular calorimeters, in which a single hadronic shower leaves thousands of energy deposits, make them more expensive still. We present CaloCHILL (Calorimeter Hits In Learned Latents), a generative model that does not produce these deposits one by one: instead it generates a compact summary of the shower in a learned latent space and expands it to full resolution only at the end. The complete shower, including the arrival time of every hit, is built in three stages: a flow-matching model first sets the number of hits and the earliest hit time in each calorimeter layer, a mean-flow model then generates the latent summary, and the decompressor of a variational autoencoder turns it into the full point cloud, giving every hit its position, energy and time. Sparse attention along the shower axis keeps this compression affordable for showers with thousands of hits. On positive-pion showers in the calorimeter of the International Large Detector, a proposed detector for the FCC-ee, CaloCHILL reproduces the main shower observables, including their time structure. This new model is 600 times faster than its predecessor, while improving on all accuracy metrics considered.

AI.tldr: CaloCHILL is a generative model for hadronic showers that samples a compact latent summary and decodes it into a full point cloud of hits, including hit times. It is 600 times faster than its predecessor while improving accuracy on all metrics considered.
AI.motivation: Calorimeter showers are the most expensive part of detector simulation, and highly granular calorimeters produce thousands of energy deposits per hadronic shower. Generating each deposit individually is too costly.
AI.method: A flow-matching model sets the number of hits and the earliest hit time per layer, a mean-flow model generates a latent summary, and a VAE decompressor expands it to the full point cloud. Sparse attention along the shower axis keeps the compression affordable for showers with thousands of hits.
AI.result: On positive-pion showers in the ILD calorimeter for the FCC-ee, CaloCHILL reproduces the main shower observables, including their time structure. It is 600 times faster than its predecessor and improves on all accuracy metrics considered.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage latent generation approach offers a much faster path to highly granular shower simulation, according to the authors.

title: AutoPYara: Next-Gen YARA Rule Generator for Malware Family Clustering
comment: To Appear In ACSAC 2026
summary: Millions of malware variants threaten users daily, such that clustering these samples is key for fast incident response. AutoYara is the current state-of-the-art for automatic YARA rule generation, but the task remains challenging on realistic datasets, where intra-family diversity and noisy clustering can degrade rule quality. We present AutoPYara, a solution armored with: (1) precise cluster centroid selection based on similarity hashing, and (2) an improved heuristic for estimating subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data. We implement AutoPYara as an open-source Python package (pip install autopyara) to support reproducibility and practical use. We show that AutoPYara, (1) increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points; (2) reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, comparing the average variance AutoPYara exhibits to that of AutoYara; and (3) improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%. AutoPYara produces robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.

AI.tldr: AutoPYara is an open-source Python tool that generates YARA rules for malware family clusters by improving centroid selection and subcluster estimation. It is reported to beat AutoYara on rule coverage, variance and threat-hunting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Clustering the large volume of malware variants is key to fast incident response, but AutoYara, the current state of the art, degrades on realistic datasets with intra-family diversity and noisy clusters.
AI.method: Cluster centroids are chosen using similarity hashing. Subclusters within a family are estimated with an improved heuristic that uses historical VirusTotal data. The method is released as a pip-installable package.
AI.result: Compared with AutoYara, AutoPYara increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points, reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, and improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that AutoPYara yields more robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.

title: Compressed Per-Player Local Methods for Multiplayer Federated Learning: Exact Convergence via Increment Sharing
summary: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates per-player local SGD for multiplayer federated learning so that players share strategy increments rather than strategies, which preserves exact convergence under compression. It extends this to variance-reduced variants with convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: PEARL-SGD does not extend cleanly to compressed communication, because compressing players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium even with deterministic gradients.
AI.method: The authors reformulate PEARL-SGD so players communicate local strategy increments. They propose C-PEARL-SGD, and also PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG for variance reduction. Convergence is established under the original MpFL assumptions through a unified parametric inequality.
AI.result: Without compression the two formulations are equivalent, while with compression increment sharing preserves exact convergence. Experiments on distributed spectrum sensing show practical benefits over vanilla PEARL-SGD.
AI.conclusion: Increment sharing is a principled way to make compressed local methods converge exactly in multiplayer federated learning.

title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
comment: 21 pages, 18 figures, 11 tables
summary: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper enables accurate inference of pretrained models on analog compute-in-memory arrays without retraining, by centering inputs and applying Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays. It restores accuracy to within a few points of floating point for CNNs, ViTs and LLMs up to 14B parameters.
AI.motivation: Converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on analog CIM arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly.
AI.method: Analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. Inputs are centered and Hadamard rotations are applied so shared reference errors are spread and input mixing is confined to each array. Calibration is low-cost and shared.
AI.result: On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, the method restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy. Across CNNs, ViTs and LLMs on PCM and ReRAM it matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights.
AI.conclusion: Retraining-free accurate inference on simple analog CIM arrays appears feasible through representation changes alone, according to the authors.

title: Functional Dependency beyond Similarity: Hierarchical Decomposition of Training Data Attribution in Music Generative Models
comment: 23 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Under review
summary: Copyright analysis focuses on the similarity between two works. However, generative AI models learn from training data through functional relations beyond similarity. Training Data Attribution (TDA) estimates the influence of each training instance on a generated output and may serve as a basis for remuneration. However, prior studies find global influence, where a few training instances rank as the most influential for almost every generation. Used directly, TDA scores would distribute part of every remuneration to these instances regardless of what was generated. To address this, we propose a new approach in which TDA scores are decomposed into three levels of influence, namely global indicating the influence of a training data to a trained model, group for its influence on a group of generated outputs (that could be clustered together), and specific for its influence on a single generated output. Our study finds that, across several music generative models and TDA methods, global- and group-level influence is non-negligible in every case. Based on these observations, we propose the term functional dependency for the relation of training data to a trained model or to its outputs. This notion both encompasses and distinguishes dependencies of different scopes, allowing TDA scores to be interpreted as distinct forms of contribution in legal, economic and ethical discussions on remuneration.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes training data attribution scores for music generative models into global, group and specific levels of influence, and argues for a notion of functional dependency beyond similarity. Global and group influence are found to be non-negligible across models and TDA methods.
AI.motivation: Copyright analysis focuses on similarity, yet generative models depend on training data through functional relations. Raw TDA scores are dominated by a few globally influential instances, so they would distribute remuneration regardless of what was generated.
AI.method: TDA scores are decomposed into three levels: global influence on the trained model, group influence on a cluster of generated outputs, and specific influence on a single output.
AI.result: Across several music generative models and TDA methods, global- and group-level influence is non-negligible in every case.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose functional dependency as the term for these relations, so TDA scores can be read as distinct kinds of contribution in legal, economic and ethical discussions of remuneration.

title: STRIDE: Learning Humanoid Locomotion in Minutes with Acceleration-Based Rewards
summary: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator. This is why we introduce \method{}, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile. To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples. Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.

AI.tldr: STRIDE learns humanoid locomotion in minutes using a reward based on the onboard IMU that follows a commanded acceleration profile rather than base velocity. It learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 in simulation within 14 minutes of samples.
AI.motivation: Locomotion rewards that track base velocity require an external motion capture system or a well-calibrated state estimator, which limits learning directly on a humanoid robot and sim-to-real transfer.
AI.method: The reward asks the robot to follow a commanded acceleration profile, measured by the onboard IMU. The method uses the off-policy XQC algorithm, a high-gain setting for joint position controllers and left-right symmetry augmentation.
AI.result: In simulation STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 within 14 minutes of samples. Without the two components, falls during training are 81% higher and the robot learns only after more than an hour.
AI.conclusion: An IMU-only acceleration reward enables fast humanoid locomotion learning, according to the authors.

title: Extending Grid Foundation Models for Phasor-Domain Dynamic Simulation
summary: Grid Foundation Models (GridFMs) are emerging as a powerful framework for learning and transferring knowledge across power grids and grid analysis tasks. This work extends GridFMs from steady-state analysis to dynamic simulation. We present DynGridFM, which uses component-wise tokenization and a structured latent operator to learn shared dynamic representations across heterogeneous grids and enable transfer to unseen systems. Pretrained on nine grids, DynGridFM is adapted to a held-out 48-machine grid, where fine-tuning on 64 trajectories achieves accuracy comparable to training from scratch on 128. On a single GPU, it achieves 924x to 1232x speedup over numerical simulators on one CPU core.

AI.tldr: DynGridFM extends grid foundation models from steady-state analysis to phasor-domain dynamic simulation, with transfer to unseen grids. It is reported to run 924 to 1232 times faster than numerical simulators on one CPU core.
AI.motivation: Grid foundation models have been developed for steady-state analysis, and the paper asks whether the same knowledge transfer can extend to dynamic simulation.
AI.method: The model uses component-wise tokenization and a structured latent operator to learn shared dynamic representations across heterogeneous grids. It is pretrained on nine grids and adapted to a held-out 48-machine grid.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on 64 trajectories achieves accuracy comparable to training from scratch on 128. On a single GPU it achieves 924x to 1232x speedup over numerical simulators on one CPU core.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained grid foundation models can reduce the data needed for dynamic simulation of unseen systems while greatly accelerating it, according to the authors.

title: Task-Contribution Dynamics of Adam in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Slow-Manifold Analysis and Gradient Modulation
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from imbalanced optimization of competing loss components, particularly when approximating solutions with high-frequency or multiscale features. Although existing balancing strategies have proven effective in alleviating this difficulty, the mechanisms governing the evolution of individual task contributions to Adam's parameter updates remain insufficiently understood. We introduce task-wise indicators to characterize this evolution and identify three distinct training regimes: smooth variation, intermittent spikes, and persistent oscillations. Focusing on the early smooth regime, we combine discrete-time analysis with a continuous-time singular perturbation framework under the full-batch setting and the parameter regime $(1-\beta_2)/(1-\beta_1)\ll1$. A first-order approximation of the locally attracting slow manifold reveals two factors governing the step-to-step redistribution of task contributions: curvature-related alignment disparities and differences in the coordinatewise distributions of preconditioned task gradients. Both factors involve Adam's shared second-moment estimate. Inspired by AdaTask, we propose Gradient-Modulated Adam (GMAdam), which modulates incoming task gradients using task-specific second-moment estimates. Numerical experiments on high-frequency Poisson and wave equations, the Allen-Cahn equation, and two-dimensional lid-driven cavity flow ($Re=100,400$) demonstrate consistent improvements in predictive accuracy over AdaTask at comparable computational cost.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how Adam allocates updates among task losses in PINN training, using a slow-manifold analysis in the early smooth regime, and proposes GMAdam, which modulates task gradients with task-specific second-moment estimates. GMAdam improves accuracy over AdaTask on several PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from imbalanced optimization of competing loss terms, and the mechanisms by which Adam distributes task contributions are insufficiently understood.
AI.method: Task-wise indicators reveal three regimes: smooth variation, intermittent spikes and persistent oscillations. In the smooth regime, discrete-time analysis and a continuous-time singular perturbation framework under full-batch training give a first-order slow-manifold approximation. GMAdam modulates incoming task gradients using task-specific second-moment estimates, inspired by AdaTask.
AI.result: Experiments on high-frequency Poisson and wave equations, the Allen-Cahn equation and 2D lid-driven cavity flow at Re=100 and 400 show consistent accuracy gains over AdaTask at comparable cost.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific second-moment modulation is a practical way to rebalance task contributions in PINN training, according to the authors.

title: Grid-Oriented Probabilistic Load Forecasting for AI Data Centers
summary: Probabilistic load forecasts for AI data centers need to represent both uncertainty under changing workloads and temporal dependence to support grid operations. This paper develops an open, grid-oriented benchmark using measured GPU power from a 448-GPU AI cluster. Forecasts are evaluated through four stages: probabilistic prediction, online uncertainty calibration, temporal scenario generation, and horizon-wide reserve sizing. Following a change in cluster utilization, a quantile LightGBM forecast achieves only 63.4% coverage for a nominal 90% interval, while online regime-conditioned calibration increases coverage to 87.3%. Even with well-calibrated marginal forecasts, independent sampling produces unrealistic ramp distributions and excessive reserve procurement. Reconstructing temporal dependence from historical forecast errors reduces the discrepancy in ramp statistics and lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4-10.6% across three forecasting tasks. These findings show that marginal forecast quality alone is insufficient for operational decisions and motivate joint evaluation of calibration, temporal structure, and decision outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper builds an open grid-oriented benchmark for probabilistic load forecasting of AI data centers from measured GPU power, and shows that calibration and temporal dependence matter for reserve decisions beyond marginal accuracy. Reconstructing temporal dependence from forecast errors lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4 to 10.6 percent.
AI.motivation: Operational use of load forecasts for AI data centers requires uncertainty under changing workloads and temporal dependence, but marginal forecast quality alone does not capture these.
AI.method: The benchmark uses measured GPU power from a 448-GPU AI cluster and evaluates four stages: probabilistic prediction, online uncertainty calibration, temporal scenario generation and horizon-wide reserve sizing. Temporal dependence is reconstructed from historical forecast errors.
AI.result: After a change in cluster utilization, a quantile LightGBM forecast achieves 63.4% coverage for a nominal 90% interval, and online regime-conditioned calibration raises it to 87.3%. Independent sampling yields unrealistic ramp distributions and excessive reserve procurement. Reconstructing temporal dependence reduces the ramp discrepancy and lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4 to 10.6% across three forecasting tasks.
AI.conclusion: Marginal forecast quality alone is insufficient for operational decisions, which motivates joint evaluation of calibration, temporal structure and decision outcomes.

title: Concordance-Optimal Continuous Music Emotion Estimation: Variance Decomposition, Dual-Branch Temporal Fusion, and Conformal Prediction Intervals
comment: 28 pages, 12 figures
summary: Continuous music emotion recognition (MER) estimates how Arousal and Valence evolve within a song, yet the field's standard metric, pooled frame-level correlation, is dominated by between-song differences and cannot distinguish a model that tracks emotional dynamics from one that only ranks songs by their average level. We decompose annotation variance into between- and within-song components and show that mean squared error (MSE) targets the former, while windowed Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC = $r \cdot C_b$) targets the latter by penalising the variance compression MSE induces. A single weight $\lambda$ controls the trade-off: on 1,764 DEAM songs, raising $\lambda$ from 0 to 1 lowers pooled Arousal $r$ from 0.843 to 0.810 while raising mean within-song $r$ from 0.204 to 0.368. Building on this objective, we present MMAS (Multimodal Music Analysis System), an open-source model that predicts Arousal and Valence every 0.5 s from raw audio. It fuses frozen MERT-v1-95M embeddings with ten symbolic features from automatic transcription through a dual-branch temporal convolutional network with cross-modal attention. Because both branches are audio-derived, one model trains jointly on DEAM and PMEmo without domain conditioning. Under song-grouped 5-fold cross-validation (2,531 songs), pooled $r$ reaches 0.801/0.685 (Arousal/Valence) on DEAM and 0.742/0.746 on PMEmo. Against a ridge baseline on identical features, within-song Arousal $r$ roughly triples (0.344 vs. 0.125; $n = 353$ songs, Wilcoxon $p = 1.7 \times 10^{-21}$, $d = 0.56$). Complete transcription failure costs at most 0.04 pooled $r$. Split-conformal intervals attain 93.7% (Arousal) and 90.0% (Valence) marginal coverage at a 95% target, with the shortfall traced to within-song dependence. MMAS is released as a pip-installable package.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes annotation variance in continuous music emotion recognition and uses a windowed concordance objective to target within-song dynamics, releasing the MMAS model with conformal prediction intervals. The within-song Arousal correlation roughly triples relative to a ridge baseline.
AI.motivation: The standard pooled frame-level correlation is dominated by between-song differences and cannot tell a model that tracks emotional dynamics from one that only ranks songs by average level.
AI.method: MSE targets between-song variance, while windowed Lin's concordance correlation coefficient targets within-song variance, with a weight lambda trading them off. MMAS fuses frozen MERT-v1-95M embeddings with ten symbolic features from automatic transcription through a dual-branch temporal convolutional network with cross-modal attention, and trains jointly on DEAM and PMEmo. Split-conformal intervals are used for uncertainty.
AI.result: On 1,764 DEAM songs, raising lambda from 0 to 1 lowers pooled Arousal r from 0.843 to 0.810 and raises mean within-song r from 0.204 to 0.368. Under song-grouped 5-fold cross-validation, pooled r is 0.801/0.685 (Arousal/Valence) on DEAM and 0.742/0.746 on PMEmo. Within-song Arousal r is 0.344 versus 0.125 for ridge. Split-conformal intervals reach 93.7% (Arousal) and 90.0% (Valence) coverage at a 95% target.
AI.conclusion: The concordance-based objective and dual-branch fusion capture within-song emotional dynamics better than pooled metrics suggest, and the released package supports practical use, according to the authors.

title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICC 2027
summary: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.

AI.tldr: VLA handover lets a robot run a small on-board VLA and switch to a large VLA on a server only when the small one is likely to fail, reducing server requests without retraining either model. In LIBERO simulations it raises success over the small model alone while sending 49 to 77% fewer requests than server-only control.
AI.motivation: Large VLAs generalize well but are hard to run in real time on robots, while small VLAs fail more often. Querying a server for every action chunk limits how many robots one server can support.
AI.method: The robot runs a small VLA and hands over to a large VLA on a server based on predicted failure of the small model. Switching is framed as minimizing request cost under a required success probability, and a heuristic framework is used because the exact problem cannot be solved directly.
AI.result: With SmolVLA and pi0.5 on three of four LIBERO suites, handover raises success by 11 to 22 percentage points over the small VLA alone and sends 49 to 77% fewer requests than server-only control. Success is 2 to 4 percentage points lower than server-only control, and completion time grows less with network latency.
AI.conclusion: Failure-prediction-based switching offers a practical trade-off between on-robot and server inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks, according to the authors.

title: Authorization Drift in LLM Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance in Multi-Step Tool Use
summary: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes authorization drift, where LLM agents exceed their authorization while pursuing user goals, and introduces the Authorization Drift Benchmark with 648 samples across seven domains. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks, more capable models show higher drift, yet most tasks admit a clean compliant trajectory.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries without any adversary, and existing evaluation does not measure this across data, tool, scope and time.
AI.method: Each benchmark sample pairs a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis validates tasks against real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Drift points are mapped to legal provisions in four jurisdictions.
AI.result: Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), frontier-capable models show drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection, and data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision. 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions.
AI.conclusion: Greater capability comes with greater drift, and drift is avoidable, so its potential privacy and information-security harms warrant attention, according to the authors.

title: Reconciling European Electricity Data with Diffusion Priors Learned from Observations Alone
summary: The ENTSO-E Transparency Platform publishes generation, load, and cross-border power flows for European bidding zones. The values carry undocumented errors and violate energy conservation, and data reconciliation consists in correcting them to satisfy that balance. In this work, we formulate data reconciliation as Bayesian inference. Classical methods implicitly take a uniform prior, which we replace with a diffusion model estimated from the observations alone by empirical-Bayes expectation-maximization. The resulting posterior is sampled with a guided process whose projection step makes every sample satisfy the balance exactly. On synthetic systems of six to thirty-five bidding zones, built from ENTSO-E resource-adequacy data, the diffusion prior gives the most accurate reconciliation, increasingly so as the system grows. Its credible intervals are calibrated or conservative, and it remains the most accurate under a misspecified noise covariance. Finally, when the generation of entire zones goes unreported, the classical methods fail while the learned prior recovers it from cross-zone structure.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates ENTSO-E electricity data reconciliation as Bayesian inference with a diffusion prior learned from the observations alone, and samples the posterior with a projection step that enforces energy balance exactly. The learned prior is most accurate on synthetic systems and recovers unreported zones from cross-zone structure where classical methods fail.
AI.motivation: ENTSO-E data carries undocumented errors and violates energy conservation. Classical reconciliation implicitly uses a uniform prior, which ignores structure in the data.
AI.method: A diffusion model is estimated from the observations alone by empirical-Bayes expectation-maximization. The posterior is sampled with a guided process whose projection step makes every sample satisfy the balance constraint exactly.
AI.result: On synthetic systems of six to thirty-five bidding zones built from ENTSO-E resource-adequacy data, the diffusion prior gives the most accurate reconciliation, with the advantage growing with system size. Its credible intervals are calibrated or conservative, and it stays most accurate under a misspecified noise covariance. When whole zones are unreported, classical methods fail while the learned prior recovers them.
AI.conclusion: A learned diffusion prior is a stronger basis than uniform-prior methods for reconciling European electricity data, according to the authors.

title: AnomSep: Bridging Optimization-Based Separation and Deep Neural Refinement for Anomaly Detection with Listenable Explanations
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures
summary: We propose AnomSep, which combines optimiza-tion-based separation with deep neural refinement to achieve accurate anomaly detection with listenable explanations. Anomaly detection requires no predefined anomalous categories, and understanding the basis for each detection helps security personnel assess the validity of each detection. End-to-end anomaly detectors can achieve high detection accuracy but output only scalar scores, and existing anomalous sound separation methods provide listenable explanations with limited detection accuracy. AnomSep first obtains preliminary normal-sound and anomalous-sound estimates through optimization-based separation using a dictionary learned from normal sounds in the target environment. Deep neural refinement then improves the preliminary estimates in a pretrained audio latent space. The separated anomalous sound serves as the listenable explanation, and its energy determines the anomaly score. Experiments on synthetic mixtures and real mixtures show improved separation quality over baseline separators. AnomSep achieves detection performance competitive with the end-to-end baseline and provides listenable explanations directly linked to each detection decision.

AI.tldr: AnomSep combines optimization-based sound separation with deep neural refinement so that anomaly detection yields listenable explanations, with the separated anomalous sound also setting the anomaly score. It is competitive with an end-to-end detector on synthetic and real mixtures.
AI.motivation: End-to-end anomaly detectors give only scalar scores, while existing anomalous sound separation methods give listenable explanations but with limited detection accuracy.
AI.method: Preliminary normal and anomalous sound estimates come from optimization-based separation using a dictionary learned from normal sounds in the target environment. Deep neural refinement then improves these estimates in a pretrained audio latent space. The energy of the separated anomalous sound determines the anomaly score.
AI.result: Separation quality improves over baseline separators on synthetic and real mixtures. Detection performance is competitive with the end-to-end baseline.
AI.conclusion: Explanations that are directly linked to each detection decision can be obtained without sacrificing detection performance much, according to the authors.

title: Bridging Spiking and Continuous Dynamics in Spiking Neural Networks: A Muscle-Inspired Model
summary: Transforming the spike trains produced by spiking neural networks (SNNs) into continuous signals through biologically inspired mechanisms remains an open challenge in generative and regression tasks. In biological systems, a similar transformation occurs when muscles integrate neural spikes to produce smooth, coordinated movements. Inspired by this mechanism, we introduce a muscle-response model, a biologically motivated dynamical layer that converts spike trains into continuous representations. Our approach uses second-order dynamics to model the temporal integration of spiking activity. We investigate how the number of spiking neurons and temporal resolution affect the quality of the generated signals in a text-to-speech task, showing that increasing representational capacity has a greater impact than increasing temporal resolution under the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, an analysis of the learned dynamics reveals that, without explicit constraints on the response type, most neurons converge toward non-oscillatory behavior. These results demonstrate the potential of biologically inspired dynamical decoders for bridging spiking neural computation and continuous signal generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a muscle-response layer that converts spiking neural network spike trains into continuous signals using second-order dynamics. In text-to-speech experiments, neuron count matters more than temporal resolution, and learned dynamics mostly converge to non-oscillatory behavior.
AI.motivation: Turning SNN spike trains into continuous signals remains an open challenge for generative and regression tasks, while muscles integrate spikes into smooth movement.
AI.method: A biologically motivated dynamical layer applies second-order dynamics to model temporal integration of spiking activity. The authors vary the number of spiking neurons and the temporal resolution in a text-to-speech task.
AI.result: Increasing representational capacity has a greater effect on signal quality than increasing temporal resolution under the configurations tested. Without constraints on response type, most neurons converge to non-oscillatory behavior.
AI.conclusion: Biologically inspired dynamical decoders may bridge spiking computation and continuous signal generation, according to the authors.

title: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction on Tabular Data
summary: Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data. Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus, withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, and same-family surrogate assumptions studied here. Our results concern default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers. They do not establish the same conclusion for other explainers, target classes, or data-free attackers.

AI.tldr: Cutpurse separates explanation-guided model extraction into attribution and coordinate channels and finds that Lime bin edges are reproducible from attacker-side data. It combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search, improving fidelity by 16.3 points over a service that withholds bin edges.
AI.motivation: Explanation APIs are often viewed as increasing extraction risk, but it was unclear whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or only supplies convenient query coordinates.
AI.method: Explanations are split into an attribution channel, which ranks features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values. The authors test whether useful bin edges are privileged or reproducible from the adversary's own data across six datasets and five target families. Cutpurse uses a self-computed grid, diverse query generation and boundary search.
AI.result: Attribution rankings give no systematic extraction advantage. Lime bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 points on continuous features, but they are quantiles of the explainer's background data. An attacker-side grid reproduces these gains without querying an explanation API. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 points on continuous-feature targets and exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 points.
AI.conclusion: Withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the assumptions studied, and the conclusions cover only default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers, according to the authors.

title: Graph representations of dislocation networks
comment: 28 pages, 15 figures
summary: The mechanical response of a crystal is governed by the evolving network of dislocations it contains, yet quantitatively linking the `state of that network' to its yield stress remains challenging. Here we represent the dislocation networks obtained from discrete dislocation dynamic simulation as graphs, using five distinct graph representations, characterize each network through a compact set of topological properties, and predict the yield stress from these graph properties and the applied strain rate using a standard random forest model evaluated with strain rate stratified cross-validation. The model predicts the yield stress with $R^2\approx0.86-0.90$ across all box sizes and $R^2\approx0.91-0.94$ for larger box sizes, and this accuracy is consistent across all five representations, indicating that the topology-stress relationship is a robust feature of the graph properties rather than an artefact of any single graph representation. We propose graph topology as a compact and robust route for connecting the microstructural state of a dislocation network to its mechanical response in addition to established variables.

AI.tldr: The paper represents discrete dislocation dynamics networks as graphs and shows that compact topological graph properties predict yield stress with a random forest, with R^2 about 0.86 to 0.90 across box sizes. The accuracy is consistent across five graph representations.
AI.motivation: The mechanical response of a crystal depends on its evolving dislocation network, but quantitatively linking the network state to yield stress has remained difficult.
AI.method: Dislocation networks from discrete dislocation dynamics simulations are represented as graphs using five representations, and each network is characterized by a compact set of topological properties. A standard random forest predicts yield stress from these properties and the applied strain rate, evaluated with strain-rate stratified cross-validation.
AI.result: The model predicts yield stress with R^2 of about 0.86 to 0.90 across all box sizes and about 0.91 to 0.94 for larger box sizes. Accuracy is consistent across all five representations.
AI.conclusion: Graph topology is proposed as a compact and robust route for connecting the microstructural state of a dislocation network to its mechanical response, alongside established variables.

title: Optimal Regret for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade
summary: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that learning both sides of a bilateral trade market is no harder in regret than learning one side, with an algorithm achieving regret of order T^(2/3) against the best fixed pair of prices. This matches the classical one-dimensional dynamic pricing rate up to logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: An intermediary profiting from trade must learn both what a seller accepts and what a buyer pays, and the question is whether the two-dimensional problem is harder than the one-dimensional one.
AI.method: An intermediary posts a purchase price to the seller and a sale price to the buyer, observing only whether trade occurs. Valuations come from an unknown joint distribution, and profit is the price difference when trade happens.
AI.result: The authors design an algorithm with regret of order T^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors, against the best fixed pair of prices, matching the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing.
AI.conclusion: The one-dimensional regret rate survives the move to two dimensions, which raises the question of whether the absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions, according to the authors.

title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
summary: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.

AI.tldr: TurtLES is a 14 TB benchmark of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes from implicit large-eddy simulations, designed to test ML surrogates on realistic time-dependent turbulence. Benchmarking neural operators on it reveals temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and difficulty learning on large irregular domains.
AI.motivation: ML surrogates for CFD are increasingly used, but progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks with realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. Existing datasets lack physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade, dense irregular meshes and long-horizon temporal dynamics.
AI.method: The dataset has 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed by high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulation. It spans variations in geometry, Reynolds number and angle of attack, and state-of-the-art neural operators are benchmarked on autoregressive rollouts.
AI.result: Neural operators show key failure modes on autoregressive rollouts: temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. The dataset is 14 TB and uses industrially relevant mesh resolution.
AI.conclusion: TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes, and the identified failure modes point to open problems for neural PDE surrogates.

title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
comment: 40 pages, 15 figures, 9 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.

AI.tldr: Running the networks of five AI weather models in fp16 while keeping the physical state in fp32 is nearly lossless and gives a 1.3-3.5x speedup on a single 16 GB GPU. bf16 is less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.
AI.motivation: AI weather prediction models are released and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. Rules of thumb for reduced precision from other applications may not transfer to these models.
AI.method: Five public models (Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet) are run on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with the networks in fp16. The physical state, its normalisation and denormalisation stay in fp32, forecasts are verified against ERA5, and sensitivity experiments probe which layers matter.
AI.result: With the state in fp32, the fp16 network changes global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, which is under one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. No systematic pattern appears by region, scale or storm type, except a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet. A 10-day fp16 forecast is 1.3-3.5x faster and uses 1.4-3.7x less energy. No value overflowed fp16's range (+/-65,504), and the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it.
AI.conclusion: For running AI weather models on one GPU, fp16 with an fp32 state is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. Sensitivity to reduced precision differs by model, so rules of thumb carry over only partly.

title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
summary: We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets. In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size. The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.

AI.tldr: The paper gives coreset constructions for capacitated k-median and k-means, where cluster-size constraints are added to the usual objectives. For finite metric spaces the coresets are of optimal size, matching the best-known unconstrained bounds, and Euclidean bounds are improved.
AI.motivation: Coresets are a central tool for scaling clustering, but the coreset complexity of capacitated clustering, which adds cluster-size constraints to choosing centers, is less well understood.
AI.method: The main technical ingredient is concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems. These bounds allow simpler and tighter analyses of the sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.
AI.result: For finite metric spaces the coresets are of optimal size and match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. In Euclidean space the paper gives improved bounds, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence on k that are independent of the dimension and input size.
AI.conclusion: Capacitated clustering admits coresets as small as unconstrained clustering on finite metric spaces, and the dual concentration technique yields simpler and tighter analyses of coreset sampling.

title: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures
summary: Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.

AI.tldr: ReplayAudit audits outsourced LLM fine-tuning by sealing training records before challenges and replaying sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints, with sampling guided by loss changes and parameter-update norms. On real LoRA training it rejects false reports and skipped updates, and cuts median audit time relative to uniform sampling in the tested settings.
AI.motivation: Auditing an untrusted provider's fine-tuning requires controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, and checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps.
AI.method: Training records are sealed before challenges, and sampled intervals are independently replayed from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling, and replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. Sampling probabilities are related to replay work, and budgets are calibrated offline.
AI.result: On a 7B BF16 prototype, a false update-norm report is rejected during a random audit, and targeted checks reject false loss reports and skipped updates. The calibrated budgets give at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. On the same honest 1.5B trajectory with two learning-rate deviation settings, median complete-audit wall time falls by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the audit costs 38% more.
AI.conclusion: Deviation capture and actual replay jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing, so the benefit of guided sampling depends on whether the anomaly signals actually catch the deviation.

title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
summary: We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds. For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt \Sigma)$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_B})$, where $\Sigma_S$ and $\Sigma_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations. We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

AI.tldr: A unified potential method gives order-tight algorithms for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback. The Bayesian bounds are trace-square-root quantities, and the worst-case regret is O(sqrt d) for both problems.
AI.motivation: The previous worst-case guarantees were O(d log d) for contextual search and O(d 6^d) for bilateral trade, and a unified potential-based analysis was needed to tighten them.
AI.method: A Bayesian model draws the unknown target, or the pair of valuations, from a known prior, and the decision maker predicts from the posterior after conditioning on past one-bit feedback. A trace-square-root potential is used, and a dual of it is adapted to the classical adversarial setting where targets and valuations lie in the unit Euclidean ball.
AI.result: The Bayesian algorithm for contextual search has total loss O(Tr sqrt Sigma), where Sigma is the target's prior covariance, and the bilateral trade regret is O(Tr sqrt Sigma_S + Tr sqrt Sigma_B). In the worst case both problems get tight O(sqrt d) regret, matching existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improving on the earlier guarantees.
AI.conclusion: One potential function yields order-tight algorithms for both problems, closing the gap to known lower bounds up to constant factors in the worst case.

title: NAVE: A Normalized, Adaptive Conformer for Antarctic Whale Vocalization Detection
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) 2026 Workshop. Code: this https URL
summary: Antarctic whale vocalization detection requires temporally localizing call boundaries in long underwater recordings and classifying them into predefined call types. Training reliable machine learning models for this task is difficult due to the variability and sparsity of whale calls in passive acoustic monitoring datasets. These difficulties are further amplified by time-varying noise that can mask whale calls and by site-specific ambient sound characteristics to which a trained model may not generalize. In this work, we present NAVE, a Conformer-based detector that improves whale-call detection via three components. First, its input representation combines per-bin complex mean subtraction, which suppresses constant site-specific ambient sound characteristics, with an additional per-channel energy normalization (PCEN) channel that adapts to temporal variations in the noise floor. Second, a frequency-dynamic stem processes these noise-aware representations with convolutions that adapt across the characteristic frequency bands of the target call types. Third, we use a Conformer backbone with a convolution kernel matched to the duration of the target calls that adds an inductive bias and improves temporal localization. We evaluate NAVE on BioDCASE 2026 Task 2 using leave-one-site-out cross-validation across the validation sites, which approximates deployment on unseen recording sites. A single NAVE model with a tuned per-class threshold exceeds the stronger WhaleVAD-BPN baseline, using no boundary-proposal network and no search over post-processing parameters. A controlled ablation study shows that the normalized front-end and a duration-matched convolutional kernel each contribute substantially to recovering the D downsweep, the hardest class for previous detectors, with the wide kernel giving the largest aggregate gain.

AI.tldr: NAVE is a Conformer-based detector for Antarctic whale calls that combines a normalized front-end, a frequency-dynamic stem and a duration-matched convolution kernel. On BioDCASE 2026 Task 2 it beats the stronger WhaleVAD-BPN baseline without a boundary-proposal network or post-processing parameter search.
AI.motivation: Whale calls are variable and sparse in passive acoustic recordings, and time-varying noise and site-specific ambient sound can mask calls and stop trained models from generalising to unseen recording sites.
AI.method: The input combines per-bin complex mean subtraction, which suppresses constant site-specific ambient sound, with a per-channel energy normalization (PCEN) channel that adapts to the noise floor. A frequency-dynamic stem applies convolutions adapted to the frequency bands of the target call types, and a Conformer backbone uses a convolution kernel matched to the duration of the calls. Evaluation uses leave-one-site-out cross-validation.
AI.result: A single NAVE model with a tuned per-class threshold exceeds WhaleVAD-BPN on BioDCASE 2026 Task 2. An ablation shows the normalized front-end and the duration-matched kernel each contribute substantially to recovering the D downsweep, the hardest class for previous detectors, and the wide kernel gives the largest aggregate gain.
AI.conclusion: Normalized input representation and a duration-matched convolution kernel both help detect whale calls, especially the hardest call type, and the leave-one-site-out design targets deployment on unseen sites.

title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures
summary: Mutation testing for deep learning (DL) faces a cost-realism trade-off. The pre-training approach produces realistic but computationally expensive mutants, whereas existing post-training operators modify trained models efficiently but produce mutants that less closely resemble real faults. This study asks whether the trade-off is necessary: can the weight-space effect of a fault-informed pre-training mutation operator be predicted from a trained model, without retraining it? We answer this question with TensorMutation, which represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) to predict parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline and reused across unseen models so that TensorMutation can generate executable mutants without retraining. We construct a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, including 25 newly curated subjects. TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects, TensorMutation achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches. The improvement over the post-training tool DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), whereas the differences from the pre-training tool DeepCrime and the norm-matched random control are not significant. These results show that fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models.

AI.tldr: TensorMutation predicts the weight-space effect of fault-informed pre-training mutations from a trained model, using a mutation-conditioned graph neural network on the model's neural graph, so realistic mutants can be generated without retraining. On 12 real-fault subjects it achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches.
AI.motivation: Mutation testing for deep learning faces a cost-realism trade-off. Pre-training mutants are realistic but computationally expensive, while existing post-training operators are efficient but less like real faults.
AI.method: A trained model is represented as a neural graph, and a mutation-conditioned GNN predicts the parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline on 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 MLP classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, and it is reused across unseen models. Direct weight-space supervision is used in training.
AI.result: TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects it has the highest median behavioral similarity. The improvement over DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), while the differences from DeepCrime and a norm-matched random control are not significant.
AI.conclusion: Fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models, which suggests a route to realistic mutants without the cost of retraining.

title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning
comment: 9 pages
summary: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning agent controls a 6-DoF manipulator carrying a camera to locate and frame hydrofoil wakes for particle image velocimetry. Trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation, the policy transfers zero-shot to a real water tunnel and resolves wakes at higher resolution than a fixed camera, in roughly half the time of a full scan.
AI.motivation: PIV reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure is resolved in the images, but the camera position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement.
AI.method: Camera placement is cast as a sequential decision problem. The agent commands the camera pose and observes only the velocity field and its uncertainty, estimated from time-separated image pairs. Training uses a photorealistic simulation of the water tunnel, with wakes from CFD simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack.
AI.result: After zero-shot transfer, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view, with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.
AI.conclusion: Learned camera placement can make PIV acquisition adaptive, and a policy trained only in simulation can transfer zero-shot to a real experimental facility.

title: Machine learning for lattice QCD
comment: 47 pages, 5 figures
summary: Machine learning (ML) methods have been explored as a means of optimizing lattice field theory calculations, with increasing interest in recent years. This chapter gives an introduction and summary to the use of ML methods to optimize lattice field theory without introducing any uncontrolled approximations. We focus on those directions which are clearly established as of late 2025, marking the 50th anniversary of the beginning of the study of lattice gauge theory. This chapter is a contribution to the online book ``Lattice QCD at 50 years,'' (LQCD@50), edited by Tanmoy Bhattacharya, Maarten Golterman, Rajan Gupta, Laurent Lellouch, and Steve Sharpe.
